text_original: Entrevista do Administrador Hlder... Entrevista do Administrador Hlder Rosalino ao ECO: BdP tem uma atitude de abertura em relao s Fintech 05 nov. 2017 O Banco de Portugal ps as Fintech no plano estratgico para 2017-2020 e tem uma atitude de abertura, afirma o administrador. Em 2018, vai criar uma porta nica de 'entrada' das Fintech. O Banco de Portugal ps as Fintech -as startup financeiras de base tecnolgica -no programa de atividades 2017-2020.  uma das prioridades, agora que est ultrapassada a pior fase do sistema financeiro, as resolues bancrias e a sua estabilizao. Na semana do Web Summit, Hlder Rosalino, administrador do banco central com o pelouro das Fintech, explica em entrevista o que est em causa e quais so os objetivos. Um deles, para 2018, passa por criar uma porta de entrada nica das Fintech no contacto com o Banco de Portugal, "para compreender os players e para lhes poder prestar servios mais alinhados". Qual  o ponto de partida para as empresas financeiras de base tecnolgica na perspetiva dos reguladores? Em primeiro lugar,  preciso fazer o enquadramento ao nvel europeu. Este tema das Fintech e do digital banking est na agenda, quer da Comisso Europeia, que tem feito questionrios sobre o tema e estudos, est na agenda da EBA, est menos, mas est na agenda do BCE. Mas o que se tem sentido, e eu tive a oportunidade h um ms de ter reunies em Bruxelas sobre isso,  a ideia do "wait and see". Ou seja Estamos a ver uma dinmica das Fintech, mas so startups e ainda no tm uma dimenso muito relevante, ainda no estamos perante um risco para a estabilidade financeira, um problema em matria de proteo dos consumidores. Portanto, h um entendimento {europeu] de que no  desejvel uma interveno prematura porque pode prejudicar a inovao e os novos 'entrantes', vital para o setor financeiro, e a Europa est atrasada em relao aos EUA. Por outro lado, as autoridades europeias reconhecem que no podem ficar indiferentes em relao aos movimentos que esto a acontecer e que prometem uma disrupo de tal ordem que no podem pr-se na posio de que este  um tema que lhes passa ao lado. O que est a ser feito em termos europeus? Foram criados grupos de trabalho, quer na Autoridade Bancria Europeia (EBA), quer no Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM ou MUS na verso portuguesa), a Comisso Europeia est a analisar os resultados de um questionrio europeu que teve 226 respostas, mas a abordagem  ainda relativamente 'soft', porque [estas entidades] no querem precipitarse em criar mecanismos e regulamentos limitadores da inovao no setor financeiro. Os bancos comeam tambm a mostrar incmodo perante a entrada de novos players sem haver um quadro regulamentar europeu Nervosismo. os bancos esto a ficar preocupados, mas os bancos vo passar por vrias fases, em primeiro lugar a fase da indiferena, depois a fase da irritao e, finalmente, vo passar para outra fase, em que percebem eles prprios que as Fintech vieram para ficar e tm de as entender como entidades que podem complementar a sua atividade e tambm sero seus concorrentes. E em Portugal, o que est a ser feito? Ainda antes disso,  importante assinalar uma interveno legislativa europeia que vai ser relevante para as Fintech,  a transposio da diretiva europeia PSD2, a diretiva dos servios de pagamentos revista, que dever entrar em vigor no dia 13 de janeiro de 2018. Porqu? A rea principal de atuao das Fintech  a rea dos pagamentos, ou seja, as Fintech cobrem muitas reas, mas cerca de 50% esto na rea dos pagamentos. Depois, h outras como o crowdfunding, o peer-to-peer lending, o machine learning, mas sobretudo os pagamentos, porque  aqui que est a receita. E, reconhecendo isso, a diretiva revista dos pagamentos vem adaptar-se a nova realidade e traz oportunidades significativas para as Fintech. Em que sentido? A diretiva revista vem enquadrar dois novos servios: os servios de informao sobre contas e os servios de iniciao de pagamentos . O que so estes servios? Sobretudo no primeiro caso, permitem que uma terceira entidade, um prestador de servios que no  um banco, possa intermediar a relao com uma instituio financeira, acedendo   s contas, obtendo informaes sobre as contas dos clientes. Estes servios so altamente inovadores e esta diretiva vem permitir que uma Fintech disponibilize uma soluo tecnolgica que ajude um cliente a gerir a relao com um banco, que consolide as contas e a situao financeira de um cliente, a gesto do oramento, os pagamentos... Pode criar um conjunto de servios de valor acrescentado, prestado por uma terceira entidade, para particulares e at para empresas. E no caso dos servios de iniciao de pagamentos, o que est em causa? Um cliente, quando se dirige a uma loja, a um qualquer prestador de servios como a Fnac ou a Worten, d autorizao para que possa, ele prprio, iniciar o respetivo pagamento. Pode autorizar que aquele prestador de servios faa pagamentos por si, entrando na conta, sem necessidade de marcar um cdigo ou de fazer um pagamento por multibanco. Ou seja, "pode iniciar pagamentos em nome do utilizador de forma cmoda e clere sem que este tenha de sair do site do comerciante ao qual est a adquirir um produto ou servio". E ns [Banco de Portugal], no PayChallenge -uma conferncia que decorre esta segunda-feira  tarde em Lisboa -lanmos um desafio s startups para desenvolverem prottipos de servios nestas duas reas. Como  que esta diretiva vai ser transposta para Portugal, em que condies? O Banco de Portugal, a pedido do Ministrio das Finanas, entregou no final de outubro uma proposta de transposio da diretiva europeia, depois de uma consulta pblica e de uma discusso com os bancos. E tivemos, creio que a possa classificar assim, uma atitude de abertura em relao s Fintech. As opes nos diversos domnios colocavam-se entre uma atitude mais protecionista e menos protecionista. Em vrias dimenses, tivemos uma avaliao que favorece a inovao, favorece a concorrncia e um ambiente de flexibilidade e competitividade no nosso sistema de pagamentos, que  a rea tratada neste diretiva. Em cada pas, a realidade das Fintech pode ser vista em nveis diferentes... Ns temos seguido este tema ao longo dos ltimos anos, mas temos de dizer... que no foi uma prioridade? Exato, no tem sido uma prioridade, porque o pas e o Banco de Portugal enfrentaram desafios em relao ao sistema financeiro muito complicados e, portanto, todos os esforos eram poucos para nos concentrarmos nesses temas. Mas no deixamos de seguir o assunto, participamos em grupos de trabalho internacionais, fizemos um estudo em 2014 e 2015 sobre as criptomoedas e publicamos alguns avisos... O Banco de Portugal seguiu este tema, mas no o colocou no topo da agenda, at agora. As Fintech e a banca digital fazem parte central do plano estratgico do Banco de Portugal 2017-2020, temos de seguir este tema, temos de ter uma estratgia e temos que estar prximo do setor. So as trs dimenses fundamentais e por isso foi criado um grupo de trabalho que produziu um relatrio apresentado em abril, uma anlise muito completa sobre as Fintech e a banca digital e o caminho a seguir. Essa anlise passa por perceber as dimenses de impacto das Fintech para as responsabilidades do Banco de Portugal e passa tambm pela nossa prpria organizao em relao ao tema. Isso quer dizer o qu? Parece simples, mas  complexo. O Banco de Portugal tem mltiplos departamentos a acompanhar o setor bancrio e o tema das Fintech impacta com a estabilidade financeira, com a superviso prudencial e os modelos de negcio dos bancos, com a superviso comportamental, at da conduo da prpria poltica monetria, o tpico, alis, que mais preocupa os bancos centrais apesar de ser o mais longnquo. Mas tambm com as questes sancionatrias, porque, no limite, estas Fintech podem facilitar o branqueamento de capitais e o financiamento do terrorismo. Por exemplo, uma das principais preocupaes que as critptomoedas trazem  a possibilidade de se fazerem pagamentos fora do circuito financeiro. Andamos a reforar cada vez mais as regras de preveno do branqueamento de capitais, as pessoas politicamente expostas, um rendilhado quase kafkiano para os bancos que tm de fazer um esforo enorme de preparao das suas estruturas de compliance para responder s exigncias cada vez maiores. Mas, o que  que o Banco de Portugal j fez? Foi criado um grupo de trabalho permanente debaixo de uma estrutura que j existe, a Comisso Especializada para o Sistema e Estabilidade Financeiro, que tem representantes dos vrios departamentos do Banco de Portugal e que eu prprio coordeno. Estamos a fazer agora debates internos e reflexes internas sobre o impacto das Fintech. Em simultneo, estamos a abordar os interlocutores... Est a falar com as Fintech? Sim, uma das grandes iniciativas que vamos fazer  a conferncia Pay Challenge, em parceria com a Cionet, para o qual convidamos as Fintech a participarem. Identificamos um conjunto de interlocutores chave, j tivemos uma reunio com o CEO da Easypay, Sebastio Lancastre, j h um conjunto de outras reunies agendadas, queremos perceber o sentimento em relao ao banco e a primeira interao foi muito esclarecedora... A avaliao das Fintech  a de que o Banco de Portugal no olha para este tema. Sim, mas ficam surpreendidos com a nova dinmica do Banco de Portugal e a aproximao a este setor, a promoo de eventos. Esto a perceber que o Banco de Portugal est a olhar para as Fintech, queremos fazer os Fintech Meetings no prximo ano. Tambm j estivemos em reunio com a secretria de Estado da Indstria, Ana Lehmann, e queremos desenvolver iniciativas conjuntas. No fundo,  aquilo que esto a fazer alguns bancos centrais que tm mais iniciativa nesta rea. Qual  a banco central de referncia? O Banco Central da Holanda  o que est  frente, criou um 'Inovation Hub', uma 'sandbox' que, basicamente, o que faz  levar estas Fintech para dentro do banco central e apoi-los na abordagem  inovao tendo em conta os requisitos que existem. Neste trabalho que desenvolvemos, identificamos tambm o Banco de Inglaterra, criou um Fintech Accelerator, mas que no serve de comparao, porque tm a 'City' e querem ter o mercado financeiro, e no esto na zona euro e vo sair da Unio Europeia. O Banco da Holanda  o que est mais desenvolvido, mas h outros dois relevantes. O Banco de Espanha criou um grupo interno para avaliar os riscos internos associados s Fintech, nomeadamente de estabilidade financeira, que  basicamente o que ns j fizemos. O Banco de Frana fez uma coisa um pouco mais interessante, criou um ponto nico de entrada das Fintech. Qual  a vantagem desse modelo? Hoje, o que  que acontece? As solicitaes das Fintech aparecem por todos os departamentos. Precisam de se relacionar com o Departamento de Superviso Prudencial para terem uma autorizao, depois, relacionam-se com o Departamento de Superviso Comportamental porque querem disponibilizar um servio, mas depois precisam de falar com Departamento de Pagamentos. Portanto, o nosso plano para 2018 tambm passa por a, por criar uma porta de entrada nica, compreender os players para lhes poder prestar servios mais alinhados. O que o Banco de Frana fez tambm foi um Fintech Frum. Ns, no Banco de Portugal, estamos tambm a preparar uma grande conferncia de pagamentos, em que envolvemos os bancos e as fintech. E queremos fazer outras iniciativas como a que fizemos com o ECO em abril deste ano [conferncia New Money], em que sentamos os bancos e os novos 'entrantes', para criar um ambiente de partilha e de reflexo. Title: Interveno do Administrador Luis Laginha de Sousa no encerramento da Conferncia "The use of narrative information in assessing the effectiveness of macroprudential policies" (apenas em ingls)
text: Intervencao do Administrador Luis Laginha de Sousa no encerramento da Conferencia "The use of narrative information in assessing the effectiveness of macroprudential policies" (apenas em ingles) 17 nov. 2017 Good afternoon, It is for me a great a pleasure and an honour to come here before you and to close this Conference which was jointly organized by the ECB and the Banco de Portugal. In the coming minutes I would like to share a few thoughts as a wrap up to this Conference. But before starting to do so, I would like to express a very deep thank you, both to the speakers, for their contributions and also to all other participants, for the lively and thorough debates weve had all day. I believe that the twelve presentations, have greatly contributed to shed light on a number of issues which are extremely important for the implementation of macroprudential policy. Before moving into the thoughts component, just two preliminary notes. The first note is to say that this Conference could not come at a more appropriate time, not just for the international audience it caters to, but also for the Portuguese audience, given the very important topic currently being discussed, concerning the future of the supervision architecture in our country. For the avoidance of doubt, I must add that having this Conference here, in the middle of such a relevant discussion, was a very fortunate coincidence. Ive used the expression fortunate coincidence because initially the Conference was planned to take place in The Netherlands, but some months ago, the ECB approached the Bank of Portugal to host this Conference in Lisbon and at that moment, there was no perception that it would coincide with the debate about the supervision architecture, at national level. The second preliminary note is to say that when it comes to effective communication there are some fundamental rules, of which I will try, as much as possible, to apply two of them. One rule is to focus on few but important messages. The other rule is to draw simple conclusions. Having this in mind, what I will try to do is to link some of the takeaways from this Conference, with key components of the already mentioned debate about the national supervision architecture. To start with, it is adequate to briefly point to Why it is important to have macroprudential policy and, which are the key supporting factors, to make it successful. To do so, particularly to answer to the why, we have to go back a few years in time. In the aftermath of the international financial crisis came the consensus that risks related to excessive leverage, the combined effect of financial institutions behaviour and signs of speculative bubbles had been largely neglected in the preceding period, therefore, the safeguard of financial stability required the implementation of an autonomous policy (and I have to stress the word autonomous) aimed at mitigating systemic risk. The urgency in operationalizing this policy led many countries to the development of a toolkit, well before a comprehensive theoretical framework and empirical evidence on the impact of these measures, was stabilized. Issues like the complementarity and substitutability between several macroprudential policy instruments, their interaction with other policies, their role when risks have already materialized and the channels for possible spill-overs, still need to be fully explored. The research that was presented in this conference is a huge step in this direction. The databases used in many papers, with aggregate and cross-country comparable information on the activation and on the release of macroprudential policy instruments, are truly a valuable tool for research and policy. This narrative information provides greater depth and coverage to the empirical studies on the effectiveness of macroprudential measures, which is of great importance both for researchers, analysts and policymakers. Information and rigorous analysis is key for decision-making (rather than feeling and prejudice). So from what we heard today, the effectiveness of macroprudential policy depends on the right combination of timely action with informed decisions. Timing is particularly relevant since the preventive nature of the policy implies that it should act before risks materialize and become too difficult to manage. Informed decisions is also a key component, which goes hand in hand with timely action. If we were to use a culinary metaphor, we could say that it is a little bit like baking a cake, the eggs and the flour have to be combined not just in the right quantity but also at the right moment. I apologize if my culinary knowledge failed to produce the right metaphor, but I hope that at least the idea was there. There are a number of features inherent to macroprudential policy which make it a very special kind of creature. In particular, I would like to draw your attention to three of the features, which have also been addressed either directly or indirectly in todays Conference. The first of these features, which is strictly linked with the timing component mentioned before, is the fact that macroprudential policy can be subject to what is described as inaction bias. There are several factors which can contribute to limiting the action of macroprudential authorities in face of vulnerabilities in financial systems. Contrary to what is normal in the corporate business world, where success has many parents and failure is an orphan, when it comes to macroprudential policy, it is not quite so. Success is orphan and, when failure materializes, there are too many parents, but none seems to be willing to accept the parental responsibility, unless it is forced to do so. So, the preventive nature of macroprudential policy implies the activation of instruments at a stage where risks have not yet materialised and because of that, the risks at such point are not perceptible for economic agents. The efficacy of the policy in preventing a crisis cannot be verified either, and thats because a crisis which has not yet occurred does not leave a trace. The fact that the financial cycle is typically longer than the business cycle makes the lag between policy benefits and its costs, wider for macroprudential policy, than for most other policies. Moreover, not having a clear and measurable objective (as there is for monetary policy) makes it more difficult to assess its effectiveness. So, in short, while the benefits of macroprudential policy may be uncertain and delayed, its costs are more observable and immediate. As such, macroprudential policy measures, are likely to be unpopular. Imposing tighter requirements when risks might not be apparent may also conflict with the objectives of other policies. Or, to put it in a more proverbial way, its like taking the punch bowl away while the party is still going. The second feature inherent to Macroprudential policy is its potential overlapping or even contradiction with monetary policy. Assessing the effectiveness of macroprudential policy implies a thorough understanding of its transmission mechanism and of all the factors which might affect its policy targets. As we have seen in the papers presented today, disentangling the effects of macroprudential and monetary policy can be quite challenging, not just because of the interdependency between the two policies, but also because of their impact on credit growth and asset prices. The liquidity conditions of an economy and their impact on aggregate demand, which are essentially of the responsibility of monetary policy, are determinant to the financial cycle. Loose monetary policy can promote the emergency of speculative bubbles and also what is usually described as the search for yield behaviour. Therefore, the orientation of monetary policy is not irrelevant to the achievement of macroprudential objectives. On the other way, macroprudential policy, by affecting credit conditions and the resilience of the financial system, can impact the transmission mechanism of monetary policy. Understanding and managing these interactions is crucial for effective policy implementation. The third and last feature of macroprudential policy I would like to mention in my final remarks, is the requirement of a strong analytical knowledge on systemic risks and financial markets, in order to achieve an effective policy implementation. I believe this a self-explanatory feature and therefore I will not elaborate on it. Having in mind the three features Ive talked about, probably a fundamental question to be raised is how to take such features into account to ensure that the right policies will be implemented when they need to be implemented. And I believe the answer to that question can be summarized into a very simple two words sentence: Good Governance. Without good governance it is impossible to guarantee that the right measures will be taken when they need to be taken, and when it comes to good governance in macroprudential policy we are talking about three basic principles that have to be present at all times (and the order does not necessarily reflect hierarchy of importance): Accountability; Credibility; and Independence. Coming to this point of my final remarks and not drawing conclusions on what Ive said before, would be a little bit like not to talk about the elephant in the room. So to conclude, it is not irrelevant which authority should be responsible to implement macroprudential policy. If we carefully and openly assess the conditions which have to be met to ensure good governance, it wont be difficult to recognize that central banks are, in general terms, better positioned to do so. They have the capacity to analyse systemic risks and to act in a timely way in preventing and mitigating such risks, independently of lack of public support or conflicts with other policies. They have the competence in the analysis of macroeconomic and financial developments, and the expertise in assessing risks to financial stability. They have the experience in the implementation of monetary policy, which is particularly relevant given the interlink between such policy and the macroprudential one. They are those enjoying a greater degree of independence as it is enshrined in their Statutes and in the Treaties of the European Union as an essential condition for the fulfilment of their mandate of ensuring price stability. It is, nevertheless, important that, at the internal level of the institution, there is a clear separation of some functions, in order to ensure autonomy and prevent conflict of interests in the pursuit of different goals. But that does not hinders all that was previously said. With this remarks, which have a strong local flavour but totally in sync with the different flavours of the topics covered during the day, I would like to conclude this conference. I hope you have not only enjoyed but also found this conference useful for the challenges that lie ahead. I wish you all a great weekend and a safe return home. And thank you for being here and for having made this conference possible and a success.

Title: Intervention of Administrator Hlder Rosalino at the closing of the "Money Conference"
text: Intervention of the Administrator Helder... Intervention of Administrator Helder Rosalino at the closing of the "Money Conference" 14 Dec. 2017 Good morning I would like to begin by thanking the invitation to participate, on behalf of Banco de Portugal, in this conference to discuss the future of money and, more generally, the future of retail payment systems. We are currently experiencing a phase of profound transformation of the retail payments ecosystem on a global scale and, of course, also in Europe. Transformation that is important to understand and follow. I therefore have to give the opportunity and merit of this conference. It is indisputable that efficient and secure retail payment systems are a precondition for the proper functioning of any modern economy. This is an area where developments have been very rapid and where the increasing digitisation of financial services has promoted an increasingly widespread use of dematerialised payment instruments as an alternative to the use of cash, although it still plays a central role in citizens' payment options. The rapid and constant evolution of digital technologies promises to offer enormous benefits, but also creates new challenges and carries great demands for payment systems and for all agents operating in this area. With widespread internet access, consumers are now continuously connected and expect commercial and financial services to be available and at their fingertips in real time and at any time. Through significant investments in technology, the banking system and other market operators have increased, in the last decade, the provision of providing more efficient solutions, ensuring more security in their use and promoting public confidence in new electronic means of payment. The creation of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) in Europe was a historic milestone in this context, developing a more comprehensive, harmonised, secure and reliable payment system for consumers. However, in recent years, the banking system has been creating inefficiencies and losing some capacity to innovate and adapt to technological changes and the growing needs of end-users. In Europe, technology outage, competition from non-banks, especially Fintechs, and regulatory pressure are forcing banks to rethink how they provide retail payment services. It is clear today that banks no longer compete only with each other, they now also compete with non-banks and have to deal with the challenges arising from the developments of financial technology offered by Fintechs. We are therefore seeing a time of profound transformation in terms of innovation and the provision of financial services, which promises to significantly change the retail payments landscape in Europe and Portugal in the near future. In this speech I will briefly address the following topics: a. The impacts of the entry into force of the new Payment Services Directive (PSD2) b. The introduction of immediate payments c. The role of Fintechs in the value chain of the financial system and the positioning of of Banco de Portugal d. The challenge of virtual currencies The Payment Services Directive (PSD2) At the level of the regulation that frames the provision of payment services, it is essential to start by addressing the main impacts associated with the entry into force of the Revised Payment Services Directive (PSD2), some of which are very disruptive to the provision of payment services at European level. This Directive responds to the increasing digitisation of financial services, which has resulted in the emergence of new payment service providers, innovative payment solutions, more demanding users and new challenges for the security of operations. The new Directive aims to contribute to the creation of a single market for payment services, which is both secure (for service providers and users), efficient, innovative and competition-promoting. And it is especially in relation to this last objective  that of promoting competition that it is important to mention the one that is the biggest novelty of the Directive, and the one that interests us most in the context of the discussions on Fintechs. The Directive regulates two payment services which have so far not benefited from a regulatory framework: account information services and payment initiation services. These services will be provided to users online by providers who consider themselves 'third parties' in the relationship between you and your bank. These third parties will have, with the consent of users, access to the data of bank customers' accounts and may, for example, in the case of account information services, provide aggregate information on accounts held in various banks and enable services to manage the budgets of households or the treasury of companies. In the case of payment initiation services, these providers may initiate payments on behalf of the user, conveniently and quickly, without having to leave the website of the merchant to whom they are purchasing a product or service. This is where the space arises for the intervention of Fintechs, which can position themselves in the market as entities specialized in the provision of certain services directly to users, but also to banks. On this point, I conclude by noting that, contrary to the usual where regulation follows innovation, with PSD2 the regulation has promoted and facilitated innovation, undoubtedly creating new opportunities for Fintechs and, ultimately, for consumers. B - Immediate Payments In the competitive context in which the banking system operates and in which society lives, the ability to provide real-time services (especially payments) will be essential for banks if they want to maintain and gain new customers in the face of increasingly comprehensive and innovative competition. From the end-user's point of view, the benefit of immediate payments is the ability to make time-sensitive payments immediately, wherever and whenever needed. Currently, and using the services offered by the banks, for a payment in euros reach the beneficiary we have to wait at least one business day. In this context of great transformation, the strategic importance of immediate payments is central to the financial system in the near future. Immediate payment solutions developed in recent decades in some European countries (based on payment cards and credit transfers) are not, as a rule, interoperable with each other and do not have a pan-European configuration. This leads to a new scenario of fragmentation of the payments market at European level. In this context, in December 2014, the European Retail Payments Board (ERPB) agreed on the need to create at least one pan-European solution for immediate payments in euro (through the use of credit transfers), accessible to any payment service provider operating in the European Union. The solution created, and already in force since November 21st, profoundly changes the paradigm of making retail payments, since establishes (through a European scheme) that: Funds should be available in the beneficiary's account for a maximum of indicative of ten seconds; The payee's payment service provider is obliged to accept all transactions of a value of EUR 15,000 or less; Operations can be ordered at any time of the day and on any day of the year, i.e. with an availability of 24/7/365; and Payment service providers of the payer and payee may established in any of the countries that are part of SEPA. At this time, around 600 payment service providers from eight European countries are already offering immediate credit transfer solutions based on the new European scheme, which will progressively cover the thirty-four European SEPA countries. Also in Portugal is being prepared a national cooperative solution of immediate credit transfers, compatible with the principles and technical requirements harmonised at European level, and framed under the Interbank Compensation System managed by Banco de Portugal. This solution is expected to be made available in the second quarter of 2018 by SIBS to the national banking community. In addition, with the aim of ensuring interoperable immediate payment solutions at European level, the Governing Council of the ECB approved on 22 June 2017 the development of a new settlement service at TARGET2, exclusively dedicated to the processing of immediate payments. This new service, called TARGET -Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS), should start 30 November 2018 and is already under development. TIPS is a solution to ensure the full interoperability and accessibility of all European payment service providers, complementing the offer provided by European clearing rooms with a central bank currency settlement service for immediate payments. The adoption of new immediate payment solutions promises to revolutionise the current ecosystem of retail payments, and many experts believe that immediate payments will soon be the new retail payment standard. In this context, the implementation of interoperable immediate payment solutions at European level is one of the main challenges facing the banking communities and European authorities, and innovation will continue in the near future. C -The role of Fintech and the positioning of Banco de Portugal It is by all to recognize that a new wave of technological innovations is accelerating change in the financial sector, with a strong push from Fintechs. Investors, private companies and other players have spent unprecedented money on global financial technology startups. According to a recent study by a consultant, more than 45 billion has been invested in almost 2,500 Fintechs since 2010. Fintechs are leveraging the collection and storage of large amounts of information (big data), advances in artificial intelligence, computing and encryption power, and, above all, the reach and breadth of the internet as a global network. The strong complementarities between these technologies give rise to an impressive range of new applications involving payment services, financing, asset management, savings and insurance solutions. Its important role in developing solutions that often respond directly to consumer needs and which are not properly addressed by the usual financial intermediaries has been notorious. The increased digital affinity of consumers (in particular millennials) and the search for more streamlined processes, along with public mistrust of the traditional financial system, are some of the main factors that help explain the success of Fintechs. In general, there are two types of Fintechs: competitive ones, which we define as direct opponents to traditional intermediaries, markets and financial infrastructures; and collaborative ones, which predominate and want to offer solutions to improve the position of players already installed in the market, usually credit institutions. Many financial services institutions already recognize the role that collaborative Fintechs can play in helping to stimulate their own evolution and change the business model. In the same way, Fintechs are increasingly coming to established institutions as possible partners. There are mutual advantages. Banks benefit from fintechs' capacity for innovation, flexibility, power of distraining and the absence of legacy. Fintechs, on the other hand, benefit from the strength, reputation, size and scale of business that credit institutions can offer them to enhance the innovative solutions they create. This seems to be the way forward, that is, that of collaboration and the integration of Fintechs into the new business models of credit institutions. Banco de Portugal has been paying increasing attention to this theme, seeking to support and stimulate, at the national level, the debate around the great challenges that digital innovation poses to the financial system and its regulation. To this end, Banco de Portugal has created a permanent, multidisciplinary internal working group, with the aim of studying the evolution of Digital Banking and Fintech and to look, in the 2020 time horizon, at the challenges that arise in the broader context of its mission and within the framework of its regulatory and supervisory responsibilities. At the same time, it has been organizing and participating in several conferences and seminars dedicated to the theme, promoting debate, the sharing of knowledge and experience among all parties involved in this transformation process, ranging from the banking system, fintechs, regulators, policy makers and even consumers. Just last month, Banco de Portugal hosted an event dedicated to the theme "The Future of Payments and FinTechs", which aimed to develop innovative technological solutions in the payments market taking advantage of the new regulatory framework established by DSP2. Banco de Portugal will intensify its activity in this area in 2018, intending to implement, among others, the following initiatives: Hold semi-annual Fintech meetings with major operators and associations national authorities; Create a dedicated channel for Fintechs to interact with Banco de Portugal; Accomplishment an annual conference on the subject; Characterise the sector at national level by means of a questionnaire to be address these entities and representative associations; Hold regular meetings with the main players of this market; Elaborate a specific regulation and supervision handbook for this segment; Reactivate the National Forum for Payment Systems, with the inclusion of representative associations of this sector. We will be increasingly active in monitoring digital innovation in the financial system, strengthening in particular the proximity and openness to the Fintechs sector. D - The challenges of virtual currencies Finally, I will not fail to address the issue of digital or virtual currencies, as they are usually called. I begin by trying to contextualize virtual currencies using some publications produced on the subject by the ECB: Virtual currency schemes, ECB, October 2012: A virtual currency is a type of unregulated digital money, which is issued and generally controlled by its creators, being used and accepted among the members of a specific virtual community. Virtual Currency Schemes  A further analysis, ECB, February 2015: Virtual currency is defined as a digital representation of value, not issued by a central bank, credit institution or e-money institution, which in some circumstances can be used as an alternative to money. Already being a phenomenon on a global scale, although still with little expression in terms of the essential characteristics of virtual currencies are as follows: They are a digital representation of a value, although unofficial; Its value is determined by the law of supply and demand and is therefore subject to a large variation in value; they are not issued by any State or central authority; No represent a claim on an issuer; No have legal status in any known country; They can be centralised (issued and controlled by a single entity) or (issued and controlled by a variable number of entities); They can be convertible or non-convertible to legal currency; Can be used as a means of payment, although not legal certainty; and No function as an account unit or as a value buffer. From the wording of the characteristics of virtual currencies, we can draw up the following findings: First ly, because there is no central entity ensuring the irrevocability and definition of payment orders, virtual currency cannot be considered secure. It also does not formally qualify as a currency as it has no legal status, nor is it certain of its acceptance as a means of payment. Second finding: Virtual currency has no legal framework, either at the level of creation or at the level of use, which defines clear rights and duties for all parties involved in the model. In this sense, as its creation is decentralised, and there is no "system owner", it is difficult to define the jurisdiction under which procedures and rules should be established for the system in which it operates. Third conclusion: Its issuance is made by entities that are not regulated or supervised and therefore not subject to any kind of prudential requirements. The system in which it operates is also not subject to any kind of superintendence activity. Therefore, its users bear all the risk, since there is no fund to protect investors and users. In fact, one of the main problems of virtual currencies created decentralisedly is the absence of specific regulation and supervision. In this table, it is appropriate to warn of some risks inherent in the use of virtual currencies, which naturally result from their characteristics, and which are generally the following: High risk of volatility (sudden and unexpected fluctuations in the value of currencies virtual systems); Possibility of loss of investment, since there is no mechanism for warranty; Risk of fraudulent performance of the trading platform, computer attack on the virtual wallet/trading platform, insolvency of trading platform, etc.; Risk of contraception (anonymity); Risk of acceptance (uncertainty as to acceptance as a means of payment and practical impossibility of converting virtual currency into currency with legal course); Risk of using virtual currencies for illicit purposes, given their global reach and the lack of supervisory mechanisms or effective prevention measures: -Possibility of use in money laundering; -Use as a form of financing of illicit activities or terrorism; -Tax avoidance facility However, it is certain that virtual currencies, even by the popularity they have achieved, present in the concept of their creators and certainly from their users some potential advantages that are briefly as follows: Speed in transaction processing; Ease cross-border transactions; Reduced costs per transaction and absence of financial intermediation; Ease receipt of the value; Impossibility revocation of the operation; Creation new types of services (innovation); Anonymity and security of personal data; and Contribution for the financial inclusion of the unbanked population. Although we are seeing a substantial increase in the value of some of the virtual currencies, we must not forget that their use as a liquidation asset is marginal and their acceptance as a means of payment is almost negligible. In fact, virtual currencies have been fueling public debate not because of their supposed payment instrument function, but mainly for their intense activity on trading and speculation platforms. And this is still a worrying reality, taking into account the developments (valuations) known in recent weeks, which are accompanied by a substantial increase in risk. Regulators and supervisors are, in all geographies, monitoring this phenomenon, while further work and studies, promoted by official entities, on the subject of virtual currencies are intensifying. Several international organisations, including the ECB, the EBA, the IMF and the BIS, have working groups studying this subject and producing papers that can generally be consulted. The main questions and questions facing regulators and supervisors are whether or not to regulate the use of these currencies and in what depth. But other questions follow: How and when to regulate? Who regulates? How to regulate on a global scale? How to monitor compliance with a possible regulation? What are the consequences of this regulation? While some countries, such as South Korea and China, have restricted the use of virtual currencies, others, such as Japan and Russia, have adopted regulations that allow their marketing and use as a means of payment. In Europe, the focus has been on consumer alerts from regulators. Recently, the European Commission proposed an amendment to the Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Prevention Directive to compel virtual currency trading platforms and virtual wallet services to meet requirements in this area. This complex reality undoubtedly represents a new challenge for regulators. However, this does not prevent them from recognizing some advantages in the use of virtual currencies, especially in transnational payment transactions, and above all in harnessing the potential of the underlying technology (DLT, Distributed Ledger Technology). In this sense, some central banks have also begun to assess the advantages and impacts of creating a Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC), which could ultimately replace the issuance of physical currency and possibly counterbalance the phenomenon of the creation of the virtual private currencies to which we have seen. A Central Bank Digital Currency can be defined as a digital currency, made available by a central bank (in the current account unit), generally accepted for making payments, and which would be used as a form of value storage in central bank currency. While central banks have historically evolved to provide services only to commercial banks and a limited set of non-bank institutions, the adoption of a Central Bank Digital Currency may correspond to a paradigm shift, and central banks can, at the limit, grant access to central bank currency deposits to a broad set of users (in a retail component). This is a discussion that is still very open and without any underlying decision in the Framework of the Eurosystem, but it will surely go its way in the near future. The theme is already on the table of several central banks around the world, and Banco de Portugal is also following the issue, both at the level of its internal teams and through their participation in international working groups. Conclusion I conclude by stating that the benefits of digital transformation and innovation for citizens can only be achieved through full cooperation between all stakeholders, involving financial institutions, Fintechs and consumers, and an appropriate regulatory framework that promotes innovation and user safety. PSD2 provides the appropriate framework to promote such cooperation, facilitate innovation and ensure user safety in the use of new payment solutions. On the other hand, immediate payments, together with the new services allowed by PSD2, can offer new business opportunities for banks and payment service providers and thereby provide citizens with a secure payment experience in real time. The banking system will have to rapidly evolve towards the adoption, availability and massification of immediate payments, taking advantage of the technological solutions already available, in order to provide an alternative covering the alleged advantages and the innovative character attributed to virtual currencies. I am convinced that future innovations in retail payments will be based on immediate payments, in combination with access to the account provided by PSD2. And this will be a field of opportunity for Fintechs, the banking system and consumers. It is in this trajectory that the national banking community is working and it is with this strategy that Banco de Portugal is committed to promoting cooperation between all agents working in the payment systems sector in Portugal, in the same way that it creates an environment favorable to innovation in the financial sector. Thank you very much.
