Title: Speech by Vice-Governor Luis Maximo dos Santos at the 2nd International Conference of the Economic Chamber of Greece
text: Speech by Vice-Governor Luis Maximo... Speech by Vice-Governor Luis Maximo dos Santos at the 2nd International Conference of the Economic Chamber of Greece 04 Jun. 2018 The conference had the central theme of The Greek Economy after the closing of the 3rd adjustment programme, and took place in Athens on 31 May with the high patronage of the President of the Hellenic Republic, who also addressed the conference. Vice-Governor Luis Maximo dos Santos was invited to speak by the President of the Economic Chamber of Greece and the Vice-Governor of the Bank of Greece, John (Iannis) Mourmouras. His address took place during the first panel session, taking as its theme: The experience from countries that have implemented adjustment programmes. Time for Reform 1. I would like to start by extend a greeting to the distinguished members of the panel and thank the Economic Chamber of Greece, namely its President, Konstantinos Kollias, and Deputy Governor Iannis Mourmouras, for their kind invitation to be part of this magnificent Conference. It is a great pleasure to be in the mythical and unique city of Athens and to be able to address such an illustrious audience, sharing with you a few thoughts on the experience of the countries that have implemented adjustment programmes. The timing of this conference could not have been more appropriate against the background of the conclusion of the third adjustment programme for Greece and the ongoing debate on the future of the European Union, in particular concerning the reform of the Economic and Monetary Union. Obviously, the experience gained from the adjustment programmes does not concern only the Member States that have implemented them. In a union with the level of integration of the European Union and, even more, when we speak of the Eurozone, a severe crisis in one Member State poses a risk to the other Members and also for that should be a common concern. The soundness of the whole is dependent on the soundness of each Member State. Furthermore, as Professor Joseph Weiller rightly said, the European Union was created to be a community of destiny. If this is forgotten, its problems will only tend to worsen. 2. Following the global financial crisis, from 2010 to 2013, Greece, Ireland, Portugal and Cyprus were subject to adjustment programmes. Spain also benefited, in 2012, from considerable financial support to its banking sector. All of these programmes have long since been concluded and the third Greek programme is well on its way. However, they gave rise to consequences so intense in the economic, social, financial and political domains and in the mutual trust among Member States that their effects have not yet dissipated. In the spring of 2011, Portugal lost access to the markets at sustainable interest rates and had to request external assistance. Consecutive years of economic stagnation or low growth, a severe imbalance in public finances, a high external deficit, a banking system with imbalances, all amplified by the effects of the international financial crisis, made this scenario unavoidable. The Economic and Financial Assistance Programme to Portugal was implemented from 17 May 2011 to 30 June 2014. A post-programme surveillance phase is currently in place. The purpose of my presentation is not to conduct a detailed analysis of the programme. There is considerable institutional and academic literature on the subject and the opinions and assessments are widely different. It is a fact that from 2011 to 2013 Portugal experienced an economic recession without precedent in its recent history. The unemployment rate grew abruptly, reaching 16.2% in 2013, with severe social consequences. However, at the end of the programme, Portugal regained access to the markets. The financing rates of the Republic fell significantly and the confidence of economic agents was gradually restored. We all know that the non-standard monetary policy measures, introduced courageously by the European Central Bank, were decisive to this. But there were also other very important factors both at Portuguese and European level. Growth returned, still very timidly, from 2014 onwards. But in 2017, domestic product grew by 2.7% in real terms, the highest rate since 2000. The main sectors of activity made a positive contribution to this momentum, with manufacturing recording its largest growth since 2010. Exports and investment were the drivers of the Portuguese economy's acceleration in 2017, which will be important for correcting some of the structural problems. These results must be seen in the context of the euro area's positive business cycle and more contingent factors such as a very dynamic tourism sector. The good performance of Portuguese exports was chiefly due to external demand for Portuguese goods and services, in particular from euro area partners. However, Portuguese exports also increased their share in external markets. The construction sector was one of the major drivers of an increase in investment, boosted by a rise in demand by non-residents and the strong growth of tourism and related real estate activities. In this environment, the unemployment rate started to follow a clear downward trend, reaching 8.9% in 2017 and according to the latest data in 2018, at less than 8%. Employment rose by 3.3%, which was the highest annual growth since Portugal's participation in the euro, especially in the youngest and oldest age groups. The public accounts have been showing fairly positive developments, in line with the consolidation targets agreed at European level. In terms of the external accounts, the current and capital account surplus was 1.4% of GDP in 2017, similar to the surplus recorded since 2014. In parallel, a set of policies designed to eliminate some measures applied under the adjustment programme were put in place from 2016. The purpose of these policies was to improve the social environment and contribute to better living conditions for some of the lower income segments of the population, but also to certain parts of the middle class. The Portuguese banking sector also strengthened its position. It is today more stable and capitalised, with higher profitability levels, undergoing restructuring to face the various challenges from regulation to the rise of the digital economy. The resolution measure applied in August 2014 to Banco Espirito Santo  at that date the third largest bank in the Portuguese financial system  was completed in October 2017 with the sale of the resulting bridge bank. The non-performing loans (NPL) portfolio has been considerably reduced, although it still remains high. 3. To strengthen and sustain these positive economic developments, past mistakes must not be repeated at national and European level. And it is crucial that growth is also inclusive, not only in individual Member States but in the European Union as a whole. Adjustment programmes did not include explicit social objectives nor monitoring requirements on the social impact. However, they could have and should have done so. Article 3, number 1, of the Treaty on the European Union states that, together with the advancement of peace and its values, the Unions aim is to promote the well-being of its peoples. Likewise, number 3 establishes that the Union shall work for the sustainable development of Europe based on balanced economic growth and price stability, a highly competitive social market economy, aiming at full employment and social progress stating also that the Union promotes economic, social and territorial cohesion, and solidarity among Member States. The Unions policies should be globally consistent, given that the rules established by the Treaties are all equally binding. 4. In the beginning of January 2019 we will celebrate the 20th anniversary of the European Monetary Union although euro banknotes and coins only began to circulate in 2002. Portugal was among its eleven founding Member States. For millions of young European citizens the euro is the only national currency they know. It is common knowledge that the establishment of the Economic and Monetary Union was the most far-reaching political step in the history of European integration. Likewise, we have always known that the architecture set up in Maastricht was incomplete and riskinducing, particularly due to the absence of mechanisms to cope with asymmetric shocks. Its architects implicitly admitted that the missing components would sooner or later be added, as a result of the integrationist momentum. However, History has repeatedly proven that determinism can be a mistake... Up until the onset of the financial crisis, we lived under a kind of spell. In many countries, the decrease in interest rates boosted indebtedness, while there were illusory improvements in living conditions. Neither the economic agents nor the authorities managed to clearly perceive that the monetary union would necessarily entail a new economic regime: the centralisation of monetary and foreign exchange policies warranted a completely different policy mix. Fiscal and income policies acquired greater importance, but, in fact, fiscal policy was also subject to heavy constraints. When the international financial crisis broke out, it progressed rapidly, quickly exposing and enhancing the accumulated imbalances within the Union. The response to the crisis focused on strengthening the coordination between fiscal policies, the development of new financing mechanisms, and the establishment of the banking union and, of course, non-standard monetary policy measures. This was far from insignificant, but, in some cases, it was perhaps a little late and surely was not enough. In many ways, we were entering a new territory as it was with the implementation of adjustment programmes, which pose unique challenges in countries within a monetary union. We need to drive the Economic and Monetary Union reform forward. It is indeed time for reform. Part of this reform merely consists in finalising the previous cycle of reforms by completing the banking union with the implementation of its third pillar and by endowing the Single Resolution Fund with the adequate financial resources to fully accomplish its mission. No debate is more sterile than the one on whether to reduce or to share risks. In truth, we must do both. And, in some ways, we have been doing just that. As many contend, it is human nature to only make important decisions when faced with necessity, during critical situations. Let us hope that it is possible to dispel that perception, by taking full advantage of the existing proposals and ongoing debate  which should be open and inclusive  to adopt the necessary measures to improve the working of the European Union and, in particular, the Economic and Monetary Union. In fact, we should avoid doing so under pressure from a new crisis. Only the future will show if we are able and willing to make the necessary decisions so that the European Union will be the "community of destiny" as Joseph Weiller put so well, and as its founders intended. Thank you for your kind attention.

Title: Intervention of the Governor, Carlos da Silva Costa, at the hearing by the Committee on Budget, Finance and Administrative Modernization on "Assessment of public and external indebtedness"
text: Intervention of the Governor, Carlos da Silva Costa, at the hearing by the Committee on Budget, Finance and Administrative Modernization on "Assessment of public and external indebtedness" 26 Jun 2018 Intervention of the Governor of Banco de Portugal, Carlos da Silva Costa [1] Madam President of COFMA, Ladies and gentlemen, very good afternoon. I thank you for your invitation to share with you banco de Portugal's perspective on issues related to the sustainability of public and external indebtedness. The relevance of the theme is unquestionable and is well mirrored in the opening sentence of the report that motivated the constitution of this Working Group and which I quote: "[the] weight of external debt, in which much of the public debt is encompassed, restricts economic growth of the country and its democratic choices." High levels of indebtedness result in slower and more volatile economic growth, for two orders of reasons: i. Undermine investment, either through the uncertainty they generate, or through the limiting the funding capacity of agents, and ii. Make economies more vulnerable to shocks  internal or external  on the confidence, the product or interest rates, also compromising the use against cyclical budget policy. The topicality of the theme remains evident. Portugal's gross foreign debt nearly quadrupled between 1996 and 2012, at 211 percent of GDP in 2017. Private non-financial sector debt increased from 89 percent of GDP in 1995 to a maximum of 220 percent in 2012, still above 173 percent in 2017. Public debt rose from 50 percent to more than 130 percent of GDP between 2000 and 2014, adhering to 126 percent in 2017. Data from the International Monetary Fund show that this level of public debt in the past year was the fourth highest among developed economies around the world, with only two economies  Japan and Greece  having a markedly higher level of debt. It follows that it is absolutely vital that all relevant actors can join forces around the debt reduction target accumulated in the Portuguese economy. The authorities responsible for conducting budgetary policy should choose the instruments and the strategy for reducing public debt. On the other, the central bank's perspective on debt focuses primarily on its impact on the conduct of monetary policy and the safeguarding of financial stability. Economic growth, financial stability and level of indebtedness are inseparable concepts: A. Sustainable indebtedness and financial stability provide financing stable to the investment that is needed to grow; B. Economic growth provides the essential return for payment of the debt and the profitability of the banking system; and C. Instability of the banking system can generate pressure on public finances, as well as, conversely, high global indebtedness may condition the functioning of the banking system. With regard to the sustainability of indebtedness, I would like to stress that in general: 1. Debt financing depends on the availability of investors for the 2. This availability is intrinsically linked to the perception that these same investors have debt sustainability and ultimately 3. The sustainability of public debt depends critically on factors such as (i) its provide dimension (in particular in view of the country's productive capacity); (ii) the currency of emission; (iii) the nationality of the holders (i.e., if the debt is mostly owned by domestic agents or external agents); and (iv) the monetary regime (in particular, it should be noted that, in the framework of a monetary union, the state is conditioned by the limits of the common monetary policy and the autonomy to issue their own currency). It should be noted that, in the absence of a credible strategy ensuring that markets the debt service will not be called into question, the economy could be vulnerable to external shocks potentially leading to an abrupt suspension of financing, with negative implications for financial stability and the conduct of monetary policy. The fact of Portugal's integration into the European Union and the Euro area represents an important factor of credibility with financial markets. Tread the path of debt reduction to the pace of preventive community rules not only credibility the path of consolidation, but also makes this effort smoother, gradual and more consistent. We know from past experience that the pace dictated by market expectations results in a much more volatile consolidation path, as these expectations can respond abruptly to sudden shocks. We all have a living memory of the consequences, efforts and constraints that can result from abrupt changes in investors' perception of debt sustainability. The hardness of the implicit adjustments typically adds to the fact that they become necessary in times of adverse shocks, periods when adjustment is more difficult and burdensome. The latest projections from Banco de Portugal indicate that the three-year period 2018-2020 will be characterized by an average annual product growth of 2 percent, after a decade of virtually zero average annual growth. Developments in economic activity will be sustained by the dynamism of exports and the recovery of investment, in a framework of accommodative monetary conditions, favourable prospects for global demand developments, but low levels of domestic savings. The Portuguese economy has shown a great capacity for macroeconomic adjustment, but we must not forget that important constraints remain to long-term growth. In recent decades, it has been evident that the reduced growth of the potential product limits the ability to sustain higher levels of consumption without incurring external imbalances. We must take advantage of the current cyclical moment to make the Portuguese economy more resilient to adverse shocks and to strengthen long-term growth. I would therefore conclude this initial intervention by stressing that it is essential and opportune to increase the room for manoeuvre in the management of our interdependencies, both commercial and financial. By 2020, a scenario of product and investment growth is expected that not only favors but also requires a path of reduction of debt stocks in the Portuguese economy, in order, on the one hand, to immunize the economy to future adverse shocks and, on the other, to make room for investment financing. I am now available to clarify the questions that you want to raise. Thank you very much. [1] Ready for presentation.

Title: Opening speech of Deputy Governor Luis Maximo dos Santos at the 7th meeting of the Forum for Behavioral Supervision
text: Opening speech of the Vice-Gov... Opening speech of Deputy Governor Luis Maximo dos Santos at the 7th meeting of the Forum for Behavioral Supervision 27 Jun 2018 1. Welcome to the seventh meeting of the Forum for Behavioral Supervision. I begin by greeting all theentities and their representatives and thanking you for your participation. Banco de Portugal has the greatest pleasure in welcoming you, seeking to maintain with everyone, without exception, a relationship of proximity and dialogue, in order to, together, contribute to the promotion of the bom functioning of retail banking markets, guided by high standards of conduct, with balanced relations between financial institutions and their customers. In fact, the greater the magnitude of the task, the greater the combination of esforcos, within the framework of their respective responsibilities. 2. Since its establishment in 2011, this Forum, which is an informal structure of an advisory nature, with regular annual meetings, has sought to provide a spacefor sharing information and views, with a view to the debate on the functioning of retail banking markets. In its first editions, the Forum met immediately after the publication of the Behavioral Supervision Report, focusing on the analysis ofthe activities developed s. However, in recent years, we chose to meet the challenges of the agenda of behavioral supervision work, enriching it with your reflections and concerns. In the past year we have been the central theme of digitization of the national retail banking market, listing the challenges it poses to institutions, regulators and supervisors and to bank customers themselves. As we read the minutes of this meeting, we realize how much of what was anticipated actually happened. But since March 9, 2017, the date of the previous edition of the Forum, many and relevant events took place, in particular  but not only in legislative matters. Without seeking to be exhaustive, it is verified that from mortgage credit to credit intermediaries, through payment accounts and without forgetting the minimum banking services and structured deposits, a whole new regulatory reality emerged. These amendments, which are mainly depending on European initiatives, are reflected both in the densification of the rights of banking customers and of the obligations of financial institutions, and in the extension of the scope of intervention of the behavioural supervision function of Banco de Portugal. For example, in the case of mortgage credit, changes in pre-contractual information, in particular through the new European Standard Information Sheet, the remuneration of the employees of credit institutions involved in the marketing of credit agreements, as well as the new requirements regarding their knowledge and competences. There has also been a strengthening of the duties on the creditworthiness assessment of consumers. Regulation on transparency and comparability of commissions in payment accounts should alsobring new rights to consumers. These and other measures necessarily promote more intrusive supervision of conduct. It should also be highlighted that the perimeter of behavioral supervision has changed, with newresponsibilities to be given to Banco de Portugal with regard to the authorization and registration of entities that act as credit intermediaries and in the certification of training entities of employees of credit institutions and credit intermediaries. Thisdensification of the regulatory framework occurs in the context of a growing digitisation of banking activity, which poses increased challenges to behavioral supervision and all market players. In today's work, the issue of the digitisation of the retail banking market will also occupy us  due to its centrality will certainly be a recurring theme for a long time  alongside the regulatory developments I referred to. 4. We are aware of the enormous challenges facing the banking sector today  far less dramatic, however, than those that have existed in the recent past  and in particular of how banking regulation has become increasingly demanding and costly in the behavioural sector. But the institutions' reaction to this requirement is not to fall into the temptation of facilitation in compliance with regulatory standards or compliance with the minimum. On the contrary. Affirming your difference in excellence in full compliance with the rules that protect consumers will have short-term costs but will undoubtedly prove to be a competitive asset and a factor of business growth in the medium and long term for the increased reputation it will bring. A client who feels that in an institution thereis a culture of compliance with the legislation that protects him is a client who will surely value that data and reward it with fidelity and trust. And if it is true that, unfortunately, the level of financial training is not yet what we want  despite the efforts made by various agents to improve  it is also a fact that, as shown by multiple indicators  starting with complaints  customers are now more attentive than in the past. Ensuring full compliance withthe comp ortamental regulation is the essential purpose of behavioural supervision, in order to ensure the protection of bank customers, obvious allies in the sense of what is not working well. Banco de Portugal wants fulfilling institutions and clients informed, informed and aware of their rights. And there is no doubt that those around this table are also what they want, because only this attitude can strengthen the retail banking market, an objective that unites us all. 5. In the apparent simplicityof its utterance, under the expression "digital society" situations and realities of enormous variety and complexity are welcomed. But let's not kid ourselves: the "digital society" isn't coming - it's already here. What will increase in the near future - and a lot - is the pace of its penetration. Since 2015, Banco de Portugal has been considering the challenges arising from the marketing of retail banking products and services through digital channels. At the end of 2016, we launched the firstionary question addressed to financial institutions on the commercialization of banking products and services in digital channels in Portugal, whose results were very important for the performance of Banco de Portugal, as conduct supervisor. And we arealready preparing the launch of a second survey this year, to obtain more current information, and the invitation to participate is already made. In 2017, through regulatory change, it became possiblefor institutions based in Portugal to make it possible to open an account to order through digital channels. In early 2018, a circular letter was issued requiring financial institutions to report credit information to consumers contracted on digital channels. With this performance, Banco de Portugal has been following the technologicalevolution in the retail banking markets, recognizing that the increasing commercialization of banking products and services in digital channels must be accompanied by compliance with the applicable standards in order not to protect the banking customer. Tecnological neutrality is one of the pillars of European regulation and supervision, with a view to ensuring that the banking customer, regardless of the channel used, benefits from the same rights and does not face increased risks. To ensure this protection, Banco of Portugal has been closely monitoring the procedures that institutions are adopting to comply with the regulatory framework in the digital context, the security requirements they implement, how they ensure that the banking customer is informed and informedabout the products they hire. The conduct supervisor is thus challenged to find appropriate answers to ensure the consumer rights framework, in particular in terms of information transparency and security, while promotingthe confidence that is essential to stimulate the use of digital channels and thereby enhance the development of new products and new business models. In this context, and with regard to, for example, the contracting of credit, Banco de Portugal began to require the prior and systematic reporting of information on the specificities of the process of contracting credit to consumers in digital channels. Banco de Portugal intends to know in depth the security mecanisms implemented in these channels and the hiring process, to evaluate the procedures adopted by the institutions and understand the technological solutions adopted. Security in the use of digital channels is a priority. Safety isa concern of regulators and supervisors, but it should also be a priority of institutions. Bank customers must themselves play an active role in promoting security, and are expected to be more attentive and demanding and more committed to the adoption of security procedures. The perception of insecurity on the part of bank customers is one of the main obstacles to the use of digital channels. Strengthening security through the adoption of resilient systems, monitoring transactions and procurement processes and applying robust authentication procedures, but also clarifying customers ' own precautions on the precautions they should take and the reasons why they should be adopted, are a key to buildingthe confidence that stimulates the development of digital channels. Since bank customers aware of security measures contribute to the mitigation of security risks and, ultimately, to the stability of the financial system, the development of information and financial training initiatives is one of the main concerns of Banco de Portugal, which we assume as a strategic objective. The training and financial (and digital) information of bank customers is an objective that will be best achieved with the support of all partners of the Forum. I can inform you that Banco de Portugal intends to launch, very soon, a multifaceted financial training strategy, with content aimed in particular at the younger populacao, using, for greater reach, also to social networks and creating electronic content. You have to be careful with simplistic visions. The granting of credit may be instantaneous but this does not free the debtor from the duty to pay it and, therefore, the credit, whatever technological modality used, must be responsible. As always, what may be wrong will never be technological evolution but the misuse that can be done of it. The digital society brings out issues withportals  in the broad sense  to the foreground. A hypertechnological society can only be successful if it is anchored in a solid culture of values and a redoubled attention to the ethical dimension. The legitimacy to act in a certain way cannot onlycome from the technological feasibility of doing so, under penalty of generating disruptive effects that will eventually limit the net gains of digital transformation. That is also why I have said on several occasions that regulation andbehavioural supervision will play an increasingly important role. I now pass the floor to Dr. Lucia Leitao, Director of the Department of Behavioral Supervision, making sure that his intervention will serve as the basis for a rich and participated dialogue, forwhat is launched the challenge.

Title: Opening speech by Administrator Hlder Rosalino at the 1st Fintech Meeting of Banco de Portugal
text: Opening speech by Administrator Helder Rosalino at the 1st Fintech Meeting of Banco de Portugal 05 jul. 2018 Good afternoon, everyone. I would like to begin by welcoming you to this 1st Fintech Meeting of Banco de Portugal. It is irrefutable that the current wave of technological innovation is accelerating change in the financial sector, with a strong push from Fintechs. Banco de Portugal has been paying increasing attention to this theme, seeking to support and stimulate, at the national level, the debate around the great challenges that digital innovation poses to the financial system and regulatory authorities. We are increasingly active in this field and this first Fintech Meeting demonstrates our closer proximity and openness to the Fintechs sector. However, it is not an isolated action. In addition to this initiative, the Bank has intensified its activity in this area and has already carried out the following actions: On May 23, 2018, it created a dedicated channel for Fintechs to interact with the Banco de Portugal, through which they will be able to ask their questions as well as have agile access to a relevant set of information; He has organized and participated in several conferences and seminars dedicated to promoting debate, the sharing of knowledge and experience among all the parties involved in this transformation process; Reactivated the National Forum for Payment Systems, the consultative structure of the Banco de Portugal, which brings together the main national players in the supply and payment services (including associations representing Fintech) and which has the mission to contribute to the implementation of payment solutions safe, efficient and innovative in the Portuguese; It has held regular meetings with market players whenever it is revealed useful. This first Fintech Meeting is dedicated to the new opportunities and challenges of the Revised Payment Services Directive (DSP2). The choice of the theme seems obvious in mind the current moment, in which the final phase of transposition of this Directive into the national legal system takes place. Still, in addition, DSP2 contributes to the creating a single market for payment services, which is both secure (for service providers and users), efficient, innovative and competition-promoting. In particular, by providing payment and access services to payment accounts, undoubtedly creating new opportunities for Fintechs and ultimately for consumers. It is essential to understand the main impacts associated with the entry into force of DSP2, some of which are very disruptive to the provision of payment services at European level. One of the biggest novelties of the Directive, and the one that interests us most in the context of the discussion with Fintechs, are the new account information services and payment initiation services. These services will be provided to users online by providers who consider themselves 'third parties' in the relationship between you and your bank. These third parties will have, with the consent of users, access to the data of bank customers' accounts and may, for example, in the case of account information services, provide aggregate information on accounts held in various banks and enable services to manage the budgets of households or the treasury of companies. In the case of payment initiation services, these providers may initiate payments on behalf of the user, conveniently and quickly, without having to leave the website of the merchant to whom they are purchasing a product or service. This is where the space arises for the intervention of Fintechs, which can position themselves in the market as entities specialized in the provision of certain services directly to users, but also to banks. As you will surely know, the Directive is complemented by the implementation of technical guidelines and requirements drawn up by the European Banking Authority (EBA). In this context, the RTS on Strong Customer Authentication and Common Secure Communication stands out, which were published on 13 March 2018 in the Official Journal of the EU, giving a period of 18 months (therefore until September 2019) for their adoption by market agents. These RTS explain essential requirements to be observed by Payment Service Providers in terms of security and secure communication procedures with third-party service providers, which are essential for the provision of such account information services and payment initiation services. Regarding the process of transposition of DSP2 into the national legal system, the proposed Law of legislative authorization, which will allow the transposition to be supported in Decree-Law, is currently under discussion in the Assembly of the Republic. It should be noted that, from an enlarged European perspective and by the end of June, transposition was carried out in 17 Member States. I note that the benefits of digital transformation and technological innovation can only be achieved through cooperation and dialogue between all stakeholders, also involving Fintechs and consumers, and guided by an appropriate regulatory framework that promotes innovation and security. However, the challenges in providing payment services are not exhausted by the implementation of DSP2. There are other initiatives that are expected to prove to be new business opportunities for Fintech operators. Examples of these initiatives are the development of immediate payment solutions, the adoption of strong authentication mechanisms and eIDAS certificates, Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) and RegTech. These may be some of the topics to be addressed in upcoming "Fintech Meetings". Banco de Portugal and FinTechs discuss opportunities and challenges of the new Payments Fineech

Como certamente sabero, a Diretiva  complementada com a implementao de orientaes e requisitos tcnicos elaborados pela Autoridade Bancria Europeia (EBA). Neste mbito, destaca-se os RTS on Strong Customer Authentication and Common Secure Communication, que foram publicados em 13 de maro de 2018 no Jornal Oficial da UE, conferindo um prazo de 18 meses (portanto, at setembro de 2019) para a sua adoo pelos agentes do mercado. Estes RTS explicitam requisitos essenciais a serem observados pelos Prestadores de Servios de Pagamentos ao nvel dos procedimentos de segurana e de comunicao segura com prestadores de servios terceiros, essenciais para a disponibilizao dos referidos servios de informao sobre contas e os servios de iniciao de pagamentos. Relativamente ao processo de transposio da DSP2 para o ordenamento jurdico nacional, a proposta de Lei de autorizao legislativa, que permitir que a transposio venha a ser suportada em Decreto-Lei, encontra-se atualmente em discusso na Assembleia da Repblica. Anote-se que, numa perspetiva europeia alargada e at ao final de junho, a transposio estava concretizada em 17 Estados-membros. Realo que os benefcios da transformao digital e da inovao tecnolgica s podem ser alcanados atravs da cooperao e dilogo entre todas as partes interessadas, envolvendo tambm as Fintechs e consumidores, e balizadas por um quadro regulamentar adequado que promova a inovao e a segurana. No entanto, os desafios que se colocam ao nvel da prestao dos servios de pagamento no se esgotam com a implementao da DSP2. Existem outras iniciativas que expectavelmente se revelaro em novas oportunidades de negcio para os operadores Fintech. So exemplo destas iniciativas o desenvolvimento de solues de pagamentos imediatos, a adoo de mecanismos de autenticao forte e de certificados eIDAS, o Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) e o RegTech. Title: Opinion article by Administrator Hlder Rosalino to Expresso: "Portugal Finlab - regulation at the service of financial innovation"
text: Administrator opinion article... Opinion article by The Administrator Helder Rosalino to Expresso: "Portugal Finlab -the regulation at the service of financial innovation" 15 set. 2018 All European countries, through governments and regulators, are creating conditions for attractiveness for fintech and innovative projects Elder Rosalino Administrator of Banco de Portugal In recent years, we have seen very significant changes in the provision of financial services, as a result of technological upheaution, pressure from banks to reduce costs, changing consumer behaviour and, especially, the entry of new players into the financial system, so-called fintech. According to recent studies, global investment in fintech increased from 9 billion in 2010 to more than 30 billion in 2017. Fintech emerged in force and attracted substantial investments, presenting itself as a direct threat to established institutions. After the denial phase (still with some followers), characterized by the idea that the financial sector is too large, complex and protected to give in to new (and small) competitors, banks have come to recognize that fintech offer interesting opportunities to stimulate their own digital transformation. There are already many banks that are creating platforms for co-creation and collaboration with some financial startups, collaboratively incorporating innovation and differentiation into their business models. In the same way, fintech increasingly sees established institutions as possible partners. Banks benefit from the ability to innovation and expand fintech, as well as the flexibility and lower cost of their infrastructure. Fintech benefits from the reputation, knowledge and the scale of business that banks can offer them. As a result, consumers benefit from cheaper products, more adapted to their specific needs, more flexible and more agile and convenient use. According to a survey recently published by the European Banking Authority, banks agree that by developing partnerships with fintech, they are generally able to increase their supply and revenues. They also believe that these partnerships allow not only to maintain existing customers but also to attract new customers and reduce costs. The results of the study also suggest that the area of payments may be the most affected with a negative impact on their profitability. On the other hand, the areas of commercial banking and trading are those where there are more opportunities to increase revenues or reduce costs by incorporating solutions offered by fintech. In this innovation ecosystem, the question arises as to what the role of regulators should be. To this question, the European Commission responded in March 2018 with the presentation of an Action Plan for Fintech (For a more competitive and innovative European financial sector) with a view to promoting competition and, where possible, encouraging innovation in the financial sector. At the same time, ensure in all circumstances the preservation of financial stability and high levels of protection for investors and consumers. This action plan reinforced the importance that European regulators have been assigning to fintech and seeks to create a favourable (and controlled) environment for their development, such as initiatives such as Innovation Hubs and Regulatory Sandboxes, already present in several countries. In general, all jurisdictions, through their governments and regulators, are creating attractive conditions for financial innovation and fintech, recognising that they can offer an important set of benefits to the financial system and consumers in general. Inspired by best practices at European level and the recommendations of the European Commission, Banco de Portugal, the Securities Market Commission and the Insurance and Pension Fund Supervisory Authority, in partnership with Portugal Fintech, have jointly launched the "Portugal FinLab Where Regulation Meets Innovation". In a special framework "regulatory laboratory to support innovation", Portugal FinLab offers an integrated view of the regulatory requirements necessary for the implementation of financial technological innovations, promoting the direct and interactive dialogue of regulators with innovators, whatever they may be. For regulators, the creation of this laboratory allows them to regularly monitor, in a controlled environment, new projects and their promoters, increasing their knowledge about innovation dynamics and reducing regulatory uncertainty and possible barriers to new business development. Portugal FinLab will be, above all, a privileged communication channel between regulators and companies, efficient and dedicated to innovative projects, which can represent a competitive advantage to attract international companies and will be addressed any project that wants to innovate in the financial sector Portuguese, be it a startup or an incumbent. It is an innovative initiative and, above all, a value-generating initiative for the national financial system, which will put Portugal on the radar of investors and innovators from other geographies.

Artigo de opinio do Administrador Hlder Rosalino ao Expresso: "Portugal Finlab -a regulao ao servio da inovao financeira" 15 set. 2018 Todos os pases europeus, atravs dos governos e reguladores, esto a criar condies de atratividade para as fintech e os projetos inovadores Hlder Rosalino Administrador do Banco de Portugal Temos assistido, nos ltimos anos, a mudanas muito significativas na oferta de servios financeiros, fruto da disrupo tecnolgica, da presso sofrida pelos bancos para reduzirem custos, da mudana de comportamento dos consumidores e, especialmente, da entrada de novos intervenientes no sistema financeiro as chamadas fintech. De acordo com estudos recentes, o investimento global em fintech aumentou de nove mil milhes de dlares em 2010 para mais de 30 mil milhes de dlares em 2017. As fintech surgiram em fora e atraram investimentos substanciais, apresentando-se como uma ameaa direta s instituies estabelecidas. Depois da fase de negao (ainda com alguns seguidores), caracterizada pela ideia de que o sector financeiro  demasiado grande, complexo e protegido para ceder face a novos (e pequenos) concorrentes, os bancos tm vindo a reconhecer que as fintech oferecem oportunidades interessantes para estimular a sua prpria transformao digital. So j muitos os bancos que esto a criar plataformas de cocriao e colaborao com algumas startups financeiras, incorporando, de forma colaborativa, inovao e diferenciao nos seus modelos de negcio. Do mesmo modo, as fintech veem cada vez mais as instituies estabelecidas como possveis parceiras. Os bancos beneficiam da capacidade de inovao e disrupo das fintech, bem como da flexibilidade e custo mais reduzido das suas infraestruturas. As fintech beneficiam da solidez, reputao, conhecimento e da escala de negcio que os bancos lhes podem oferecer. Em consequncia, o consumidor beneficia de produtos mais baratos, mais adaptados s suas necessidades especficas, mais flexveis e de utilizao mais gil e conveniente. Em contrapartida, as reas de banca comercial e de trading so aquelas onde existem mais oportunidades de aumentar receitas ou reduzir custos pela incorporao de solues oferecidas pelas fintech. Neste ecossistema de inovao, coloca-se a questo de saber qual deve ser o papel dos reguladores. A esta questo a Comisso Europeia respondeu, em maro de 2018, com a apresentao de um Plano de Ao para as Fintech (For a more competitive and innovative European financial sector), tendo em vista promover a competio e, sempre que possvel, incentivar a inovao no sector financeiro. Ao mesmo tempo, garantir em todas as circunstncias a preservao da estabilidade financeira e elevados nveis de proteo dos investidores e dos consumidores. Este plano de ao reforou a importncia que os reguladores europeus tm vindo a atribuir s fintech e procura criar um ambiente favorvel (e controlado) para o seu desenvolvimento, de que so exemplo iniciativas como os Innovation Hubs e as Regulatory Sandboxes, j presentes em vrios pases. De um modo geral, todas as jurisdies, atravs dos respetivos governos e reguladores, esto a criar condies de atratividade para a inovao financeira e para as fintech, reconhecendo que podem oferecer um importante conjunto de vantagens ao sistema financeiro e aos consumidores em geral. Inspirados nas melhores prticas ao nvel europeu e nas recomendaes da Comisso Europeia, o Banco de Portugal, a Comisso de Mercado de Valores Mobilirios e a Autoridade de Superviso de Seguros e Fundos de Penses, em parceria com a Portugal Fintech, lanaram, em conjunto, o Portugal FinLab Onde a regulamentao encontra a inovao. Num enquadramento especial laboratrio de regulao para apoio  inovao , o Portugal FinLab oferece uma viso integrada dos requisitos regulatrios necessrios para a implementao de inovaes tecnolgicas financeiras, promovendo o dilogo direto e interativo dos reguladores com os inovadores, quaisquer que eles sejam. Para os reguladores, a criao deste laboratrio permite-lhes um acompanhamento regular, em ambiente controlado, dos novos projetos e dos seus promotores, aumentando o seu conhecimento sobre as dinmicas de inovao e reduzindo a incerteza regulatria e eventuais barreiras ao desenvolvimento de novos negcios. O Portugal FinLab ser, acima de tudo, um canal de comunicao privilegiado entre os reguladores e as empresas, eficiente e vocacionado para projetos inovadores, que poder representar uma vantagem competitiva para atrair empresas internacionais e ter como destinatrio qualquer projeto que queira inovar no sector financeiro portugus, seja uma startup ou um incumbente. Trata-se de uma iniciativa inovadora e, sobretudo, geradora de valor para o sistema financeiro nacional, que colocar Portugal no radar de investidores e inovadores de outras geografias.

Title: Opening speech of Administrator Hlder Rosalino at the First Meeting of the Forum for Payment Systems
text: Opening speech of Administrator Helder Rosalino at the First Meeting of the Forum for Payment Systems 17 set. 2018 I thank the presence of all entities invited to participate in the Forum for Payment Systems, which is formally relaunched with the holding of this first meeting in its new format and composition. Banco de Portugal, as the entity responsible for regulating and promoting the proper functioning of payment systems, is strongly committed to promoting cooperation between all agents operating in this market in Portugal, involving the supply and demand of payment services, just as it intends to create an environment favorable to innovation and value generation in this crucial dimension for the development of our economy. It is indisputable that efficient and secure retail payment systems are a precondition for the proper functioning of any modern economy. This new formulation follows an earlier phase, which has occurred since this Forum was originally created at the end of 2009, at the time focusing its mandate and objectives on the implementation of the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA) and consequent national migration. This phase ran until the end of 2014. Given the set of challenges that have been facing the retail payments market, we understand that there were broad reasons to promote the relaunch and recomposition of this structure, leading to the new model that is now formed and which, we hope, provide guarantees of cooperation between agents with an interest in this area, while also will allow an articulation with European bodies, or counterparts, from other countries. Exactly 4 months ago, on 14 May, Banco de Portugal hosted the first conference organized in the context of the Forum for Payment Systems, dedicated to the theme "A new era in payments?". Many of the representatives in this plenary were present and several took the floor, in particular in the panels organised there. We also had the opportunity at the time to have interventions from representatives of relevant international bodies on the governance of retail payments in Europe, from the outthen the European Central Bank, the European Commission and the European Payments Council. Indeed, it was an initiative that Banco de Portugal considers successful, in which we sought to provide an overview of trends and give visibility to a set of topics on the agenda and which will benefit from involvement and knowledge, both on the supply side (banks, payment and electronic money institutions, card schemes, clearing boards, among others), both on the demand side (public administration bodies, companies representing different segments of use of payment instruments and, of course, consumer representatives). Following this conference, we have prepared for today's session an agenda to reflect the challenges that arise, taking into account the model defined for the functioning of the Forum, as set out in its mandate, as well as to address topics to be addressed jointly, at this early stage of activities and at a later stage. One of the inevitable themes is the recent evolution of the European regulatory framework, which will have a significant impact on the provision of payment services. In particular, the Revised Payment Services Directive (DSP2) creates conditions for the provision of services by new players, removing barriers to innovation and fostering greater security, by imposing strong user authentication and the use of secure communication channels based on harmonised practices. At the same time, the habits of payment service users have also evolved, in an increasingly digital economy and with continuous technological advances. The ease of use of diverse solutions that improve the user experience quickly and safely is increasingly an indecible expectation of customers. In connection with this trend, in November 2017 the foundations were laid at European level for the launch of immediate payment solutions in the different markets, aiming at their interoperability and pan-European reach. In Portugal, in a few days, we will have available a national solution of immediate transfers, framed by Banco de Portugal in the Interbank Clearing System (SICOI). This solution will work in real time and will allow the execution of transfers in a maximum time of 10 seconds, for processing unit values up to 15 thousand euros (as a starting basis). Similar national solutions already exist in other countries. However, the trend will be in Europe for coverage to gradually become wider and the use of these solutions more widespread. This example illustrates a path of innovation and creates a significant margin of progression for the Portuguese community. The same is true in other quadrants, such as the use of cards with contactless technology. With the relaunch of the Forum, especially from today, we have a structure that will allow the development of joint work, in cooperation between various actors, for the benefit of the national community as a whole and the interests of customers, which is very pleased with Banco de Portugal. We will certainly have the possibility to identify areas of improvement, in terms of efficiency, in general or in specific sectors, represented here. With this perspective, I reiterate an idea left at last May's conference: we have well-founded expectations as to the results that can be achieved in this new phase, in the different areas of work that may be covered by the Forum. Banco de Portugal will ensure the further work and seek the involvement of all actors in an open and transparent way of ensuring that all actors are adequately involved in a model that will enable us to respond adequately to the various challenges that arise for us. Payment Systems Forum will work on promoting payments Electronic

Title: Intervention of the Governor, Carlos da Silva Costa, at the Great Banking Meeting of the Future
text: Intervention of the Governor, Carlos da Silva Costa, at the Great Banking Meeting of the Future 25 set. 2018 Closing session of the Governor of Banco de Portugal, Carlos da Silva Costa (i) Good morning It is a great pleasure for me to participate in this meeting dedicated to the Banking of the Future. The phenomenon of digitisation in economies and societies is irreversibly changing the behaviour and expectations of economic operators in various contexts. The financial system is no exception. Bearing in mind the permanent technological evolution, the change in payment systems and the discussion about the future of money, it is important to discuss what the future of banking will be in order to identify potential risks in advance and act on them in order to overcome or mitigate them. I will therefore seek in this speech in my speech to identify some of the challenges we face. The challenges facing the digital age In the face of exponential technological development, I begin by leaving a question to everyone in the audience: how did they stop banking activity in 10 years, 5 or even 2 years? The 2007 financial crisis and subsequent developments called into question the high levels of confidence and reputation enjoyed by the banking sector. There are even those who advocate that banking brands today suffer from an existential crisis, in a context in which brands are increasingly able to empathise with consumers are the great technological icons. (ii) Currently, and to have a point of comparison, Apple's appreciation in the market shareholder almost exceeds the valuation of the 48 largest European banks,(iii) while FinTech companies attract investment rounds of increasing size with valuations beginning to exceed billions of euros. (iv) In this context there are some issues that require reflection: (i) banks will be condemned to a progressive reduction in their size and their added value, becoming backoffices, or they could be players in the market in the digital age? (ii) Will banks be able to anticipate consumer needs? (iii) And how will the ecosystem in which the various agents interact? It is expected that the availability of large amounts of data (big data) and the use of this data through the use of artificial intelligence will become central to a customer's digital ecosystem, both financial and non-financial, in the future. Rather than offering a rearview mirror perspective, the digital financial ecosystem will provide consumers with a forward-looking, GPS view of their financial life in the future. The pressure to reduce costs and the push for simplification will create a new paradigm of organization in which it will be common for banks to rely on third parties for non-essential infrastructure and talent. Banks will thus become increasingly interconnected through a complex network of providers and third parties such as account information services and payment initiation services introduced by the new Service Directive. Payment (DSP2). (v) Customers will be offered, in real time, products segmented to suit their needs retail level, by promoting credit or savings products adjusted to the preferences of the financiers or the alysers (robo-advice), wealth management. (vi) At the same time, financial institutions will be able to improve the assessment of their clients' risk profile through an accurate and up-to-date view of their financial position, with the large-scale use of credit scoring models. Recent research shows that simple variables in the digital footprint have a predictive power that can match, or sometimes exceed, traditional credit assessments bureaus. (vii) This may represent an opportunity to increase financial inclusion in developing countries as well as significantly expand the customer base. Investment by companies such as Google in India through the expansion of Google Pay is an example of this. (viii) On the other hand, the increased use of personal information, including the potential sale of anonymised aggregated data, by enabling perfect discrimination against consumers, could call into question consumer privacy by confronting society with a number of issues related to financial and technological literacy, cybersecurity and other broader philosophical issues. Is society willing to share every detail of its financial life by subjecting itself, in extreme cases, to potential manipulations? Recently, cases such as those involving Facebook and Cambridge Analytica have sensitized society to the risks associated with third parties' use of information shared on the internet. Can this case be understood as a challenge for society to establish a tolerance limit? Can we imagine ourselves in the future turning to a bank through apps as obsessively as we check social networks, or do we already do so today? And what are the implications of that? For incumbent banks this scenario poses a number of challenges, but it is also an opportunity. There are already several examples of banks that currently invest, cooperate and develop from scratch FinTechs, not seeing them as competitors but as complementary institutions or partners. This type of investment allows these banks to position themselves strategically to deal with the expansion of the big digital giants  commonly known as GAFAA (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon and Alibaba)  in the field of financial services. The extensive databases of the large digital giants, combined with a clear analytical and data processing capacity, are very relevant competitive factors vis-a-vis incumbents. While banks have in their favor the (re)knowledge of the public and the accumulated fiduciary capacity, their databases are geographically limited by comparison with those of technology companies on a global scale and are based on heavy legacy systems, which are characterized by little agility to treat large amounts of information in near real time. The banking business model as we know it will undergo profound changes. The design, cost of production and the margin of financial products destined for the mass market will require scale to make possible a fine segmentation of the market, diversify the risk and dilute the technological cost, becoming increasingly dependent on the supply of large players. Local banks without technological capacity and scale will thus tend to work: (i) as complementary networks of financial products in a distribution model (ii) and as financing networks for small-sized enterprises that require type of 'white mark', collecting and applying client funds; proximity relationship in risk assessment. As large fully digital players enter the market, and guarantee licenses to operate in free service provision, one begins to question how much will be needed as a wide network of branches as the one that still characterizes the banking systems of several European countries: (i) Will the rational counters be completely abolished, or will banks have to reinvent the (ii) Banks will seek inspiration in cafes, Apple stores or others to customer experience? redesign the concept of the counters in order to make the experience of going more enjoyable to the bank? (iii) How far can banks go without losing the confidence and credibility that are essential in the relationship with the client? From a risk point of view, there are still not enough empirical studies to assess the implications of digitising the banking sector. Some point to the existence of lower volatility, but also to an increase in systemic risk due to the increased use of artificial intelligence,(ix) while others argue that the use of technologies will tend to cause a faster and more widespread response to market indicators, resulting in increased volatility and prociclicalidade(x). The increase in the operational risk associated with increasing dependence on third parties is also reported, and the third party may be systemic in that several entities may be dependent on the same supplier or infrastructure. (xi) However, the most pressing risk is that of cyber-attacks, a topic of importance on a currently mainly associated with payment systems. (Xii) In addition, the extent of the geographical coverage promoted by digitization and the interaction between the different players will put new challenges in safeguarding the financial stability that will matter to be taken. The new architecture of the financial system and new business models require a multidisciplinary response from central banks and regulators, require new approaches, resources and skills and collaboration between countries, in order to maximize opportunities and minimize risks to society. It is very important that the competent authorities do not interrupt the ongoing dynamic, but to frame it and ensure, in particular: (i) the neutrality of regulation, (ii) fair and balanced treatment between incumbents and new entrants, as well as as between jurisdictions, (iii) the identification of new risks and challenges posed and the adoption of appropriate regulatory and supervisory conditions, (iv) and coordinated action between regulators and supervisors. These challenges are even more pressing in a context of rapid development of artificial intelligence. (xiii) On the other hand, the supervision practice should be given new tools, for example associated with the use of artificial intelligence, to accelerate the development and intervention (aka SupTech) (xiv) in a context of permanent expansion of the use of technological innovation applied to banking regulation and compliance (called RegTech). I would also like to devote some time to the theme of cryptocurrencies and the digital currency of central bank. Much has been said about the emergence of cryptocurrencies and the promises they carry, however reality has shown the existence of various risks that matter have gifts. (xv) The most promising of cryptocurrencies seems to be the application of the underlying technology (distributed ledger technology) in other applications, such as process simplification in the settlement of financial transactions. (xvi) On the other hand, the creation of a central bank digital currency is an innovation whose implications are only now beginning to be assessed, particularly from the point of the transmission of monetary policy. (xvii) And although the Central Bank european does not plan to issue a digital currency,(xviii) this discussion already begins to take place in other geographies not as far from us as Sweden. (xix) Conclusion I'd finish with a few final notes. As was very clear from today's session, the challenges posed to banking by digital are many, varied, relevant and are already in the distant future. To do this, banks need to act more and react less, reinventing their business model. However, for European banks, and particularly for Portuguese banking, digital is not the only major immediate challenge. In addition to topics that have been widely debated and which I will not address today  such as asset management and the fulfilment of much more stringent regulatory requirements (notably in MREL)  the disappearance of fragmentation in the European financial market also entails a number of challenges that we cannot ignore. The current European debate focuses on further harmonisation of rules by removing remaining national options and discretion, as well as on the use of Direct-implementing Community Regulations rather than Directives requiring national transposition. (xx) Such harmonisation is seen as necessary for cross-border financial integration, which enhances greater risk-sharing in Europe. The concomitant acceleration cross-border banking mergers will in this context be a long-term reality. This concentration process will be as fast as less prepared banks to compete in Europe. At national level, it will be important to assess what investment needs are and where to bet to compete in a market where the delimitation of the national border is less and less relevant, against the background of the discussion on the location of decision-making centres. text_original: Interveno do Governador, Carlos da Silva Costa, no Grande Encontro Banca do Futuro 25 set. 2018 Sesso de encerramento do Governador do Banco de Portugal, Carlos da Silva Costa (i) Bom dia,  para mim um grande prazer participar neste encontro dedicado  Banca do Futuro. O fenmeno da digitalizao nas economias e nas sociedades est a alterar, de forma irreversvel, os comportamentos e as expetativas dos agentes econmicos em vrios contextos. O sistema financeiro no  exceo. Tendo presentes a permanente evoluo tecnolgica, a mutao dos sistemas de pagamentos e a discusso sobre o futuro do dinheiro, importa discutir o que ser o futuro da banca para se identificarem antecipadamente potenciais riscos e atuar sobre os mesmos no sentido de os superar ou mitigar. Procurarei, assim, nesta minha interveno, identificar alguns dos desafios com que nos confrontamos. Os desafios que se colocam na era digital Em face do desenvolvimento tecnolgico exponencial, comeo por deixar uma pergunta a todos na audincia: como anteveem a atividade bancria daqui a 10 anos, a 5 ou mesmo a 2 anos? A crise financeira de 2007 e desenvolvimentos subsequentes puseram em causa os nveis elevados de confiana e de reputao de que beneficiava o setor bancrio. H mesmo quem advogue que as marcas bancrias sofrem hoje de uma crise existencial, num contexto em que cada vez mais as marcas capazes de criar empatia com os consumidores so os grandes cones tecnolgicos. (ii) Atualmente, e para termos um ponto de comparao, a valorizao da Apple no mercado acionista quase ultrapassa a valorizao dos 48 maiores bancos europeus,(iii) ao mesmo tempo que empresas FinTech atraem rondas de investimento de dimenso cada vez maior, com valorizaes que comeam a ultrapassar os milhares de milhes de euros. (iv) Neste contexto h algumas questes que requerem reflexo: (i) Estaro os bancos condenados a uma reduo progressiva da sua dimenso e do seu valor acrescentado, tornando-se backoffices, ou podero ser atores no mercado global na era digital? (ii) Sero os bancos capazes de antecipar as necessidades dos consumidores? (iii) E como ser o ecossistema em que os diversos agentes iro interagir?  expectvel que a disponibilidade de grandes quantidades de dados ( big data) e a utilizao destes dados atravs do recurso a inteligncia artificial se tornem centrais ao ecossistema digital, tanto financeiro como no financeiro, de um cliente no futuro. Ao invs de oferecer uma perspetiva de espelho retrovisor, o ecossistema financeiro digital fornecer ao consumidor uma viso prospetiva, um GPS da sua vida financeira no futuro. A presso para reduzir custos e o impulso para a simplificao criaro um novo paradigma de organizao em que ser comum os bancos dependerem de terceiros para infraestruturas e talentos no essenciais. Os bancos ficaro assim cada vez mais interligados atravs de uma rede complexa de fornecedores e terceiros como sejam os servios de informao sobre contas e os servios de iniciao de pagamentos introduzidos pela nova Diretiva de Servios de Pagamento (DSP2). (v) Sero oferecidos aos clientes, em tempo real, produtos segmentados  medida das suas necessidades quer ao nvel do retalho, atravs da promoo de produtos de crdito ou poupana ajustados s preferncias dos financiados ou dos aforradores (robo-advice), quer ao nvel de gesto de patrimnio (wealth management). (vi) Ao mesmo tempo, as instituies financeiras sero capazes de melhorar a avaliao do perfil de risco dos seus clientes atravs de uma viso precisa e atualizada da posio financeira destes, com a utilizao em larga escala de modelos de credit scoring. Investigao recente mostra que simples variveis da pegada digital tm um poder preditivo que pode igualar, ou por vezes ultrapassar, as tradicionais avaliaes de credit bureaus.(vii) Tal pode representar uma oportunidade para aumentar a incluso financeira nos pases em desenvolvimento, bem como expandir significativamente a base de clientes. O investimento de empresas como a Google na ndia atravs da expanso do Google Pay  um exemplo disso. (viii) Por outro lado, o maior uso de informao pessoal, incluindo a potencial venda de dados agregados anonimizados, ao permitir a discriminao perfeita dos consumidores, poder colocar em causa a privacidade dos consumidores, confrontando a sociedade com diversas questes relacionadas com a literacia financeiro-tecnolgica, a cibersegurana e outras questes mais vastas de cariz filosfico. Est a sociedade disposta a partilhar todos os pormenores da sua vida financeira sujeitando-se, em casos extremos, a potenciais manipulaes? Recentemente, casos como os que envolveram o Facebook e a Cambridge Analytica, sensibilizaram a sociedade para os riscos associados ao uso por terceiros de informao partilhada na internet. Pode este caso ser entendido como um repto a que a sociedade estabelea um limite de tolerncia? Conseguimos imaginar-nos no futuro a recorrer a um banco atravs de aplicativos ( apps) to obsessivamente quanto verificamos as redes sociais, ou j o fazemos hoje? E quais as implicaes disso? Para os bancos incumbentes este cenrio coloca diversos desafios, mas constitui tambm uma oportunidade. Diversos so j os exemplos de bancos que atualmente investem, cooperam e desenvolvem de raiz FinTechs, no as vendo como concorrentes mas sim como instituies complementares ou parceiras. Este tipo de investimento permite a estes bancos posicionar-se estrategicamente para lidar com a expanso dos grandes gigantes digitais  comumente conhecidos como GAFAA (Google, Apple, Facebook, Amazon e Alibaba)  no domnio dos servios financeiros. As extensas bases de dados dos grandes gigantes digitais, aliadas a uma assinalvel capacidade analtica e de processamento de dados, constituem fatores competitivos muito relevantes face aos incumbentes. Embora os bancos tenham a seu favor o (re)conhecimento do pblico e a capacidade fiduciria acumulada, as suas bases de dados so limitadas geograficamente por comparao com as das empresas tecnolgicas  escala global e assentam em sistemas legacy pesados, que se caracterizam pela pouca agilidade para tratar grandes quantidades de informao em tempo quase real. O modelo de negcio bancrio como o conhecemos sofrer profundas alteraes. A conceo, o custo de produo e a margem de produtos financeiros destinados ao mass market vai requerer escala para tornar possvel uma segmentao fina do mercado, diversificar o risco e diluir o custo tecnolgico, ficando cada vez mais dependente da oferta dos grandes players. Os bancos locais sem capacidade tecnolgica e escala tendero, assim, a trabalhar: (i) como redes complementares de produtos financeiros num modelo de distribuio (ii) e como redes de financiamento de empresas de dimenso pequena que requerem tipo de marca branca, recolhendo e aplicando os fundos de clientes; uma relao de proximidade na avaliao do risco.  medida que grandes players totalmente digitais entram no mercado, e garantem licenas para operar em livre prestao de servios, comea-se a questionar at quando ser necessria uma to vasta rede de balces como aquela que ainda caracteriza os sistemas bancrios de vrios pases Europeus: (i) Sero os tracionais balces totalmente abolidos, ou tero os bancos de reinventar a (ii) Iro os bancos procurar inspirao em cafs, lojas da Apple ou outros para experincia do cliente? redesenhar o conceito dos balces por forma a tornar mais agradvel a experincia de ir ao banco? (iii) At onde podero os bancos ir sem perder a confiana e credibilidade que so essenciais na relao com o cliente? Do ponto de vista de risco, ainda no existem estudos empricos suficientes para aferir quais as implicaes da digitalizao do sector bancrio. H quem aponte para a existncia de menor volatilidade, mas tambm para um aumento do risco sistmico devido ao maior uso de inteligncia artificial,(ix) enquanto outros sustentam que o uso das tecnologias tender a provocar uma resposta mais rpida e generalizada a indicadores de mercado, resultando numa maior volatilidade e prociclicalidade(x). O aumento do risco operacional associado  cada vez maior dependncia de terceiros  tambm referido, podendo este assumir um carcter sistmico na medida em que diversas entidades podem estar dependentes de um mesmo fornecedor ou infraestrutura. (xi) Contudo, o risco mais premente  o de ciberataques, tema de importncia  escala global, atualmente maioritariamente associado a sistemas de pagamentos.(xii) Alm disso, a extenso da cobertura geogrfica promovida pela digitalizao e a interao entre os diferentes players vai colocar novos desafios no que toca  salvaguarda da estabilidade financeira que importar acautelar. A nova arquitetura do sistema financeiro e os novos modelos de negcio obrigam a uma resposta multidisciplinar dos bancos centrais e reguladores, exigem novas abordagens, recursos e competncias e colaborao entre pases, de forma a maximizar as oportunidades e a minimizar os riscos para a sociedade.  muito importante que as autoridades competentes no interrompam a dinmica em curso, mas a enquadrem e assegurem, nomeadamente: (i) a neutralidade da regulao, (ii) o tratamento justo e equilibrado entre incumbentes e novos participantes, bem como entre jurisdies, (iii) a identificao de novos riscos e desafios colocados e a adoo de iniciativas regulatrias e de superviso adequadas, (iv) e uma atuao coordenada entre reguladores e supervisores. Estes desafios so ainda mais prementes num contexto de rpido desenvolvimento de inteligncia artificial. (xiii) Por outro lado, a prtica de superviso dever dotar-se de novas ferramentas, por exemplo associadas ao uso de inteligncia artificial, para acelerar a deteo e interveno (vulgo SupTech) (xiv) num contexto de permanente expanso da utilizao de inovao tecnolgica aplicada  regulao e compliance bancria (denominada de RegTech). Gostaria, ainda, de dedicar algum tempo ao tema das criptomoedas e  moeda digital de banco central. Muito se tem dito sobre o surgimento das criptomoedas e as promessas que as mesmas comportam, contudo a realidade tem mostrado a existncia de vrios riscos que importa ter presentes. (xv) O mais promissor das criptomoedas parecer ser a aplicao da tecnologia subjacente (distributed ledger technology) noutras aplicaes, como a simplificao de processos administrativos na liquidao de transaes financeiras. (xvi) J a criao de uma moeda digital de banco central constitui uma inovao cujas implicaes s agora comeam a ser objeto de avaliao, nomeadamente do ponto de vista da transmisso da poltica monetria. (xvii) E muito embora o Banco Central Europeu no planeie a emisso de uma moeda do tipo digital,(xviii) esta discusso comea j a ter lugar em outras geografias no to afastadas de ns como a Sucia. (xix) Concluso Concluiria com algumas notas finais. Como resultou de forma muito clara da sesso de hoje, os desafios colocados  banca pelo digital so muitos, variados, relevantes e colocam-se j hoje e no num futuro distante. Para tal,  necessrio que os bancos ajam mais e reajam menos, reinventando o seu modelo de negcio. Contudo, para os bancos europeus, e muito particularmente para a banca portuguesa, o digital no  o nico grande desafio imediato. Para alm de temas que tm sido amplamente debatidos e que hoje no vou abordar  como sejam a gesto dos ativos no produtivos em balano e o cumprimento de requisitos regulatrios muito mais exigentes (designadamente em sede de MREL)  tambm o desaparecimento da fragmentao no mercado financeiro europeu comporta um conjunto de desafios que no podemos ignorar. O debate europeu atual centra-se na maior harmonizao de regras atravs da remoo de opes e discricionariedade nacional que ainda subsiste, bem como no recurso a Regulamentos Comunitrios de aplicao direta em vez de Diretivas que requerem transposio nacional. (xx) Tal harmonizao  vista como necessria  integrao financeira transfronteiria, potenciadora de maior partilha de risco no espao europeu. A concomitante acelerao de movimentos de concentrao bancria transfronteiria ser neste contexto uma realidade a prazo. Esse processo de concentrao ser to mais rpido quanto menos preparados estiverem os bancos para concorrer no espao europeu. Ao nvel nacional, importar avaliar quais as necessidades de investimento e onde apostar para concorrer num mercado em que a delimitao da fronteira nacional  cada vez menos relevante, tendo como pano de fundo a discusso sobre a localizao dos centros de deciso.
