Title: Speech by Governor Carlos da Silva Costa in the panel "European Union and challenges of monetary, economic and financial integration" at the Colloquium in honor of Professor Antnio Barbosa de Melo
text: Colquio in honor of Professor Antnio Barbosa de Melo 60 years of the European Union: balance sheet and prospects May 5, 2017 Speech by Governor Carlos da Silva Costa in the panel "European Union and challenges of monetary, environmental and financial integration" 1. Framing The international financial crisis and the subsequent sovereign debt crisis in the have had a considerable impact on the global and European financial system and have made clear the need to reform regulatory and supervisory models. This has led to profound and unprecedented changes in international financial regulation and architecture and has joined forces globally. The European Union has played a major role in this area by introducing extensive reforms in the financial sector, with emphasis on the implementation of the European System of Financial Supervision (based on a sector-based supervisory model and a cross-cutting entity with macroprudential competences) and, above all, for the establishment of the Banking Union. This process Implied: (i) on the one hand, the definition of a model for the shared exercise of regulatory and supervisory powers, with a European institutional framework and a common framework of rules, procedures and practices; and (ii) On the other hand, a redefinition of the perimeter of competences and the role of national regulatory, supervisory and resolution authorities. 2. Regulation and supervision The current framework for financial regulation and supervision of the European Union can be illustrated by the following diagram: Financial regulation and supervision in the European Union While the institutional and regulatory framework in which European banks currently operate is undeniably more robust than before the crisis erupted, there remain inmere limitations and challenges that need urgent action. In view of the multiplicity of national and supranational authorities working in the legislative, regulatory, supervisory and resolution fields, it is essential to ensure effective coordination and articulation of the legislative, regulatory, supervisory and resolution areas. As shown in the diagram above, regulation in the European Union is exercised at various levels, with diverse powers and attributes. Member States participate at all these levels, with different degrees of intensity and with different interlocutors. Supervision, both at macro and microprudential level, also involves a myriad of institutions and actors. It is important to promote the efficient and coherent functioning of this whole structure, minimizing gaps, conflicts and redundancies. The experience gained in recent years has increasingly shown the importance of distinguishing regulatory functions from supervisory functions: between those who produce the regulation (the legislator/regulator) and who applies it (the supervisor). In other words, greater segregation and specialisation of these functions  the creation of Chinese walls  should be introduced, both at European and Member State level. The preparation of the regulatory framework, the detail of the regulation and the way in which it is interpreted should be the responsibility of the regulatory function, and it is for the supervisory authorities to carry out their activity in compliance with the defined regulatory framework. 3. Completing the Banking Union On the other hand, the Banking Union remains incomplete, with one of its three fundamental pillars missing: a common system for guaranteeing pits. In the presence of all the pillars  and the necessary safety nets  the link between sovereign risk and banking risk in the euro area can be permanently broken. The current framework shows clear limitations, in particular in terms of coordination, sharing of responsibilities and risks, powers and instruments, as well as the application of competition rules. There is currently an asymmetry between those who have the power to make decisions about an institution and who have responsibility for financial stability. National authorities remain responsible for financial stability, but their action is conditional on the decisions on supervision, resolution and enforcement of competition rules that are taken at European level. Maintaining the status quo could jeopardise the banking union project and its original objectives, namely: (i) safeguarding financial stability; (ii) the protection of depositors and taxpayers; (iii) improving the financing of the real economy. 4. Continue reflection on the regulation and supervision of the financial sector The European Financial Supervision System, its articulation with the Banking Union and national authorities, as well as national regulatory and supervisory models need adjustments that correct deficiencies and suit new realities. The reflection on the regulation and supervision of the financial sector must therefore continue, benefiting from the recent experience. Banco de Portugal is deeply committed to the discussion of these matters, of which are examples the White Paper on the Regulation and Supervision of the Financial Sector and the contributions to (i) the reflection on the Financial Supervision Model in Portugal, promoted by the Minister of Finance and (ii) the consultation of the European Commission on the revision of the macroprudential policy framework. The Bank has also been actively involved in the discussion of the legislative package presented by the Commission to complement the regulatory programme launched in the wake of the financial crisis. 5. Supervisory models in the European Union Looking at the situation of the various Member States, it is clear that, while acting in a common institutional framework, the paths to the performance of supervisory and resolution functions are very diverse. This results in very different institutional designs for the regulation and supervision of the national financial system, the articulation of which is not always easy and which, in some cases, will justify adjustments. 5.1. Microprudential supervision Microprudential supervision in the Member States of the European Union is mostly allocated to their national central banks. In the euro area, of the 19 competent national authorities that are part of the Single Supervisory Mechanism (SSM), 11 are central banks and in France the supervisory authority, although autonomous, is also in the central bank. Within the SSM, the ECB is responsible for the effective and consistent functioning of the entire integrated prudential supervision system and is directly responsible for significant credit institutions. In this context, supervision is based on common supervisory methodologies and tools, defined at Facility level. With the implementation of the SSM, the progress made in the creation of the Banking Union was very significant in a short period of time. However, progress must be made rapidly in the construction of the missing elements in the remaining pillars. 5.2. Macroprudential policy The European macroprudential institutional framework had as its starting point the report de Larosiere which led to the creation of the European Systemic Risk Board (ESRB) and continued to be built gradually, eventually resulting in a particularly complex architecture involving inmere entities: (i) first, the ESRB, with a broad coordination mandate covering the entire EU, with non-binding powers; (ii) Secondly, the ECB/SSM with specific macroprudential powers and binding powers, but limited to the scope of the Banking Union; (iii) Finally, 28 macroprudential authorities at national level, established in the last few years, either by granting a specific macroprudential mandate to existing entities or through the creation of dedicated authorities. The situation at national level is very diverse between Member States, not without the choice of the Macroprudential Authority, as well as the tasks and powers assigned: In 13 Member States (10 in the euro area) the Macroprudential Authority is its central bank; In 13 others (8 in the euro area) this role was assigned to a separate Committee and; In the cases of Finland and Sweden, the Macroprudential Authorities are their integrated supervisory authorities. This heterogeneity does not facilitate cross-border coordination of macroprudential poilytic. Furthermore, in a number of situations (e.g. Austria, the Netherlands, Spain and Letia) the Macroprudential Authority is not responsible for the use of prudential macroprudential instruments specified in the CRDIV/CRR and is authorities "designated" for that purpose or the supervisors of the Prudential. The EU macroprudential policy framework undoubtedly needs to be revised, including to reflect the consequences of the creation of the Banking Union, in particular the SSM. This review should take into account the following general principles: (i) ensure a clear allocation of responsibilities and instruments; (ii) allocate the use of pillar 2 to the competent authorities to the extent that macroprudential authorities are endorsed in sufficient and flexible alternative instruments; (iii) extend the coverage of macroprudential policy beyond the banking sector; (iv) preserve sufficient national flexibility to address specific systemic risks; (v) provide macroprudential authorities with sufficient powers and instruments; (vi) ensuring an extended composition of the ESRB, reflecting developments at Bank Union level. 5.3. Behavioral Supervision The banking union supervisory model does not include powers of behavioural supervision, and this responsibility falls within the national authorities, despite the tasks assigned to European supervisory authorities, which are fundamentally regulatory in nature. Both across the European Union and in the euro area, the allocation of national powers of behavioural supervision is distributed in a balanced way between central banks and integrated supervisory authorities. Whatever the institutional model chosen by the Member States for the exercise of behavioural supervision powers, it is important to: (i) avoid the existence of gaps in action; (ii) ensure clarity in the allocation of responsibilities; and (iii) align prudential and conduct assessments. In the years to come, behavioural supervision will also have to be prepared to meet the new challenges of the digital age, arising both from the widespread use of digital channels and from the marketing of innovative banking products and services. 5.4. Resolution At the national allocation of the resolution function too, the situation is heterogeneous within the European Union, but the option of cumulation of prudential supervision and resolution functions within the same authority prevails. In the 19 Euro Area Member States, it is noted that: In 17 there is accumulation of functions in the same authority, and in 11 of them, this cumulation occurs at the level of the central bank; Only in 2 (Slovakia and Finland) a total institutional separation of prudential supervision and resolution functions was chosen in different authorities. It should be seen that, in the model adopted in France, the national supervisory and integrated resolution authority is based in the central bank, but as an automation entity (modelo agency-within-an-agency). Whatever model adopted by the Member States, the regulatory requirements of the European Union, enshrined in brrd, in particular: (i) ensure operational independence and the prevention of conflicts of interest; (ii) ensure close functional cooperation in the development, planning and implementation of resolution decisions, either where the resolution authority and the supervisory authority are different entities either when the functions are exercised within the same entity; (iii) to reduce to a minimum the negative effects on financial stability and the adverse social and social impacts. With the entry into operation of the Single Resolution Mechanism (SRM), responsibility for the vast majority of resolution decisions has been transferred from the national to The European sphere to the Single Resolution Council (SRB). The SRB has mechanisms to ensure the mandatory and binding implementation of its resolution decisions relating to: (i) significant entities and groups; (ii) less significant cross-border groups; and even (iii) to the other less significant entities and groups where resolution requires the use of financing mechanisms. The full entry into operation of the SRM also entails the replacement of national financing mechanisms by a single financing mechanism at Union level. 6. Final considerations The architecture of European regulation and financial supervision is complex, involves the action of a multiplicity of entities and agents and presents gaps and limitations to which it is urgent to address. It is important, inter alia, to: i) Complete the Banking Union; (ii) revisit the regulatory framework; (iii) distinguish the functions of regulation and supervision; (iv) reassess and adjust, if necessary, national regulatory and supervisory models; (v) ensure better coordination and articulation of all entities involved.
text_original: Colquio em homenagem ao Professor Antnio Barbosa de Melo 60 anos de Unio Europeia: balano e perspetivas 5 de maio de 2017 Interveno do Governador Carlos da Silva Costa no painel Unio Europeia e desafios da integrao monetria, econica e financeira 1. Enquadramento A crise financeira internacional e a subsequente crise das dvidas soberanas na rea do euro tiveram um impacto considervel no sistema financeiro mundial e europeu e tornaram evidente a necessidade de reformar os modelos de regulao e superviso. Esta constatao conduziu a alteraes profundas e sem precedentes na regulamentao e na arquitetura financeiras internacionais e congregou esforos a nvel global. A Unio Europeia desempenhou um papel de relevo nesta matria, atravs da introduo de amplas reformas no setor financeiro, com destaque para a implementao do Sistema Europeu de Superviso Financeira (assente num modelo de superviso de base setorial e numa entidade transversal com competncias macroprudenciais) e, sobretudo, para a criao da Unio Bancria. Este processo implicou: i) Por um lado, a definio de um modelo de exerccio partilhado dos poderes de regulao e superviso, com um quadro institucional europeu e um quadro comum de regras, procedimentos e prticas; e ii) Por outro lado, uma redefinio do permetro de competncias e do papel das autoridades nacionais de regulao, superviso e resoluo. 2. Regulao e superviso O atual quadro de regulao e superviso financeira da Unio Europeia pode ser ilustrado pelo seguinte diagrama: Regulao e superviso financeira na Unio Europeia Embora o quadro institucional e regulamentar em que os bancos europeus operam atualmente seja inegavelmente mais robusto do que o que existia antes do eclodir da crise, persistem inmeras limitaes e desafios que carecem de atuao urgente. Desde logo, face  multiplicidade de autoridades, nacionais e supranacionais que atuam nos domnios legislativo, regulamentar, de superviso e de resoluo,  essencial assegurar uma efetiva coordenao e articulao das mesmas. Conforme demonstrado no diagrama acima, a regulao na Unio Europeia  exercida a vrios nveis, com poderes e atribuies diversificados. Os Estados-Membros participam em todos esses nveis, com graus distintos de intensidade e com diferentes interlocutores. A superviso, quer a nvel macro quer microprudencial, envolve tambm uma mirade de instituies e de atores. Importa promover o funcionamento eficiente e coerente de toda esta estrutura, minimizando lacunas, conflitos e redundncias. A experincia colhida nos ltimos anos tem vindo a evidenciar, cada vez, mais a importncia de distinguir as funes de regulao das de superviso: entre quem produz a regulamentao (o legislador/regulador) e quem a aplica (o supervisor). Ou seja, importa introduzir uma maior segregao e especializao destas funs  criao de Chinese walls , quer a nvel europeu quer dos Estados-Membros. A preparao do quadro normativo, o detalhe da regulamentao e a forma de a interpretar devem ser competncia da funo regulatria, competindo s autoridades de superviso exercer a sua atividade no respeito do quadro regulamentar definido. 3. Completar a Unio Bancria Por outro lado, a Unio Bancria permanece incompleta, faltando-lhe um dos seus trs pilares fundamentais: um sistema comum de garantia de depitos. Sna presena de todos os pilares  e das necessrias redes de segurana  se poder romper definitivamente o elo de ligao entre risco soberano e risco bancrio na rea do euro. O quadro atual apresenta evidentes limitaes, designadamente em termos de coordenao, de partilha de responsabilidades e de riscos, de poderes e de instrumentos, bem como de aplicao das regras de concorrncia. Existe atualmente uma assimetria entre quem tem poder de tomar decises sobre uma instituio e quem tem a responsabilidade pela estabilidade financeira. As autoridades nacionais permanecem responsveis pela estabilidade financeira, mas a sua atuao est condicionada pelas deciss em matria de superviso, de resoluo e de aplicao das regras de concorrncia que so tomadas no plano europeu. A manuteno do status quo poder comprometer o projeto de Unio Bancria e os objetivos que estiveram na sua gnese, designadamente: (i) a salvaguarda da estabilidade financeira; (ii) a proteo dos depositantes e dos contribuintes; (iii) a melhoria do financiamento da economia real. 4. Prosseguir a reflexo sobre a regulao e a superviso do setor financeiro O Sistema Europeu de Superviso Financeira, a sua articulao com a Unio Bancria e com as autoridades nacionais, bem como os prprios modelos de regulao e de superviso nacionais precisam de ajustamentos que corrijam deficincias e os adequem s novas realidades. A reflexo sobre a regulao e a superviso do setor financeiro tem pois de prosseguir, beneficiando das lies da experincia recente. O Banco de Portugal est profundamente empenhado na discusso destas matrias, de que so exemplos o Livro Branco sobre a Regulao e Superviso do Setor Financeiro e os contributos para (i) a reflexo sobre o Modelo de Superviso Financeira em Portugal, promovido pelo Senhor Ministro das Finanas e (ii) a consulta da Comisso Europeia sobre a reviso do quadro de poltica macroprudencial. O Banco tem estado tambm ativamente envolvido na discusso do pacote legislativo apresentado pela Comisso para complementar o programa regulamentar lanado na sequncia da crise financeira. 5. Os modelos de superviso na Unio Europeia Analisando a situao dos diversos Estados-Membros, constata-se que, embora atuando num enquadramento institucional comum, so muito diversificadas as vias seguidas para o desempenho das funes de superviso e de resoluo. Da decorrem desenhos institucionais muito dspares para a regulao e superviso do sistema financeiro nacional, cuja articulao nem sempre  fcil e que, em alguns casos, justificaro ajustamentos. 5.1. Superviso microprudencial A superviso microprudencial nos Estados-Membros da Unio Europeia est maioritariamente (em 18 pases) atribuda aos respetivos bancos centrais nacionais. Na rea do euro, das 19 autoridades nacionais competentes que integram o Mecanismo nico de Superviso (MUS), 11 so bancos centrais e, em Frana, a autoridade de superviso, embora autonomizada, est tambm no banco central. No mbito do MUS, o BCE  responsvel pelo funcionamento efetivo e consistente de todo o sistema integrado de superviso prudencial, sendo responsvel direto pelas instituis de crdito significativas. Neste contexto, a superviso assenta em metodologias e ferramentas de superviso comum, definidas a nvel do Mecanismo. Com a implementao do MUS, os avanos registados na criao da Unio Bancria foram muito significativos, num curto espao de tempo. Importa, no entanto, progredir rapidamente na construo dos elementos que faltam nos restantes pilares. 5.2. Poltica macroprudencial O quadro institucional macroprudencial europeu teve como ponto de partida o relatio De Larosire que conduziu  criao do Comit Europeu do Risco Sistmico (ESRB)e continuou a ser construdo de forma gradual, acabando por resultar numa arquitetura particularmente complexa e envolvendo inmeras entidades: i) Em primeiro lugar, o ESRB, com um amplo mandato de coordenao, abrangendo a totalidade da UE, com poderes no vinculativos; ii) Em segundo lugar, o BCE/MUS com competncias macroprudenciais especficas e poderes vinculativos, mas limitados ao mbito da Unio Bancria; iii) Por fim, 28 autoridades macroprudenciais a nvel nacional, estabelecidas nos ltimos anos, quer atravs da atribuio de um mandato macroprudencial especfico a entidades existentes, quer atravs da criao de autoridades dedicadas. A situao a nvel nacional  muito diversificada entre Estados-Membros, no sem termos da escolha da Autoridade Macroprudencial, como das tarefas e dos poderes atribudos:  Em 13 Estados-Membros (10 na rea do euro) a Autoridade Macroprudencial  o respetivo banco central;  Em 13 outros (8 na rea do euro) esse papel foi atribudo a um Comit separado e;  Nos casos da Finlndia e da Sucia, as Autoridades Macroprudenciais so as respetivas autoridades de superviso integrada. Esta heterogeneidade no facilita a coordenao cross-border da poiltica macroprudencial. Acresce ainda que, em diversas situaes (por exemplo, na ustria, Holanda, Espanha e Letia) a Autoridade Macroprudencial no  responsvel pela utilizao de instrumentos macroprudenciais prudenciais especificados na CRDIV/CRR, estando estes a cargo de autoridades designadas para o efeito ou dos supervisores prudenciais. O quadro de poltica macroprudencial da UE carece indiscutivelmente de reviso, incluindo para refletir as consequncias da criao da Unio Bancria, em especial do MUS. Esta reviso deveria levar em conta os seguintes princpios genricos: i) Assegurar uma clara afetao de responsabilidades e instrumentos; ii) Atribuir o uso do pilar 2 s autoridades competentes na medida em que as autoridades macroprudenciais sejam dotadas de instrumentos alternativos suficientes e flexveis; iii) Alargar a cobertura da poltica macroprudencial para alm do setor bancrio; iv) Preservar suficiente flexibilidade nacional, para fazer face a riscos sistmicos especficos; v) Dotar as autoridades macroprudenciais de poderes e instrumentos suficientes; vi) Assegurar uma composio alargada do ESRB, refletindo os desenvolvimentos a nvel da Unio Bancria. 5.3. Superviso Comportamental O modelo de superviso da Unio Bancria no comporta poderes de superviso comportamental, ficando essa responsabilidade no mbito das autoridades nacionais, no obstante as tarefas atribudas s autoridades de superviso europeias, fundamentalmente de ndole regulamentar. Quer no conjunto da Unio Europeia, quer na rea do euro, a atribuio dos poderes nacionais de superviso comportamental est distribuda de forma equilibrada entre bancos centrais e autoridades de superviso integrada. Qualquer que seja o modelo institucional escolhido pelos Estados-Membros para o exerccio das competncias de superviso comportamental, importa: (i) evitar a existncia de lacunas de atuao; (ii) assegurar clareza na atribuio de responsabilidades; e (iii) alinhar consideras prudenciais e de conduta. Nos prximos anos, a superviso comportamental ter tambm de estar preparada para enfrentar os novos desafios da era digital, decorrentes quer da generalizao da utilizao de canais digitais quer da comercializao de produtos e servios bancrios inovadores. 5.4. Resoluo Tambm a nvel da atribuio nacional da funo de resoluo a situao  heterognea no seio da Unio Europeia, prevalecendo, no entanto, a opo de cumulao de funes de superviso prudencial e de resoluo na mesma autoridade. Nos 19 Estados-Membros da rea do euro, constata-se que:  Em 17 existe cumulao de funs na mesma autoridade, sendo que em 11 deles, essa cumulao se verifica a nvel do banco central;  Apenas em 2 (Eslovquia e Finlndia) se optou por uma total separao institucional das funs de superviso prudencial e de resoluo em autoridades distintas. Refira-se que, no modelo adotado em Frana, a autoridade nacional de superviso e resoluo integrada est sedeada no banco central, mas como entidade automa (modelo agency-within-an-agency). Qualquer que seja o modelo adotado pelos Estados-Membros importa garantir as exigncias normativas da Unio Europeia, consagradas na BRRD, nomeadamente: i) Assegurar a independncia operacional e a preveno de conflitos de interesses; ii) Garantir uma cooperao funcional estreita na elaborao, na planificao e na aplicao das deciss de resoluo, quer quando a autoridade de resoluo e a autoridade de superviso so entidades diferentes quer quando as funes so exercidas no seio da mesma entidade; iii) Reduzir ao mnimo os efeitos negativos sobre a estabilidade financeira e os efeitos econicos e sociais adversos. Com a entrada em funcionamento do Mecanismo nico de resoluo (MUR), a responsabilidade pela grande maioria das decises de planeamento e de aplicao de medidas de resoluo foi transferida da esfera nacional para a europeia, para o Conselho nico de Resoluo (CUR). O CUR est dotado de mecanismos tendentes a garantir a execuo obrigatia e vinculada das suas deciss de resoluo relativas: (i) s entidades e grupos significativos; (ii) aos grupos transfronteirios menos significativos; e inclusivamente (iii) s restantes entidades e grupos menos significativos quando a resoluo exija a utilizao de mecanismos de financiamento. A entrada em funcionamento pleno do MUR implica tambm uma substituio dos mecanismos de financiamento nacionais por um mecanismo nico de financiamento ao nvel da Unio. 6. Consideraes finais A arquitetura de regulao e de superviso financeira europeia  complexa, envolve a atuao de uma multiplicidade de entidades e agentes e apresenta lacunas e limitaes a que  urgente fazer face. Importa, designadamente: i) Completar a Unio Bancria; ii) Revisitar o quadro regulamentar; iii) Distinguir as funs de regulao e de superviso; iv) Reavaliar e ajustar, se necessrio, os modelos de regulao e superviso nacionais; v) Assegurar uma melhor coordenao e articulao de todas as entidades envolvidas.

Title: Speech by Governor Carlos da Silva Costa at the 23rd Lisbon Meeting between the Central Banks of Portuguese-speaking Countries
text: XXIII Lisbon Meeting between the Central Banks of Portuguese-speaking Countries October 30, 2013 Intervention of the Governor of Banco de Portugal, Carlos da Silva Costa Sustained growth and economic development1 1 Prepared for presentation. Taking performance in the United States over the past 50 years as a benchmark, the potential for welfare gains from better long run, supply-side policies exceeds by far the potential from further improvements in short-run demand management Premio Nobel Robert Lucas, 2003 Presidential address to the American Economic Association 1. Introduction Mr Minister of State and President, Ambassadors, Governors, Ladies and gentlemen, I thank you all for being present at this 23rd Meeting of Central Banks of the Lusophone Countries. The longevity of the Lisbon Meeting is a testament to its relevance to the community of central banks in portuguese-speaking countries and Macao. This is a privileged occasion for evaluating and deepening our interconnections, providing a joint debate on topics of common interest, such as recent economic and financial developments, the cooperation aspect and the issues on the agenda of the imf/world bank annual meetings. My goal today is to talk to you about "Sustainable growth and economic development", which is undoubtedly a topic of common interest. With developed economies showing some signs of recovery and developing economies showing a slowdown trend, discussion of growth support factors is at the top of the international agenda. It should be in mind that, although economic growth alone is not synonymous with development, it is difficult to conceive of further development and higher levels of well-being without the underlying presence of a process of sustained economic growth. But what is sustained economic growth? Sustained growth is growth with scant fluctuations  which means sustainability of public debt and external debt  generating jobs and able to provide populations with higher levels of well-being in parallel with a reduction in social inequalities. 2. Luke's Paradox I propose to address the question of the factors supporting economic growth and development, starting from one of the biggest puzzles of the development economy, the so-called "Lucas Paradox": Why doesn't capital flow from rich to poor countries?. 2 2 Lucas (1990). Lucas' Paradox is nothing more than the realization that, contrary to the neoclassical theory, the flow of capital from developed countries to developing countries is relatively limited, although the latter have lower levels of capital per worker. Indeed, neoclassical theory predicts that, by the effect of decreasing yields, capital moves from more developed countries to developing countries, where the relative scarcity of capital in relation to work means that returns on capital investment are higher. Put another way, the policymakers of developed countries look to developing countries as profitable places to invest. But in practice, things don't seem to work that way. For example, from 1991 to the beginning of the current crisis, three-quarters of the world's flows of Foreign Direct Investment (EI) were captured by developed countries.3 3 World Investment Report 2009, UNCTAD. There are numerous studies of a theoretical and empirical nature that investigate the reasons behind the "Paradox of Luke". The main conclusions of these studies point to explanations associated with differences in the fundamentals affecting the productive structure of the poorest economies, such as the quality of human capital, macroeconomic, regulatory and fiscal stability and the quality of institutions. This means that, from the point of view of the economies competing on the international market, it is essential to create the conditions that make them attractive places to invest. From a broader perspective, I would say that countries should be concerned about creating conditions that attract mobile production factors at international level, such as financial capital, technology and human capital, and that, at the same time, they are able to retain the mobile factors of domestic production. Addressing the challenge of sustained growth and economic development therefore requires comprehensive, long-term strategies based on vocational education and training, a framework of stability and certainty and the creation of inclusive economic and political institutions. 3. Conditions for sustainability of growth and economic development Quality of human capital The focus on education and human capital is central as a source of economic growth and an explanatory element of the differences between countries in terms of growth trajectories and per capita income. This result is robust to several theoretical approaches to economic growth (namely neoclassical theory4, endogenous growth theory5 and technological diffusion theory6) but is also robust to a multiplicity of empirical approaches based on analysis methodologies and very differentiated samples7. In an illustrative way, it is worth noting the results of an empirical study by Sala-i-Martin, Doppelhofer and Miller (2004), which in growth regressions for 88 countries in the period 1960-1996 show that, among 67 explanatory variables, primary education is the most robust variable with a positive impact on gdp growth per capita. 4 Solow (1956), Mankiw, Romer e Weil (1992). 5 Lucas (1988), Romer (1990), Aghion e Howitt (1998). 6 Nelson e Phelps (1966) , Welch (1970) e Benhabib e Spiegel (2005). 7 Barro (1991), Mankiw, Romer and Weil (1992), Levine and Renelt (1992) and Barro and Lee (1993, 2001). In fact, it is easy to see that more skilled workers are more productive. Education facilitates the transmission of knowledge necessary for the adoption of new working methods and new technologies, but also increases the innovation capacity of the economy through the development of new ideas. One of the most extraordinary examples of success in terms of economic development based on a strategy of continuous improvement of the level of education of the population is the case of Singapore. Indeed, when Singapore became a sovereign republic in 1965, it was a poor island with rapid population growth, few natural resources, precarious housing and recurring conflicts between the ethnic and religious groups that made up the population. There was no compulsory school education and only a very small group of the population had secondary or university education. Today, Singapore is one of the richest countries in the world, with a GDP per capita of more than 50 000 USD (in 2012). In just one generation, it has become a modern economy, being one of the world's largest trading and transport platforms and a major international financial center. Currently, all children receive a minimum of 10 years of schooling and singapore's education system is referred to by several international organizations as one of the best in the world. The fact that the education system is forward-looking to the needs of a competitive economy is particularly important. Singapore's example illustrates the importance of investment policies in education but also of the benefits of linking these policies with vocational training and research and development. There are three interdependent areas that constitute the vertices of a triangle that determines the quality and sustainability of the development process. This triangle conditions the standard of specialization of a given economy and, in particular, productivity and innovation both incremental and radical. It must therefore be designed and driven according to the present and future needs of the productive system of a competitive economy. In a context of strong global competition, where scientific and technological paradigms are rapidly being broken, innovation has been a driving force for growing global factor productivity, economic growth and improving living conditions. This means that it is essential that knowledge production centers have the capacity to detect the present and future needs of the productive fabric and articulate with the business fabric. Framework of stability and certainty Investment is an intertemporal bet that requires confidence and stability in various forms: macroeconomic, financial, but also legislative, regulatory and fiscal stability. This means that instability and uncertainty have a depressing effect on investment and therefore on growth and economic development. It is therefore no wonder that, in contexts of high uncertainty about the economic environment, high tax incentives and/or other related incentives have to be used to achieve a positive impact on investment. The crisis has clearly shown us that: (i) High levels of public debt increase uncertainty, undermine the countercyclical use of fiscal policy and may undermine the credibility and effectiveness of monetary policy; (ii) A successful price stability policy is crucial for sustainable economic growth, but does not in itself guarantee financial stability; (iii) Financial instability can generate major imbalances and harm economic growth. The sustainability of public finances is a necessary condition for sustained economic growth and this, in turn, is crucial to reversing unsustainable public debt trajectories. In fact, the existence of very high levels of public debt increases the uncertainty and financing costs of the economy, penalising economic growth. In view of the high levels of public debt of the majority of advanced economies and the unfavourable dynamics arising from the ageing population, credible fiscal consolidation plans are needed in these economies to help reverse the upward trajectory of public debt and restore the confidence of economic operators. The high financial instability that was observed in the context of the crisis showed that price stability does not guarantee financial stability. It also showed that the objectives of price stability, financial stability and the sustainability of public debt are interlinked and cannot be seen in isolation. This has called into question the previously prevailing paradigm, which gave central banks the mandate to ensure only nominal stability. It is now globally accepted that financial stability must be an explicit objective of central banks. Financial stability is necessary for sustainable growth. In fact, volatility and uncertainty make it difficult to finance the economy, damaging investment and therefore the long-term economic outlook. Conversely, sustained growth is also key to preserving financial stability. A prolonged recessionary environment negatively affects the employment and financial situation of companies, weakening banks' balance sheets and creating risks to financial stability. We can reach similar conclusions on the relationship between stability of the financial system and sustainability of public finances: problems in the financial system may call into question the sustainability of public debt; unsustainable public debt trajectories negatively affect the financing capacity and stability of the financial system. The crisis in euro area sovereign debt markets and their impact on the conditions of access to finance by the financial sector are well illustrative of this relationship. Institutional framework In recent years, a vast economic literature has emerged that highlights the role of the quality of institutions in the different results achieved in terms of growth and economic development between countries. In fact, the framework of values, norms and institutions  called in the economic literature "social capital"  has a central place in economic development by enhancing the productive impact of physical capital, the qualification of the active population and the accumulation of technical and organizational knowledge. This framework includes laws that uphold the rule of law and guarantee property rights, but also those that define political institutions and interaction between the social partners. The framework of values, standards and institutions influences the confidence with which economic agents interact and the levels of security they place in the relationship with third parties. This means that it conditions the way the economy works and also the motivations of individuals. When there is no trust, there are transactions that do not take place. This point was highlighted by economist Kenneth Arrow, nobel prize winner for economics in 1972, stating that: "Virtually all trade transactions have in themselves an element of trust, certainly all that are repeated in time. It can be argued that the examples of weak economic development in the world are largely explained by the lack of mutual trust." In fact, a 2011 OECD study shows that mutual trust is greater in richer countries with lower income distribution inequalities. The countries of Northern Europe are the countries with the highest levels of confidence. A good institutional environment is generally synonymous with a transparent and impartial legal environment that protects the right to property, with low levels of corruption, with public services that ensure a level playing field for all and the participation of individuals in the activities that best fit their talents and competencies. Thus, the introduction of improvements in legal and judicial systems, in the execution of contracts or the adoption of laws establishing compulsory schooling are examples of areas in which relevant gains can typically be generated in terms of growth potential. For example, a recent study by Banco de Portugal (Julio, Alves and Tavares, 2013) indicates that, in Portugal, improvements in institutional performance towards convergence towards European best practices can increase The GIS directed to Portugal by about 60 percent. Institutions cannot be immutable, just as reality is not immutable. In particular, the ruptures introduced by technological progress (new products, new techniques, new forms of work organisation) require them to transform and adapt so as not to compromise economic dynamics and the process of economic growth. If the institutions, once adequate, do not reform and adapt, we can see a sharp deterioration in economic conditions and the economic decline of the countries or regions concerned. Institutional reforms must, however, start from existing social capital. The transposition into a given economy of successful institutional models in other countries is not synonymous with success. While there are lessons to be learned from the practices of other countries, in some cases, particularly in developing countries, it may be preferable to opt for "second-best" institutions that take into account the context in which they are included, including specific governance and market failures that cannot be quickly eliminated. In reforming, we must focus on horizontal power relations, where the social partners interact at the same level of responsibility and where institutions are a factor in promoting social capital and having broad participation in decision-making. These institutions are inclusive, as defined by Acemoglu and Robinson (2012). They promote the adaptation of societies to technological shocks through processes of creative destruction. On the contrary, societies characterized by extractive institutions, which oppose the process of self-regeneration, are based on vertical power structures and tend to impoverish as a result of their difficulty in responding to the shocks to which they are subjected. Indeed, in these societies groups extracting resources from the rest of society by being threatened by their power are vigorously opposed to transformations. A recent example of an extraordinary economic rise associated with the reform of political and economic institutions towards inclusive institutions is Brazil from the 1970s on. The Brazilian institutional transformation arose with the increase of civic participation in local administrations, as a result of the approximation of various social movements and trade unions, and later extended at the national level. Social empowerment was a key factor in the emergence of a government committed to the provision of public services, education and the creation of a level playing field for all. Since 1990, Brazil has seen rapid economic growth (average growth of 3.7 percent in the last two decades), average schooling increased from six years in 1995 to eight and a half years in 2009, and the proportion of population living in poverty decreased from 45 to 21 percent in the same period. More importantly, the process of transformation of institutions in Brazil occurred progressively without a radical revolution that often generates great destruction and suffering and whose success is not certain. 4. The importance of the financial system for economic development The development of the financial system is fundamental to economic development. According to Schumpeter, credit and financing are necessary conditions for the realization of the entrepreneur's innovative spirit, which determines long-term growth. In fact, an economy grows because of the savings it generates and the capacity it has to turn that savings into productive investment. It is precisely in channeling savings into investment that the financial system plays a key role. The financial system is indispensable for contacting agents with financing capacity and agents in need of funding. To illustrate the importance of the financial system, Alan Blinder (2013) likes it to the circulatory system of the human body: Finance is more like the circulatory system of the economic body. And if the blood stops flowing  well, you dont want to think about it. The financial system enhances the efficient use of savings through maturity transformation, risk pooling, pooling large amounts of funds and accumulating and monitoring information. Transformation of maturities Aphorizers and investors typically have very different time horizons. There are few deposits with maturities of more than two years and few investment projects with maturities of less than two years. Without the financial system, it would be very difficult to make the liquidity preferences of the borrowers compatible with the needs of investors. The financial system operates this transformation of maturities: on the one hand, it receives funds from the aphorizers, making them available within the agreed deadlines; on the other hand, it finances entrepreneurs by establishing repayment periods compatible with the profitability of their investments. Risk mutualisation In addition to the transformation of maturities, the mutualization of risk is also an important function of the financial system. The financial system has instruments and mechanisms to exchange, group and diversify risk. This function of the financial system is crucial for the implementation of high-return and risk investment projects and very long-term projects. Risk mutualization allows optimal allocation of resources. Investment choices and opportunities are expanded by relationships with a multitude of policymakers and investors and, at the same time, risk is distributed and assumed by more agents. Consequently, the financial system not only mutualizes risks but broadens the view on the possibilities of resource allocation and, in this sense, enhances a better use of savings. Aggregation of large amounts of funds In addition, the financial system has the ability to aggregate large amounts of funds from various players, which allows the financing of large-scale investment projects. Accumulation, production and monitoring of information Financial intermediaries process and accumulate substantial information on businesses and economic conditions, enabling better evaluation of investment projects and discrimination based on the risk of economic actors and projects. This means that financial intermediaries do professionally what no saver is able to do individually. This function has a fundamental importance in the efficient allocation of resources. The financial intermediation function of the banking sector presupposes a relationship of trust between banking institutions and their customers. It also presupposes confidence of the general public and investors in the banking system as a whole. The financial system therefore assumes a general interest, ensuring that resources are used efficiently and ensuring that the trust of those who give up their resources remains intact. It is therefore necessary to ensure a sound and resilient financial system with enhanced solvency levels, properly regulated and supervised. For this, strict supervision is indispensable and based on a regulatory framework focused on the essential interests of the system: maintaining confidence, using resources adjusted to objectives compatible with the financing needs of the economy. text_original: XXIII Encontro de Lisboa entre os Bancos Centrais dos Pases de Lngua Portuguesa 4 de outubro de 2013 Interveno do Governador do Banco de Portugal, Carlos da Silva Costa Crescimento sustentado e desenvolvimento econmico1 1 Preparado para apresentao. Introduo Senhor Ministro de Estado e Presidente, Senhores Embaixadores, Senhores Governadores, Minhas Senhoras e meus Senhores, Agradeo a todos a presena neste XXIII Encontro de Bancos Centrais dos Pases Lusfonos. Trata-se de uma ocasio privilegiada de avaliao e aprofundamento das nossas interligaes, proporcionando um debate conjunto sobre temas de interesse comum, como a evoluo econmica e financeira recente, a vertente de cooperao e os assuntos da agenda das reunies anuais do FMI/Banco Mundial. O meu objetivo hoje  falar-vos sobre Crescimento sustentado e desenvolvimento econmico, que  sem dvida um tema de interesse comum. Com as economias desenvolvidas a darem alguns sinais de recuperao e as economias em desenvolvimento a evidenciarem uma tendncia de desacelerao, a discusso dos fatores de sustentao do crescimento est no topo da agenda internacional. Importa ter presente que, embora crescimento econmico por si s no seja sinnimo de desenvolvimento,  difcil conceber maior desenvolvimento e maiores nveis de bem-estar sem a presena subjacente de um processo de crescimento econmico sustentado. Mas o que  um crescimento econmico sustentado? Um crescimento sustentado  um crescimento com flutuaes pouco acentuadas  o que significa sustentabilidade da dvida pblica e da dvida externa , gerador de emprego e capaz de proporcionar s populaes nveis de bem-estar superiores em paralelo com uma reduo das desigualdades sociais. 2. O Paradoxo de Lucas Proponho abordar a questo dos fatores de sustentao do crescimento e do desenvolvimento econmico, partindo de um dos maiores puzzles da economia do desenvolvimento, o chamado Paradoxo de Lucas: Why doesnt capital flow from rich to poor countries?. 2 2 Lucas (1990). O Paradoxo de Lucas no  mais do que a constatao de que, ao contrrio do previsto pela teoria neoclssica, o fluxo de capitais dos pases desenvolvidos para os pases em desenvolvimento  relativamente limitado, apesar de estes ltimos terem nveis mais baixos de capital por trabalhador. Efetivamente, a teoria neoclssica prev que, por via do efeito dos rendimentos decrescentes, o capital se mova dos pases mais desenvolvidos para os pases em desenvolvimento, onde a escassez relativa de capital em relao ao trabalho significa que os retornos do investimento em capital so mais elevados. Dito de outra forma, os aforradores dos pases desenvolvidos olham para os pases em desenvolvimento como lugares rentveis para investirem. Mas, na prtica, as coisas no parecem funcionar desta maneira. Por exemplo, de 1991 at ao incio da atual crise, trs quartos dos fluxos mundiais de Investimento Direto Estrangeiro (IDE) foram captados pelos pases desenvolvidos.3 3 World Investment Report 2009, UNCTAD. Existem numerosos estudos de natureza terica e emprica que investigam as razes subjacentes ao Paradoxo de Lucas. As principais concluses destes trabalhos apontam explicaes associadas s diferenas nos fundamentos que afetam a estrutura produtiva das economias mais pobres, tais como a qualidade do capital humano, a estabilidade macroeconmica, regulamentar e fiscal e a qualidade das instituies. Isto significa que, do ponto de vista das economias que concorrem no mercado internacional,  fundamental criar as condies que as tornem locais atrativos para investir. Numa perspetiva mais abrangente, diria que os pases devem preocupar-se em criar condies que atraiam os fatores mveis de produo a nvel internacional, como o capital financeiro, a tecnologia e o capital humano, e que, simultaneamente, sejam capazes de reter os fatores mveis de produo nacionais. Abordar o desafio do crescimento e do desenvolvimento econmico sustentado exige, por conseguinte, estratgias abrangentes, de longo prazo, assentes na educao e formao profissional, num quadro de estabilidade e de certeza e na criao de instituies econmicas e polticas inclusivas. 3. Condies de sustentabilidade do crescimento e do desenvolvimento econmico Qualidade do capital humano A aposta na educao e no capital humano  central como fonte de crescimento econmico e elemento explicativo das diferenas entre pases em termos de trajetrias de crescimento e de rendimento per capita. Este resultado  robusto a vrias abordagens tericas sobre crescimento econmico (designadamente  teoria neoclssica4,  teoria do crescimento endgeno5 e  teoria da difuso tecnolgica6) mas  tambm robusto a uma multiplicidade de abordagens empricas que assentam em metodologias de anlise e amostras muito diferenciadas7. A ttulo ilustrativo, vale a pena salientar os resultados de um estudo emprico de Sala-i-Martin, Doppelhofer e Miller (2004), que em regresses de crescimento para 88 pases no perodo 1960-1996, evidenciam que, de entre 67 variveis explicativas, o ensino primrio  a varivel mais robusta com impacto positivo no crescimento do PIB per capita. 4 Solow (1956), Mankiw, Romer e Weil (1992). 5 Lucas (1988), Romer (1990), Aghion e Howitt (1998). 6 Nelson e Phelps (1966) , Welch (1970) e Benhabib e Spiegel (2005). 7 Barro (1991), Mankiw, Romer e Weil (1992), Levine e Renelt (1992) e Barro e Lee (1993, 2001). Na realidade,  fcil perceber que trabalhadores mais qualificados so mais produtivos. A educao facilita a transmisso de conhecimentos necessrios  adoo de novos mtodos de trabalho e de novas tecnologias, mas tambm aumenta a capacidade de inovao da economia atravs do desenvolvimento de novas ideias. Um dos mais extraordinrios exemplos de sucesso em termos de desenvolvimento econmico assentes numa estratgia de melhoria contnua do nvel de educao da populao  o caso de Singapura. Efetivamente, quando Singapura se tornou uma repblica soberana, em 1965, era uma ilha pobre, com rpido crescimento populacional, poucos recursos naturais, habitaes precrias e conflitos recorrentes entre os grupos tnicos e religiosos que compunham a populao. No existia ensino escolar obrigatrio e apenas um grupo muito reduzido da populao tinha formao secundria ou universitria. Hoje em dia, Singapura faz parte dos pases mais ricos do mundo, com um PIB per capita superior aos 50 000 USD (em 2012). Em apenas uma gerao, transformou-se numa economia moderna, sendo uma das maiores plataformas de comrcio e transporte mundiais e um grande centro financeiro internacional. Atualmente, todas as crianas recebem um mnimo de 10 anos de escolaridade e o sistema de educao de Singapura  referenciado por diversas organizaes internacionais como um dos melhores do mundo.  particularmente destacado o facto de o sistema de ensino estar orientado para o futuro, para as necessidades de uma economia competitiva. O exemplo de Singapura  ilustrativo da importncia das polticas de investimento em educao mas tambm dos benefcios da articulao destas polticas com a formao profissional e com a investigao e desenvolvimento. So trs reas interdependentes que constituem os vrtices de um tringulo que determina a qualidade e a sustentabilidade do processo de desenvolvimento. Este tringulo condiciona o padro de especializao de uma dada economia e, em particular, a produtividade e a inovao tanto incremental como radical. Por isso, tem de ser concebido e dirigido em funo das necessidades presentes e futuras do sistema produtivo de uma economia concorrencial. Num contexto de forte concorrncia mundial, em que os paradigmas cientficos e tecnolgicos esto a ser rapidamente quebrados, a inovao tem sido uma fora motriz do crescimento da produtividade global dos fatores, do crescimento econmico e da melhoria das condies de vida. Quer isto dizer que  fundamental que os centros de produo de conhecimento tenham capacidade para detetar as necessidades presentes e futuras do tecido produtivo e articular-se com o tecido empresarial. Quadro de estabilidade e de certeza O investimento  uma aposta intertemporal que exige confiana e estabilidade sob vrias formas: estabilidade macroeconmica, financeira, mas tambm legislativa, regulamentar e fiscal. Isto significa que a instabilidade e a incerteza tm um efeito depressivo sobre o investimento e, por conseguinte, sobre o crescimento e o desenvolvimento econmico. No , assim, de admirar que, em contextos de elevada incerteza quanto ao enquadramento econmico, se tenha de recorrer a elevados incentivos fiscais e/ou outros incentivos relacionados para se conseguir um impacto positivo no investimento. A crise mostrou-nos de forma clara que: (i) Elevados nveis de dvida pblica aumentam a incerteza, comprometem a utilizao contra-cclica da poltica oramental e podem minar a credibilidade e a eficcia da poltica monetria; (ii) Uma poltica bem-sucedida de estabilidade de preos  crucial para o crescimento econmico sustentvel, mas no garante, por si s, a estabilidade financeira; (iii) A instabilidade financeira pode gerar importantes desequilbrios e prejudica o crescimento econmico. A sustentabilidade das finanas pblicas  uma condio necessria para o crescimento econmico sustentado e este, por seu turno,  crucial para inverter trajetrias insustentveis de dvida pblica. De facto, a existncia de nveis muito elevados de dvida pblica aumenta a incerteza e os custos de financiamento da economia, penalizando o crescimento econmico. Atendendo aos elevados nveis de dvida pblica da generalidade das economias avanadas e  dinmica desfavorvel decorrente do envelhecimento da populao, so necessrios, nestas economias, planos de consolidao oramental credveis que contribuam para inverter a trajetria ascendente da dvida pblica e restaurar a confiana dos agentes econmicos. A elevada instabilidade financeira que se observou no contexto da crise mostrou que estabilidade de preos no garante estabilidade financeira. Mostrou tambm que os objetivos de estabilidade de preos, estabilidade financeira e a sustentabilidade da dvida pblica esto interligados e no podem ser vistos isoladamente. Esta constatao veio pr em causa o paradigma anteriormente prevalecente, que atribua aos bancos centrais o mandato de assegurar exclusivamente a estabilidade nominal.  hoje globalmente aceite que a estabilidade financeira deve ser um objetivo explcito dos bancos centrais. A estabilidade financeira  necessria para o crescimento sustentvel. De facto, a volatilidade e a incerteza dificultam o financiamento da economia, prejudicando o investimento e, por conseguinte, as perspetivas econmicas de longo prazo. Inversamente, o crescimento sustentado tambm  fundamental para preservar a estabilidade financeira. Um enquadramento recessivo prolongado afeta negativamente o emprego e a situao financeira das empresas, fragilizando os balanos dos bancos e criando riscos para a estabilidade financeira. Podemos chegar a concluses similares sobre a relao entre estabilidade do sistema financeiro e sustentabilidade das finanas pblicas: problemas no sistema financeiro podem pr em causa a sustentabilidade da dvida pblica; trajetrias insustentveis de dvida pblica afetam negativamente a capacidade de financiamento e a estabilidade do sistema financeiro. A crise nos mercados de dvida soberana da rea do euro e os seus impactos sobre as condies de acesso ao financiamento por parte do sector financeiro so bem ilustrativos desta relao. Quadro institucional Nos ltimos anos surgiu uma vasta literatura econmica que destaca o papel da qualidade das instituies nos diferentes resultados alcanados em termos de crescimento e desenvolvimento econmico entre os pases. Com efeito, o quadro de valores, normas e instituies  denominado na literatura econmica de capital social  tem um lugar central no desenvolvimento econmico ao potenciar o impacto produtivo do capital fsico, da qualificao da populao ativa e da acumulao de conhecimento tcnico e organizacional. Este quadro inclui as leis que sustentam o Estado de direito e garantem os direitos de propriedade, mas tambm as que definem as instituies polticas e a interao entre os parceiros sociais. O quadro de valores, normas e instituies influencia a confiana com que os agentes econmicos interagem e os nveis de segurana que colocam no relacionamento com terceiros. Isto significa que condiciona a maneira como a economia funciona e tambm as motivaes dos indivduos. Quando no h confiana, h transaes que no se realizam. Este ponto foi salientado pelo economista Kenneth Arrow, prmio Nobel da economia em 1972, ao afirmar que: Virtualmente todas as transaes comerciais tm em si mesmas um elemento de confiana, certamente todas as que se repetem no tempo.  possvel argumentar que os exemplos de fraco desenvolvimento econmico no mundo so em grande parte explicados pela ausncia de confiana mtua. Um bom ambiente institucional  geralmente sinnimo de um ambiente legal transparente e imparcial, que protege o direito de propriedade, com baixos nveis de corrupo, com servios pblicos que asseguram condies equitativas para todos e a participao dos indivduos nas atividades que melhor se adaptam aos seus talentos e competncias. As instituies no podem ser imutveis, tal como a realidade no  imutvel. Em particular, as ruturas introduzidas pelo progresso tecnolgico (novos produtos, novas tcnicas, novas formas de organizao do trabalho) exigem que elas se transformem e se adaptem, de modo a no comprometerem a dinmica econmica e o processo de crescimento econmico. Se as instituies, outrora adequadas, no se reformarem e adaptarem podemos assistir a uma forte deteriorao das condies econmicas e ao declnio econmico dos pases ou regies em causa. As reformas institucionais tm, no entanto, de partir do capital social existente. A transposio para uma determinada economia de modelos institucionais bem-sucedidos noutros pases no  sinnimo de sucesso. Embora haja lies a retirar das prticas de outros pases, em alguns casos, nomeadamente nos pases em desenvolvimento, poder ser prefervel optar por instituies second-best que levem em considerao o contexto em que se inserem, incluindo falhas especficas de governao e de mercado que no se conseguem eliminar rapidamente. Ao reformar, devemos privilegiar as relaes de poder horizontais, em que os parceiros sociais interagem ao mesmo nvel de responsabilidade e em que as instituies so um fator de promoo do capital social e de uma participao alargada nas tomadas de deciso. Estas instituies so inclusivas, tal como definidas por Acemoglu e Robinson (2012). Promovem a adaptao das sociedades aos choques tecnolgicos, atravs de processos de destruio criativa. Pelo contrrio, as sociedades caracterizadas por instituies extrativas, que se opem ao processo de auto-regenerao, esto assentes em estruturas de poder vertical e tendem a empobrecer em consequncia da sua dificuldade em responder aos choques a que so sujeitas. Efetivamente, nestas sociedades os grupos que extraem os recursos do resto da sociedade ao verem ameaado o seu poder opem-se energicamente s transformaes. Um exemplo recente de extraordinria ascenso econmica associada  reforma das instituies polticas e econmicas no sentido de instituies inclusivas  o Brasil a partir da dcada de 1970. A transformao institucional brasileira surgiu com o aumento da participao cvica nas administraes locais, em resultado da aproximao de diversos movimentos sociais e dos sindicatos, e posteriormente estendeu-se a nvel nacional. O empoderamento social foi um fator fundamental no aparecimento de um governo empenhado na prestao de servios pblicos, na educao e na criao de condies equitativas para todos. Desde 1990, o Brasil tem verificado um rpido crescimento econmico (crescimento mdio de 3,7 por cento nas duas ltimas dcadas), a escolaridade mdia aumentou de seis anos, em 1995, para oito anos e meio, em 2009, e a proporo de populao que vive na pobreza diminuiu de 45 para 21 por cento no mesmo perodo. Mais importante, o processo de transformao das instituies no Brasil ocorreu progressivamente sem que houvesse uma revoluo radical que frequentemente gera grande destruio e sofrimento e cujo xito no  certo. 4. A importncia do sistema financeiro para o desenvolvimento econmico O desenvolvimento do sistema financeiro  fundamental para o desenvolvimento econmico. De acordo com Schumpeter, o crdito e o financiamento so condies necessrias para a concretizao do esprito inovador do empresrio, a qual determina o crescimento de longo prazo. Na verdade, uma economia cresce em funo da poupana que gera e da capacidade que tem para transformar essa poupana em investimento produtivo.  precisamente na canalizao da poupana para o investimento que o sistema financeiro desempenha um papel fundamental. O sistema financeiro  indispensvel para colocar em contacto agentes com capacidade de financiamento e agentes com necessidade de financiamento. Para ilustrar a importncia do sistema financeiro, Alan Blinder (2013) compara-o ao sistema circulatrio do corpo humano: Finance is more like the circulatory system of the economic body. And if the blood stops flowing well, you dont want to think about it. O sistema financeiro potencia a utilizao eficiente da poupana, atravs da transformao de maturidades, da mutualizao do risco, da agregao de grandes montantes de fundos e da acumulao e monitorizao de informao. Transformao de maturidades Os aforradores e os investidores tm, tipicamente, horizontes temporais muito diferentes. Existem poucos depsitos com prazos superiores a dois anos e poucos projetos de investimento com prazos inferiores a dois anos. Sem o sistema financeiro, seria muito difcil compatibilizar as preferncias de liquidez dos aforradores com as necessidades dos investidores. O sistema financeiro opera esta transformao de maturidades: por um lado, recebe os fundos dos aforradores, disponibilizando-os nos prazos acordados; por outro lado, financia os empresrios, estabelecendo prazos de reembolso compatveis com a rendibilidade dos seus investimentos. Mutualizao do risco Para alm da transformao de maturidades, a mutualizao do risco  tambm uma importante funo do sistema financeiro. O sistema financeiro dispe de instrumentos e mecanismos que permitem trocar, agrupar e diversificar o risco. Esta funo do sistema financeiro  crucial para a concretizao de projetos de investimento de elevado retorno e risco e projetos de muito longo prazo. A mutualizao do risco permite uma afetao tima dos recursos. As escolhas e oportunidades de investimento so ampliadas pelas relaes com uma multiplicidade de aforradores e investidores e, paralelamente, o risco  distribudo e assumido por mais agentes. Consequentemente, o sistema financeiro no s mutualiza os riscos como amplia a viso sobre as possibilidades de alocao de recursos e, neste sentido, potencia uma melhor utilizao da poupana. Agregao de grandes montantes de fundos Adicionalmente, o sistema financeiro tem a capacidade de agregar grandes montantes de fundos oriundos de vrios aforradores, o que permite financiar projetos de investimento de grande envergadura. Acumulao, produo e monitorizao de informao Os intermedirios financeiros processam e acumulam informao substancial sobre as empresas e as condies econmicas, o que possibilita uma melhor avaliao dos projetos de investimento e uma discriminao em funo do risco dos agentes econmicos e dos projetos. Isto significa que os intermedirios financeiros fazem profissionalmente o que nenhum aforrador  capaz de fazer individualmente. Esta funo tem uma importncia fundamental na afetao eficiente dos recursos. A funo de intermediao financeira do sector bancrio pressupe uma relao de confiana entre as instituies bancrias e os seus clientes. Pressupe, igualmente, uma confiana do pblico em geral e dos investidores no conjunto do sistema bancrio. O sistema financeiro assume, por conseguinte, um carcter de interesse geral, assegurando que os recursos so utilizados de forma eficiente e garantindo que a confiana daqueles que lhe cedem os seus recursos se mantm intacta. , por isso, necessrio assegurar um sistema financeiro slido e resiliente, com nveis de solvabilidade reforados, devidamente regulado e supervisionado. Para isso,  indispensvel uma superviso rigorosa e assente num quadro regulatrio focado nos interesses essenciais do sistema: manuteno da confiana, utilizao dos recursos ajustada a objetivos compatveis com as necessidades de financiamento da economia. Title: Speech by Governor Carlos da Silva Costa - Symposium of the fiftieth anniversary of BCEAO (DAKAR, 5 and 6 November 2012)
text: SYMPOSIUM OF THE 50th ANNIVERSARY OF THE BCEAO (DAKAR, 5 AND 6 NOVEMBER 2012) THEME: "MONETARY INTEGRATION AND CHANGES IN THE INTERNATIONAL FINANCIAL SYSTEM: CHALLENGES AND PERSPECTIVES" SESSION 3: "CHANGES IN THE FINANCIAL SECTOR, ECONOMIC GROWTH AND FINANCIAL STABILITY: WHAT ANSWERS CAN CENTRAL BANKS GIVE?" Mr. Carlos Costa, Governor of Banco de Portugal: Ladies and gentlemen, First of all, I would like to thank Governor KONE and bceao for their invitation to participate in this high-level symposium on the occasion of the celebrations of the fiftieth anniversary of the BCEAO. I would like to congratulate the BCEAO on its anniversary and, above all, on the future project that the Bank itself represents. Yesterday's discussions on the central theme of the conference, "Monetary integration and changes in the international financial system: challenges and perspectives", highlighted not only the gradual but progressive evolution towards economic integration of the region, but also the role that the Bank played in the path of building real economic integration from monetary integration. The decision to focus the theme of this symposium on the future  and I congratulate Governor KONE on this wise decision  demonstrates that THE BCEAO intends to continue to play a catalyst role in this integration process. And to ensure the future, we must think and reflect on the future, a reflection that we will continue in this symposium. I also thank you for the invitation (to participate as one of the Governors of the European System of Central Banks), because it has enabled me to enjoy the benefits of implicit knowledge arising from presentations and participation in the debates. In this context, I am also very honoured to have been chosen to speak to you after and about Professor FIELDING's intervention. In this regard, I would like to underline the pleasure you have given me to read and listen to Professor FIELDING's communication. I don't just want to make some comments. I wish to deepen reflection by exploring the paths opened by their communication. There is a relationship of continuity between yesterday afternoon's discussions and those now in place. Professor FIELDING pointed out this by referring to the communications of Mrs GUILLAUMONT and Professor COLLIER, and I believe that we can sum up all two issues: the extremely important role we must play, on the one hand, in promoting and allocating savings to ensure sustainable development and, on the other hand, to creating a stable macroeconomic environment, where the intertemporal consistency of economic policies and, in particular, the role of monetary and budgetary policy are key factors. We have always been victims of a short-term vision. And in a short-term view, we focus our attention on aggregate demand as a growth engine. However, in the long run it is above all the savings that should be at the heart of the reflection, as well as the quality and size of the investment. I think it is very opportune for our President to quote Schumpeter in this regard, because if we want to act over time, we must think of phenomena that take into account savings and investment. The second dimension of yesterday morning's discussion is also very important, as it sets the bridge between the short and the long term. It referred to the need to create a stable macroeconomic environment. Indeed, the temporal dimension of economic policies and, in particular, the importance of ensuring a stable macroeconomic environment cannot be ignored from the point of view of sustainable development. I think there are four criteria for assessing the durability of a country's growth or development. First, gdp growth per capita. Secondly, employment, its evolution and the evolution of unemployment. The third criterion is the durability of external accounts, mainly current accounts, and finally, the fourth criterion relates to public finances and their sustainability. We can find periods in the economic history of a country where apparently everything is fine, even if we are aware that everything is wrong. It seems to be all right because there is an increase in GDP per capita or employment. But if we deepen our reflection, we are able to detect an unsustainable trajectory both on the side of external accounts and on the public finance side. It's a bit like the phenomenon of doping in cycling. It's all right until the moment we suddenly find out that there's something that doesn't add up. And then it is important to take into mind the sustainability framework as a whole. From the point of view of economic theory, we can admit the existence of an external deficit for a well-limited period, provided that the savings raised externally are allocated to productive investments that allow the subsequent repayment of their debt. We can also accept a public deficit, provided that the aim is to temporarily correct an aggregate demand deficit. However, there is always a tomorrow, and it is necessary to take into account the structural consequences that a temporary imbalance can generate. And Professor COLLIER showed this problem well with the example of countries that today, by possessing raw materials, have a very important public or private domestic savings. Consequently, the great responsibility is not to move forward on a path of consumption, because this will call into question the growth of GDP per capita in the future, which will have an impact on employment and, therefore, on the maintenance of the initial level of development, as we have created anticipations and consumption habits and, after the course of this period, it is very difficult to go back and return consumption to the level and previous patterns. The case referred to by Professor COLLIER and the case we are talking about show the importance of saving management: even if there is an abundance of savings, its management must be oriented towards the long term and should not focus on the short term and the ephemeral. If we focus on the ephemeral, forgetting the long-term effects, one day we will pay the bill. This leads me to another finding. It is always necessary to look closely at what is happening with internal savings, but also to the capacity and purpose of the investment. Virtuous investment must be effective and productive in two directions. It must be an investment of a directly productive nature and must be effective from the point of view of its profitability. It is that we may have a problem, or trap, on the side of the size of the savings, but we can also have it on the side of the allocation of investment. If the allocation of investment, even if it is public, is made, for example, with a huge imbalance between infrastructure and the productive investment that should follow, a situation will be reached that I have known, and I know, that is the situation that companies arrive to when the investment budget is not well managed. There are manufacturing facilities, but there is no longer money to buy machines and, consequently, start all the productive activity that would allow the repayment of the loans obtained or the recovery of the savings used. For all these reasons, it is necessary to ensure that the national system of allocation of savings and investment works optimally, allowing to affect the savings to investments with the best return. The second problem pointed out by Professor COLLIER is what relates to entrepreneurial capacity. This ability is not invented overnight. We do not have entrepreneurial capacity if we do not have a history of entrepreneurship based on a mentality, education and culture of innovation, risk, as well as an attitude of response and adaptation to the competitiveness challenges imposed by market rules. A framework should be promoted that favours entrepreneurship and, without entrepreneurial capacity, it needs to be generated, even if it takes some time and this process does not have significant short-term effects. Thirdly, we need mechanisms to channel savings for those who have entrepreneurial capacity and willingness to invest. This role belongs to the financial system. The financial system, in particular the banking system, guarantees the certainty of reimbursement by saverand, at the same time, the liquidity of its savings or, in other words, its availability within the time limits required by the saver. But at the same time, the investor cannot be forced to repay the financing within the time limits requested by the saver. The financial system plays a very important role here in the intermediation and transformation of maturities. On the one hand, it receives the funds from the aides, making them available within the deadlines agreed with them and, on the other hand, finances the entrepreneurs, requesting repayment periods compatible with the profitability of their investments. In a way, the banking system aggregates and transfers savings to investors. However, in addition to financial intermediation and maturity transformation, risk pooling is also an important role of the economic and financial role played by banks. And, as Professor FIELDING implicitly pointed out through the question asked, this function can never be ignored. The pooling of risk and an optimal allocation of resources stem from the multiplicity of policymakers and investors who establish financial relationships with banks. Investment choices and opportunities are expanded and, at the same time, the risk is distributed and assumed by more people. A relationship between an saver and an investor would have increased risks and would represent a suboptimal allocation of resources. Consequently, banks are necessary not only to pool risks, but also to broaden the field of view on all possibilities for allocating resources and, in this sense, are necessary to optimise the use of internal savings. And finally, we must understand that, from the point of view of those who obtain credit, banks are equally useful, since they do professionally what no saver is capable of doing. You will then tell me that I am talking to you about the banks, but not the capital markets. We must not be deceived, the capital market implies a level of knowledge of risks and financial education on the part of the aphorizers, factors that must be taken into account before pushing the aphorizers to investments in complex products and with a very high risk. First, it is necessary to develop the bond market and only then the stock market and other investment products. For example, if people are not used to the risks associated with the venture capital market, and if we encourage them to make too much progress in this direction, we will suffer a huge blow in the future, so that everyone will start to distrust the financial system and ultimately the savings capacity will be affected. There is useful social savings and useless social savings, even if it is useful for the person who owns it. If you have five thousand euros and put them in your safe, or in a book hidden in some corner, that money is very useful to you, but you are subtracting funds from the economy that could be invested. The role of the banking system is to make savings useful for the saver, the investor and society at large. If we generate mistrust of the banking system, we can provoke undesirable responses from savers, who will tend to take away from the circuit the savings that are necessary for investment. Thus, it is appropriate to ensure that confidence, ensuring that all savings enter the banking and financial circuit. Once constituted, the savings must be borrowed in order to have a social function. If it remains hidden in one corner of the house, it weakens aggregate demand and has no long-term counterpart on the supply potential side, which means it will have no impact on growth. All these reasons demonstrate the need for a banking system that is effective in order to ensure, on the one hand, the collection of savings and, on the other hand, the financing of investments. The effectiveness and optimal nature of the banking allocation mechanism work on the basis of balances between the interests of bankers, policymakers and investors.
