Our vast exclusive economic zone provides criticai biodiversity Services and has a huge potential for carbon capture, which can be an important source of revenue in the context of a well-functioning carbon emissions market. In addition to pricing carbon emissions or the use of natural capital, other policy instruments can also play an important (even if complementary) role. Im referring to environmental regulations, public investment in R&D and in green infrastructure, or even subsidies for clean energy. The key challenge lies in the fact that these policies have massive distributional consequences both within and across countries, and it is often the most vulnerable households and the poorest countries that suffer the most. The Gillets Jaunes movement in France and the protests in several countries following the rise in energy prices clearly showed there is no way around this. We need fair compensation measures to make sure decarbonisation policies are (politically) feasible. In addition to the right policies, if we want to extract the most from the opportunities offered by the imperative to decarbonise the economy,we must also be able to finance the transition. And on the topic of financing the transition I would like to share three very brief notes. The first note is about the volume of finance needed. To say the green transition implies a very substantial amount of additional investment is clearly an understatement as were talking about both public and private investment that needs to be deployed over several decades. The European Investment Bank estimates that in order to reach its climate target of a 55% decline in emissions by 2030, the EU will need additional investment of 2.1 % of GDP each year for the entire current decade. This extra-investment is both a challenge and an opportunity, since it will help innovation, growth and jobs. According to the IMF, a policy mix of carbon taxes and green investment stimulus could increase the levei of global GDP in the next 15years by about 0.7 percent and create around 12 million new jobs by 2027. The second note I would like to share is about the instruments that need to be used to finance the transition. Sustainable investment projects typically involve new technologies and significant R&D costs. They also tend to be capital intensive and have very long implementation horizons. The characteristics lve just mentioned are not properly dealt with by traditional bank loans and bonds, which are the predominant instruments in the European financial landscape We will definitely need other instruments as sources of finance such as equity, quasi-equity or venture capital. Again, this challenge can be an opportunity to substantially expand market-based finance throughout the EU and particularly in Portugal. My third and final note is about data. The green transition cannot be achieved by delegating to a central authority the extreme power of defining where we can or cannot invest. Achieving this goal has to rely on the capacity of those who invest being able to make the right choices. For this, investors need to be able to assess the risks, the expected returns and the ESG credentials of alternative investments. And allthis requires good data. Lack of data has been a key obstacle to implementing sustainable investment strategies and measuring progress towards a greener economy. To handle this obstacle, there are promising avenues, such as classification systems, labeis, harmonised reporting standards and, externai verification requirements. But it is also fundamental to ensure transparency and a broad coverage, otherwise, we might end up with a situation that was addressed in a recent article in The Economist. The Economist reported that dirty assets are heading into the shadows. This is because listed firms are selling their most polluting assets to meet their carbon reduction targets, but these assets continue to operate in the hands of more opaque organisations (who may even increase production!). To wrap-up this second topic, I believe its fair to conclude that the financial sector and financial policies play an irreplaceable role in the transition to a sustainable economy. That is because the energy transition will only be possible if the financial system is able to finance the tremendous volume of (green) investments, which will be needed over the coming decades. And for such financing to occur, the lending decisions have to reflect a fair assessment of environmental risks. This brings me directly into the third and final topic I would like to address today which is how can central banks help? Central banks: action drivers and boundaries! To start this third and final topic, I would like to share another quote, but this time from the former Governor of the Bankof Japan, Masaaki Shirakawa: ... central banks always have to be aware where they can best contribute to a sustainable economy. For me it is price stability and financial stability where central banks have a com para ti ve advantage. It is clear from what I said before that environmental concerns must be addressed, first and foremost, by the political authorities who conduct economic policy, because the root of the problem is essentially economic. However, it also goes without saying that the central banks need to contribute because their core missions are significantly affected by climate change and energy transition. One of the most important missions, if not the most important, is to preserve and reinforce financial stability, which is a pre- requisite for an economy to function properly, for all economic agents, be it individuais or companies, being able to take their decisions of consumption, saving and investment. For this to happen, central banks are required to promote the resilience of the financial sector throughout the transition towards a carbon neutral economy. This means that central banks must assess and deepen their understanding of climate-related financial risks in order to properly manage them. As far as the Banco de Portugal is concerned, this has been an important item on our agenda for the pastthreeyears. Afew months ago, we published a study that quantifies the Portuguese banking systenYs exposure to firms more sensitive to the transition to a low-carbon economy. The results suggest that around 60% of banks exposures to non-financial corporations are in climate policy-relevant sectors, especially in the construction and real estate sectors, and to a lesser extent in transport and energy-intensive industries. We are also upgrading our Prudential framework to encourage financial institutions to measure and price environmental risks. The ECB has set supervisory expectations on climate-related and environmental risks for the larger euro area banks and Banco de Portugal has extended these expectations to the less significant institutions, which fali under our direct supervision. Besides safeguardingfinancial stability and maintaining price stability, central banks can also use their analytical capacity to contribute to the transition to a more sustainable economy. Although its up to governments to implement economic policy, our mandate as a central bank, includes providing advice to the government on economic and financial issues. In this capacity, we have contributed to shaping multiple sustainable finance initiativesand we published research on the effects of climate change, in order to inform public policies and society as a whole. Concluding remarks Let me conclude by saying that veryfew global challenges were able to remain under the spotlight during the pandemic as the climate emergency. This means that climate emergency is here to stay, even if other events take the centre stage in the media and in our attention, as is the case of the situation currently developing in Ukraine. Bearing this in mind, we cannot afford to miss the opportunity of setting in motion a virtuous cycle of investment, growth and environmental sustainability. The big question that remains is to knowwhether we are willingto bearthe cost of the green transition when confronted with the need to pay (much) more for the carbon-intensive goods we consume? In other words, whether or not we are willing to change the way we live? One last word to say that after I started preparing the messages to share here today, I happened to listen to Vivaldis Four Seasons. As I was listening to it, I wondered whether he would have been able to compose such a masterpiece and to name it that way if he had lived three centuries later, in our time, given the impact of climate change. I stop here, leavingyou with this open question that combines hope with a dose of scepticism. Thankyou again for the invitation and I am happy to take any questions or comments you may have. Title: Speech by the Director Lus Laginha de Sousa at the ASWP/Serralves 2022 Conference  Smart Growth: the Role of the Circular Economy
text: Speech by Director Luis Laginha de Sousa at the ASWP/Serralves 2022 Conference - Smart Growth: the Role of the Circular Economy 06 MAY 2022 18 minutes Good afternoon to all. On my own behalf and on behalf of Banco de Portugal, I would like to begin by thanking you for inviting you to be here today. I would like to thank in particular the Smart Waste Portugal Association, in the person of its president, Eng. Aires Pereira. It is always a great pleasure to come to Porto and be in Porto. And when the visit includes a space like the Serralves Foundation, the pleasure is doubled. I know I have a particularly difficult challenge in this slot that has been assigned to me. And the difficulty results not only from the fact that we have already had a long day, but also from the fact that a lot of and very relevant information has already been shared by all the previous speakers. In addition, there is the difficulty that results from the fact that the interventions of the Central Banks are not exactly associated with the ability to make audiences vibrate. Under normal conditions, I would move on to the subject of intervention. However, before I get into the topic itself, let me share a few words that are an imperative of conscience. These are words to express deep solidarity with the Ukrainian people. And, through it, to all those who are denied the right to live in peace in their own country. This living in peace was something that we took for granted in Western Europe, but recent reality has shown that this assumption is not true after all. And bearing in mind this note of solidarity and the reasons that justify it, there is sometimes the feeling that everything else loses relevance in the face of the magnitude, not only of what has happened and is happening in Ukraine, but also in the face of the risks inherent to what may still happen. Abstracting ourselves from the War in Ukraine, to talk about other topics, almost suggests the image of the Music Band playing on the Titanic. However, even if it is difficult to abstract ourselves from what is happening in Ukraine, if we use the historical perspective, one of the lessons we can learn from this perspective is that, regardless of the difficulties of the situation, it has always been possible to find a way to overcome them, even if often at an overwhelming cost. It is in light of this focus on the future that I would like to believe that the notes I have to share with you can make a little more sense. And when we think about the future, the challenge of sustainability - and, in particular, the challenge linked to the environmental dimension of sustainability - occupies a prominent place, if not the first place, in terms of importance. An example of this importance is the fact that this challenge is often described as an existential threat. And to deal with this "existential threat", the so-called "green transition" has been increasingly universally accepted as the way forward. And that is why, especially since the signing of the Paris Agreement on climate change, just over six years ago, both the financial system and the Central Banks have been devoting increasing attention to this issue. To exemplify this growing attention, I can cite an analysis that the Economist magazine recently presented on the public interventions of central bankers. The results obtained indicated that 29% of the interventions made in 2021 contained references, more or less extensive, to the topic of climate change. For comparison, in 2007, the topic was mentioned in only 1 % of the interventions. However, this is a topic that is not limited to words alone. As with any economic activity, which requires financing to be developed, the green transition is not only no exception, but also brings financing challenges that have rarely found a parallel in economic history. I am referring to the order of magnitude, the variety and the complexity of that funding. And so it is also with great pleasure that I come here today to address the topic of "how to finance sustainability", framing it in this annual conference that is increasingly asserting itself in the panorama of ESG sustainability in Portugal. In order to try to make the best of the time I have spoken, I shall concentrate the messages on five main points, which are necessarily synthetic. In the first two points I will recall and highlight the essential features of what is the biggest problem that concerns everyone in the sphere of sustainability. I am referring to the impact of climate change. But I will also broaden the scope a little further to other topics that are evolving rapidly and consistently in the scale of concerns. In the third and fourth points, I will address not only what can be expected from the financial system, in the context of the profound economic transformation that is already underway, but also the role of public policies, including their limits. Finally, as a fifth point, I will also indicate what central banks - and in particular the Bank of Portugal - can do and are doing in terms of sustainability, ESG and climate change. Starting with the first point - the problem that most concerns us in the sphere of sustainability, precisely climate change. The set of analyses and projections that seek to scalp and predict the foreseeable impact of climate change and the implications for society and the economy is already very broad. One of the most in-depth angles of the analyses is the need to respond to the problem, a response that implies going so far as to reverse the secular trend of increasing greenhouse gas emissions and achieve so-called climate neutrality. And I open a parenthesis to say that there are already several countries, including Portugal, that have assumed 2050 as the year by which this goal of climate neutrality (or carbon, if we consider only CO2 emissions) must be achieved. Regarding the set of analyses I mentioned above, one of the documents that deserve to be highlighted is the most recent report by the IPCC (Intergovernmental Panei on Climate Change), which is the scientific entity of reference for climate change, operating in the orbit of the UN. Without underestimating all the wealth of information in the report, there are two elements, in particular, that justify an emphasis. The first of these elements is the concept of carbon budgeting - or climate budget. Science takes it for granted that, with regard to greenhouse gases, what is relevant is their accumulated concentration in the atmosphere. This means that it is the stock, rather than the annual flow of emissions, that is important in determining the pace and degree of global warming. Based on this scientific certainty, the report estimates that, in order to make the 1.5C temperature increase limit viable, this implies that the stock of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere could not increase by more than about 500 Gigatons (Gt) compared to the accumulated value until 2019. In other words, our common climate budget, on a planetary scale, is 500 Gt. If this threshold is reached, it would be necessary to ensure net-zero emissions to prevent the global temperature from rising more than 1.5C. With these data, the scale of the challenge is perfectly clear: at the current rate, which is approximately 59 Gt of net new emissions per year, the climate budget will be exhausted by 2028. The second element that I would like to highlight in the IPCC report is the broad approach that the report takes to ways of responding to the challenge. And this approach includes, for example, the removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, through ways such as traditional tree planting or various forms of carbon capture and storage. But it is also a crucial contribution in terms of a real change in individual behaviour patterns and in concrete ways of functioning in society and the economy. If this change happens, estimates point to the possibility of a 40 to 70% reduction in annual emissions by 2050. Clearly, the idea of circular economy, which brings us here today, fits into this change that is necessary to reduce GHG/GHG emissions. As if the challenge of climate change and the need to move towards a low-carbon economy were not enough, there is another topic that has been growing in importance and it is this topic that leads me to the second point that I would like to share with you. It is the issue of biodiversity loss. Biodiversity loss was considered the third largest global risk, in terms of ten-year impact, in the World Economic Forum's 2021 and 2022 Surveys. As a curiosity, the first of the risks in 2021 was that of a possible failure of climate action. The loss of biodiversity, in addition to contributing to global warming, also affects the ability of ecosystems to provide a set of fundamental services to the economy. This is the case of the supply of food and raw materials or the so-called ecosystem regulation services, such as pollination. Regarding pollination, it is an activity for which there is no technically viable substitute. It is estimated that the economic value of pollination could be 5 to 8% of the market value of global agricultural crops. Everything I have mentioned, as I believe will be easily understood, involves matters that are not yet familiar to central banks, but in relation to which the path is being made. And although the main approach of Central Banks is to look at reality with the filter of concerns, especially in order to identify potential risks to financial stability, there are several elements of this theme that can translate into relevant opportunities and benefits for a country with the characteristics of Portugal. It is enough, for example, to bear in mind that our vast exclusive economic zone (EEZ) provides effective biodiversity services to all humanity. And if so, these services can and should be translated into financial compensation. Within this same line of reasoning, and returning to the topic of climate change, the carbon capture potential of our EEZ can be a huge opportunity. Especially if the carbon allowance market becomes increasingly developed and comprehensive. This was, in fact, one of the guidelines that resulted from COP-26. A crucial way to counteract biodiversity loss is to foster the possibility that ecosystems can also be a source of income. And, by the way, that this yield is greater the healthier the ecosystems are. Finding ways to attribute income to those who preserve or increase natural capital and to charge the appropriate price to those who use and consume that same natural capital is what economic theory suggests should be done. In other words, and thinking for example about inland forest lands, if it is recognized that it is important to preserve them, it might be interesting to find a way to remunerate those who preserve these areas. Perhaps in return for a cost to be borne by activities or economic agents that consume natural capital. Conceptually, dealing with these questions is relatively simple. However, the operationalization of the concept is anything but easy and requires several conditions to be met. One of these conditions, perhaps the most important, is that we have the ability to measure natural capital. And with this note I would now like to move on to the third of the five points I mentioned at the beginning. This is the point concerning the financial system. More specifically, than can be expected from the financial system, in the context of the profound economic transformation that is already underway. This transformation is inevitable so that the economy can follow the path of the so-called energy transition, which is the path that can lead us to carbon neutrality. This means that if this path involves very broad and profound transformations, then we will inevitably be faced with the need to make large investments. Investments that, in order to be implemented, will have to be financed. There are several approaches that seek to quantify this challenge, but I will mention only two, made by reference entities, such as the EIB (European Investment Bank) and the IMF. In the case of the EIB, the estimate it makes is that the European Union will need additional investments equivalent to 2.1% of GDP per year if it is to reach the target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 55% by 2030. In the case of the International Monetary Fund, the estimates that the Fund presented, and which it even considered conservative, pointed to additional investments of 0.6 to 1% of global GDP each year, to achieve climate neutrality by 2050. And it is also important to take into account three elements in relation to these two estimates:  These are incremental values, that is, they add to the gross investments to replace productive capital, which would have to be carried out anyway.  It will be an effort to be sustained for decades.  Finally, when it comes to global values, this means that for some countries and sectors the effort will have to be substantially greater than for others. In the face of figures of this order of magnitude, public investment certainly has its place, but it must be accompanied by a greater volume of private investment. And this is where the participation of the financial sector becomes crucial, which is responsible for enabling and channeling this investment. This responsibility of the private financial sector, although it can and should be seen as a huge opportunity, has several implications. Since it is not possible to address all of them, I will highlight two that seem especially relevant to me:  First, the contours of the investment will have to be adjusted. Typically, sustainable investment projects deal with innovative technologies, involve considerable R&D costs, incorporate a high capital intensity and have very long realisation horizons, often over decades. These are characteristics that require instruments that go far beyond those made available by the traditional bank credit and bond markets. Equity, quasi-equity, venture capital and other less common financing instruments are needed, especially in Europe.  Secondly, it is necessary to ensure a good assessment of the risks and opportunities raised by the energy transition, in order to put the right pricing in financing. And for that, there is a long way to go in terms of data availability, quality, comparability and cost. Which are a critical element for a good assessment of the risks and opportunities that I mentioned earlier. This is one of the areas where there is latitude for intervention by public authorities, including central banks. And this reference allows me to bridge the gap with the fourth point that I wanted to share with you. It is the point relating both to the scope of action and to the limits of public policies. I believe that it makes perfect sense to start by referring to what is an irreplaceable role of public policies. It is the ability to deal with the so-called negative externalities. Understood here as the situations that result from the fact that the private cost of certain activities is below, or even much below, their true social cost. And for economists, climate change or the degradation of natural capital can be explained as a problem of externalities. The way to correct the problem of externalities, although it can be based on the functioning of the market, can only be ensured and led by the political powers, by the governments. Because they are the ones who have the legitimacy to act and they are also the ones who have the most effective instruments to do so. I am referring, for example, to carbon taxes or emission allowances. These examples should exist in parallel with stricter environmental regulation, but one that is well calibrated and does not unjustifiably penalise wealth-creating business activity. Governments can also play an important role in encouraging environmentally sustainable activities. For example, by making use - in a balanced way - of subsidies aimed at promoting "green" innovation or public investments in "green" infrastructure. Nor can we ignore the costs of these policies - which are very significant and unequal, and are already clearly visible. Therefore, to ensure that the transition is understood and accepted by citizens, governments will have to adopt redistributive policies that compensate those who are most affected by the climate transition. Be it families, regions or even countries. Despite the unavoidable role of governments and public policies, the dimension of the challenges of sustainability, climate change, biodiversity loss and energy transition requires that everyone feels summoned. And of course, the Central Banks could not ignore this issue. Therefore, I left the last note to share with you precisely to address the role of Central Banks. I would like to start by mentioning that, for some years now, the issue of sustainability, and in particular that of climate change, has entered the front door of the Central Banks. And he never left. The decisive moment for Central Banks to start looking very seriously at the issue was when it became clear that phenomena such as climate change are a major source of risk for financial institutions. Whether they are banks, insurance companies or asset managers and pension funds. If, to the risks associated with climate change, we add those related to the energy transition and the loss of biodiversity, we easily realize that all these issues affect economies and societies in a transversal and profound way. To that extent, they have a material impact on the mandate of central banks, in particular in the sphere of financial stability, but also in the area of monetary policy. The so-called physical and transition risks, associated with climate change, can compromise financial stability, first of all by inducing the devaluation of assets. Whether these assets have been directly financed by the banking system, whether they are given as collateral for loans, whether they are part of the portfolios of investment funds, or whether they are covered by insurance companies. In the specific case of Banco de Portugal, we have been allocating more and more resources - human, technical and financial - to respond in the best possible way to the mandate entrusted to us. Special priority has been given to two aspects:  One is to deepen knowledge about the economic and financial risks arising from climate change.  The other is to seek to assess the exposure and resilience of the Portuguese banking system to these risks. In terms of supervision, it is also appropriate to point out two initiatives:  One was the fact that supervisory expectations on the management of climate risks by banks were defined, expectations that were extended to all banking institutions operating in Portugal.  The other initiative concerns the climate stress test for the largest banks in the euro area, which is being prepared. In addition to the implications for financial stability and supervision, climate change and the energy transition also affect a set of macroeconomic variables that are fundamental to the framework in which monetary policy is conducted. In this context, what the Bank is doing is actively participating in the action plan defined by the ECB to adapt this framework (refining the models and methodologies underlying monetary policy). There are also two other areas in which central banks not only can, but must also contribute.  The first is the reduction of its own ecological footprint. Whether in the operational domain, like any other organization, or also in the management of its own asset portfolios. Or even in the mechanisms and procedures for issuing banknotes and coins, since we are one of the Central Banks that have a banknote factory, producing not only for Portugal, but also for Portugal. also for the outside.  The second area in which the Bank's contribution is also of great importance is the role of investigating and advising governments in the economic and financial fields. On this point, I would have many references to make. In relation to studies already published, to others that are in preparation, to the various technical contributions that have been provided, or even active participation in the project coordinated by the Portuguese Environment Agency, to assess the vulnerability of the national territory to climate change in the 21st century. But in order not to dwell on details, I invite all interested parties to visit the official website of the Bank of Portugal where they can find a section dedicated to these issues. The section has an easy-to-remember designation, which is precisely "Sustainability". And with this suggestion I come to the end of the five points I had to share with you. Before finishing, I want to leave, by way of conclusion, three very brief final notes. These are three points that stem from the fear that the impression may have been left that a large part of what I said in the course of my speech is not linked to the subject of this item of the conference. I remember that this theme was: "How to finance sustainability?" Therefore, the first note is to recover two expressions that are two of the "mantras" of the universe of corporate finance (in the sense of corporate finance). One of the expressions is that "the riskier the activity, the more solid the financing structure should be". The other expression is that "the level of return is associated with the level of risk". The conclusion drawn from the combination of those two expressions, although obvious, must be underlined. And it is in the sense that, in the face of the risks and opportunities that are associated with climate change, the energy transition and the loss of biodiversity, it is absolutely critical that ways are found to encourage access to capital. Despite the fact that this word, in Portugal, generates very negative feelings. The second point I would like to make is to emphasise that, although the financing needs that result from the imperative to face the risks I mentioned earlier are unavoidable, it is no less true that these needs can be substantially mitigated. Whether through an advance in the management of natural capital, or through the incorporation of externalities, negative and positive, in the prices of goods and services. Be also, and no less important, for the promotion of the circular economy, as this conference reminds us so well. The last note is what the Anglo-Saxons would say as "very cyose to the heart". It is to be emphasised that the many and very important decisions that the various economic agents will have to make must be based on solid and comprehensive data. There we certainly have a way to go, which is a common path for all our international partners. And this path is crucial to ensure that we are aligned with the phrase that appears in the stained glass window of the National Institute of Statistics and that faithfully translates this last note of mine. It's a phrase that says "in numbers, prosperity." And with this I end by thanking you once again for your attention and for the invitation that has been addressed to me to be here with you.
text_original: Interveno do Administrador Lus Laginha de Sousa na Conferncia ASWP/Serralves 2022 - Smart Growth: o Papel da Economia Circular 06 MAI 2022 18 minutos Muito boa tarde a todos.
