Title: Opening speech by Governor Mrio Centeno at the 1st Meeting of Portuguese Regulatory Authorities
text: Opening speech by Governor Mario Centeno at the 1st Meeting of Portuguese Regulatory Authorities 09 MAY 2023 04 minutes Your Excellency the President of the Assembly of the Republic, Prof. Augusto Santos Silva, Your Excellency the Minister of Finance, Dr. Fernando Medina, Hon. Madam President of the Mobility and Transport Authority, Eng.to Ana Paula Vitorino, Ladies and Gentlemen, I would like to start by thanking you for the invitation and congratulating the organization of this initiative that brings together all Portuguese regulators. Although we have responsibilities in markets of a very different nature, this is an excellent opportunity to discuss together the challenges of regulation in Portugal. Naturally focusing on the banking system, I could not fail to mention the enormous evolution of regulation at the international, European and national levels. The international financial crisis of 2007/2008 exposed several vulnerabilities and regulatory failures in the global financial system. It made visible the misalignment between the sophistication of the financial markets and the underlying institutional and normative framework of regulation and supervision. As we know, from the country's own experience, safeguarding financial stability requires robust and effective rules and institutions that preserve confidence and support the economy. For the stability of the financial system and for the good performance of our economy, it is essential that the financial system is solid and capable of facing adversity. It must have adequate solvency and liquidity, appropriate governance and management models, and be properly regulated and supervised. The promotion of financial stability is therefore one of our goals. Looking at the model of regulation and supervision of the financial system in Portugal, it is important to highlight the coordination and articulation work carried out in the National Council of Financial Supervisors. The cooperation between the Insurance and Pension Funds Supervisory Authority, the Bank of Portugal and the Portuguese Securities Market Commission has made it possible to create synergies and foster integrated regulation. Banco de Portugal, in its role as regulator and supervisor of the financial system, is disaggregated into different areas: prudential, macroprudential, behavioural, payment systems and the prevention of money laundering and terrorist financing. As a regulator, Banco de Portugal intervenes in the processes of discussion, production and amendment of laws and regulations, closely monitoring the work carried out in Portugal and internationally. He participates in the work of drafting regulations at the European Central Bank and the European Banking Authority. In its advisory activity, it also participates in the negotiation of legislation of the Council of the European Union and the European Parliament, playing a crucial role in the drafting of their implementing legislation. In its supervisory activity, it acts in an integrated and cooperative manner, in an increasingly harmonised European regulatory framework. Its sanctioning powers enhance its role as an important deterrent and contribute to full compliance with the regulations in force. However, the Bank of Portugal's action is not limited to a one-way action by the regulator-supervisor for the market. We understand that our role must be much broader. We bet on a bi-directional and sharing relationship. Being an "open-door" organization is a requirement for us to intervene with more quality and in a more timely manner, especially in the challenging context we are experiencing. Regular interaction with the various economic agents provides us with a deeper knowledge of the various dimensions of our activity. It allows us to improve our analyses so that they are useful for defining a strategy and policies that enable the country to overcome challenges. At the same time, it generates a greater public understanding of what we do. And this understanding brings credibility and confidence indispensable to monetary policy and to the safeguarding of financial stability. Banco de Portugal also has an irreplaceable role in promoting the economic and financial literacy of citizens, for example through the National Plan for Financial Education. Conscious and informed action by economic agents is also a form of market regulation. Our work has been crucial for people to have access to complete and timely information about the Portuguese and European economies and for them to better understand the main underlying concepts. Only then will they be able to make informed decisions and intervene, with full awareness, in the definition and evaluation of public policies. Basically, benefiting financial and macroeconomic stability. Fostering proximity and building trust is at the heart of the Bank's Strategic Plan Portugal, because we believe that we have a duty to contribute to the strengthening of the country's social capital. With this proximity, we promote public debate on the economy and on Europe. We continue to deepen information sharing and coordination between the different authorities. We are at the service of the country, contributing to the development of Portugal and the European Union. Today we are a Bank closer to citizens, companies, civil society institutions, education and research. To conclude, I would like to highlight that all regulators were actors in the evolutionary process that occurred in the last decade in regulation in Portugal. They were, therefore, decisive in shaping the Portuguese economy today. A more competitive economy with more informed agents. An economy equipped with a stronger institutional framework capable of acting. A more demanding economy, the result of the productive potential of younger generations who are increasingly educated and capable of taking Portugal to higher levels of socio-economic development. You can count on a Bank of Portugal capable of responding and contributing to an institutional framework that best serves the interests of Portugal. Thank you.

Senhor Presidente da Assembleia da Repblica, Prof. Augusto Santos Silva, Exmo. Senhor Ministro das Finanas, Dr. Fernando Medina, Exma. Senhora Presidente da Autoridade da Mobilidade e dos Transportes, Eng.a Ana Paula Vitorino, Minhas senhoras e meus Senhores, Gostaria de comear por agradecer o convite e felicitar a organizao desta iniciativa que junta todos os reguladores portugueses. Em simultneo, gera um maior entendimento pblico sobre o que fazemos. O Banco de Portugal tem ainda um papel insubstituvel na promoo da literacia econmica e financeira dos cidados, por exemplo atravs do Plano Nacional de Formao Financeira. Uma atuao consciente e informada dos agentes econmicos  tambm ela uma forma de regulao dos mercados. O nosso trabalho tem sido crucial para que as pessoas tenham acesso a informao completa e tempestiva sobre as economias portuguesa e europeia e para que melhor compreendam os principais conceitos subjacentes. S assim podero tomar decises informadas e intervir, com plena conscincia, na definio e na avaliao das polticas pblicas. No fundo, beneficiando a estabilidade financeira e macroeconmica. Promover a proximidade e reforar a confiana est no centro do Plano Estratgico do Banco de Portugal, porque consideramos que temos o dever de contribuir para o reforo do capital social do pas. Com esta proximidade, promovemos o debate pblico sobre economia e sobre a Europa. Continuamos a aprofundar a partilha de informao e a coordenao entre as diferentes autoridades. Estamos ao servio do pas, contribuindo para o desenvolvimento de Portugal e da Unio Europeia. Somos hoje um Banco mais prximo dos cidados, das empresas, das instituies da sociedade civil, do ensino e da investigao. Para finalizar, gostaria de evidenciar que todos os reguladores foram atores do processo evolutivo ocorrido na ltima dcada na regulao em Portugal. Foram, assim, determinantes para moldar a economia portuguesa de hoje. Uma economia mais competitiva e com agentes mais informados. Uma economia munida de um quadro institucional mais forte e capaz de atuar. Uma economia mais exigente, fruto do potencial produtivo de geraes mais novas cada vez mais educadas e capazes de levar Portugal a patamares superiores de desenvolvimento scio-econmico. Title: Closing speech by Governor Mrio Centeno at the presentation of the Digital Financial Literacy Strategy
text: Closing speech by Governor Mario Centeno at the presentation of the Digital Financial Literacy Strategy 10MAY2023 05 minutes Hon. European Commissioner for Cohesion and Reforms, dear Elisa Ferreira, Hon. Madam Deputy Secretary-General of the OECD, Fabrizia Lapecorella, Hon. Colleagues of the Board of Directors of Banco de Portugal, Luis Maximo dos Santos and Francisca Guedes de Oliveira, Hon. Speakers and partners of financial education initiatives, Ladies and gentlemen, The rapid and significant digital transformation that we have experienced in recent years has changed the way we contact, work or shop. The financial system has followed these changes with the digitalization of financial products and services and also with the emergence of new providers based on digital channels. Digitalisation has also brought about the dilution of borders. Consumers can access services that are marketed across borders, not all of which are subject to the same regulatory and protection framework. This is the case of crypto-assets, and the implementation of European regulation is expected soon. From the perspective of consumers, as a counterpoint to the benefits of convenience and speed, we have the risks of fraud. Almost every day we hear about social engineering scams. There is also the risk of incorrect use of new products, due to lack of knowledge of the characteristics or how digital financial products and services work. Digital channels are designed to exacerbate behavioral biases. The architecture of digital choice facilitates consumption and power decisions and the poorly considered use of credit. In a time of buy-now-pay-later online trading platforms , this is a particularly important risk. Recognizing these risks, it is important to know if Portuguese consumers are prepared for digitalization and financial innovation. The diagnosis of digital financial literacy in Portugal reveals that there is much to do in this area. In Portugal, many prefer to continue managing their personal finances without resorting to digital channels. For example, only half of respondents to the 2022 Digital Financial Literacy Survey of the Portuguese Population indicate that they use home banking or bank APPs to manage their personal finances. They are therefore unable to take advantage of the opportunities and benefits of innovation. Among those using digital channels, there are also significant knowledge gaps. Their attitudes and behaviors are not always the most appropriate to ensure digital security and the protection of personal data. The Strategy we are discussing today is therefore of the utmost importance to promote digital financial services, based on appropriate financial attitudes, behaviours and knowledge. With its implementation, we hope to make our consumers more resilient to fraud and cyberattacks; with a greater awareness of behavioural biases in accessing financial services on digital channels. And we hope to contribute to reducing the digital financial divide. For all these reasons, I thank the European Commission for having placed its trust in Banco de Portugal and for supporting the drafting of this Strategy. I also thank the OECD for its support in diagnosing digital financial literacy in Portugal and designing the Strategy. From an early age, the Bank of Portugal assumed financial education as a line of action. Thus, in 2008, the Bank launched the Bank Customer Portal and, in 2010, conducted the first national survey on financial literacy. Since then, there have been many financial education initiatives, always aware of the importance of financial inclusion and education, not only for individual financial well-being, but also for the stability of the financial system. The last two decades have been of collective learning, forced more times than we wanted, on how to deal with our financial dimension. The country, accused and harassed internally and internationally, understood that financial stability should be part of its self-esteem. Consequently, he values the achievements of this stability more than those of other areas equally relevant to national life. In 2017, the exit from the excessive deficit procedure or the reclassification of the Portuguese debt with an investment recommendation were more relevant to this self-esteem than the achievements that have always been in our collective imagination, obtained on the football fields of France or in European music competitions. Banco de Portugal cannot be separated from this collective feeling; In its areas of expertise, it has closely followed the trends and risks of technological evolution, eliminating regulatory barriers, ensuring technological neutrality and promoting financial education. The Bank has also worked to promote digital financial literacy with campaigns to alert about security precautions in the use of these channels. The concern with financial inclusion led the Bank to include as a priority in its Strategic Plan for 2021-25 the promotion of a medium/long-term digital financial literacy strategy. The National Plan for Financial Education for 2021-25 also establishes digital financial education as a strategic dimension of action. The three financial supervisors have made a commitment to implement in Portugal the financial literacy skills framework for the adult population of the European Union, prepared by the European Commission and the OECD/INFE. Of the approximately 560 skills listed in this framework, 114 are related to digital financial literacy. The Digital Financial Literacy Strategy for Portugal presented at this conference defines essential public policies to promote enlightened digital financial inclusion, which allows people to benefit from the advantages of digital financial services, while mitigating risky behaviors. Banco de Portugal is committed to the implementation of this Strategy and takes on this ambitious challenge. To bring this project to a successful conclusion, it needs to rely not only on its usual partners, but also on new partners, so that the initiatives are comprehensive and can reach the entire population. Everyone's collaboration is essential for the implementation of the Strategy and for achieving the ultimate goal of improving people's resilience and financial well-being. We are living through a unique moment in our history, one of the longest among European countries: the improvement of our school qualifications. Never before have so many families invested so much in their children's education. The obstacles posed by the transmission of education from parents to children are being overcome for the first time in Portugal. Financial inclusion is also crucial for this. If our institutions, public and private, policy makers and policy makers, are not up to this effort, they will not be entitled to the investment of families, sometimes with many personal sacrifices, and which is so necessary for the progress of the country. We have been able to overcome the constraints that the delay in literacy, among others financial literacy, placed on us, we cannot use this freedom, conquered with a unique effort in Europe, to destroy the dream that financial stability brings to Portuguese families. I understand this initiative as a contribution, a strategy to put digital and finance at the service of this noblest and highest objective, which is the convergence and integration of Portugal in a Europe that must show the world, also through Portugal, the example of inclusion and breaking with a past that, we know, it took us a long time to overcome. Thank you very much for the work already done, but even more for what still remains to be done, which we know is a lot.

Senhores oradores e parceiros de iniciativas de formao financeira, Minhas senhoras e meus senhores, A rpida e significativa transformao digital que temos vivido nos ltimos anos veio alterar a forma como contactamos, como trabalhamos ou como fazemos compras. O sistema financeiro tem acompanhado estas mudanas com a digitalizao de produtos e servios financeiros e, tambm, com o aparecimento de novos prestadores assentes em canais digitais. A digitalizao trouxe igualmente a diluio de fronteiras. No conseguem, por isso, tirar partido das oportunidades e benefcios da inovao. Entre os que utilizam os canais digitais, verifica-se que existem tambm importantes lacunas de conhecimentos. As suas atitudes e comportamentos nem sempre so os mais apropriados para garantir a segurana digital e a proteo dos dados pessoais. A Estratgia que hoje debatemos , por isso, da maior importncia para promover servios financeiros digitais, com base em atitudes, comportamentos e conhecimentos financeiros adequados. Com a sua implementao, contamos tornar os nossos consumidores mais resilientes  fraude e a ataques cibernticos; com uma maior conscincia dos enviesamentos comportamentais no acesso a servios financeiros em canais digitais. Desde cedo, o Banco de Portugal assumiu a formao financeira como uma linha de ao. Assim, em 2008, o Banco lanou o Portal do Cliente Bancrio e, em 2010, conduziu o primeiro inqurito nacional  literacia financeira. Desde ento, muitas foram as iniciativas de formao financeira, sempre cientes da importncia da incluso e formao financeira, no s para o bem-estar financeiro individual, mas tambm para a estabilidade do sistema financeiro. As duas ltimas dcadas foram de uma aprendizagem coletiva, forada mais vezes do que desejvamos, de como lidar com a nossa dimenso financeira. Em 2017, a sada do procedimento por dfices excessivos ou a reclassificao da dvida portuguesa com recomendao de investimento foram mais relevantes para essa autoestima do que as conquistas que sempre estiveram no nosso imaginrio coletivo, obtidas nos campos de futebol de Frana ou nos concursos musicais europeus. O Banco tem trabalhado igualmente na promoo da literacia financeira digital com campanhas de alerta sobre os cuidados de segurana na utilizao destes canais. A preocupao com a incluso financeira levou o Banco a inscrever como prioridade no seu Plano Estratgico para 2021-25 a dinamizao de uma estratgia de mdio/longo prazo de literacia financeira digital. Tambm o Plano Nacional de Formao Financeira para 2021 -25 estabelece a formao financeira digital como uma dimenso estratgica de atuao. Os trs supervisores financeiros assumiram o compromisso de implementar em Portugal o referencial de competncias de literacia financeira para a populao adulta da Unio Europeia, elaborado pela Comisso Europeia e pela OCDE/INFE. Das cerca de 560 competncias elencadas neste referencial, 114 esto relacionadas com a literacia financeira digital. A colaborao de todos  indispensvel para a implementao da Estratgia e para alcanarmos o objetivo ltimo de melhoria da resilincia e do bem-estar financeiro das pessoas. Os entraves colocados pela transmisso de pais para filhos da educao esto a ser, pela primeira vez, ultrapassados em Portugal. Tambm para isso a incluso financeira  crucial. Se as nossas instituies, pblicas e privadas, decisores de polticas e executantes de polticas, no estiverem  altura desse esforo, no faro jus ao investimento das famlias, por vezes com muitos sacrifcios pessoais, e que to necessrio  para o progresso do pas. Entendo esta iniciativa como um contributo, uma estratgia para pr o digital e as finanas ao servio desse objetivo mais nobre e elevado, que  a convergncia e a integrao de Portugal numa Europa que deve mostrar ao mundo, tambm atravs de Portugal, o exemplo de incluso e de rompimento com um passado que, sabemos, nos custou a ultrapassar. Title: Speech by Governor Mrio Centeno at the opening of the Banco de Portugal Conference on Financial Stability
text: Intervencao do Governador Mario Centeno na abertura da conferencia Banco de Portugal Conference on Financial Stability (apenas em ingles) 02 outubro 2023 04 minutos Good morning to everyone gathered here and for the ones joining us online. I welcome you today to the 2023 Banco de Portugal Financial Stability Conference. It is my pleasure to address such a distinguished audience and our esteemed speakers, who bring a wealth of diverse expertise to engage in deep discussion on matters crucial to financial stability. Todays conference is dedicated to the overarching theme of Financial stability: why does economic policy coordination matter?. In its 5th edition, our aim remains unchanged: to provide a platform for policymakers, academics, and practitioners to engage in substantive discussions on key topics. Todays discussions will cover monetary policy, fiscal policy, and financial regulation, but also climate change and digitalization. To kick start the discussion, let me point out linkages between monetary and macroprudential policies. A persistently high inflation may have disruptive effects on households and businesses. The recent ECB Governing Council decisions reflect this concern. High inflation introduces uncertainty into real incomes, requires a firm monetary policy to generate a more predictable economic environment. The distributional effects of inflation include a measurable transfer of real wealth among households. Savers who invest in fixed-income instruments see their financial positions erode, while debtors with fixed-rate debt witness a dilution of the real value of their obligations. For loans or mortgages with variable interest rates or short maturities, the sudden increase in short- term interest rates, driven by monetary policy, places a heavy burden. The current interest rates cycle with the largest increase in the shortest time - 450 basis points in little more than a year - has been demanding. When it comes to addressing the accumulation of risks to financial stability, the primary lines of defense are microprudential and macroprudential policies. National macroprudential policies may be designed to fine-tune the impact of transversal monetary policy. This can be achieved, for instance, through revised borrower-based measures. Furthermore, in situations where risks are sector specific, for instance in real estate markets, capital- based instruments remain at the disposal of policymakers. However, there is a delicate balance between the stance in macroprudential policies in the running up to the end of the financial cycle and the stance in which macroprudential authorities perceive that the risks are already materialising. Macroprudential buffers are built to encourage banks to retain profits, in tandem with the actions of microprudential supervisors. However, when risks are starting to materialize a more aggressive easing of macroprudential policies might be warranted, recognising that microprudential supervisors tend to adhere to more stringent policies. Numerous other key policy dilemmas confront policymakers, including new risks to financial stability arisingfrom bigtechs, fintechs, cybersecurity, and climate change. Todays financial landscape is evolving at an increasingly rapid pace, driven by continuous innovation, greater reliance on digital platforms, and the emergence of mixed-activity groups. It would be short-sighted to believe that regulating and supervising these global risks and international players at the national levei will suffice. We need international cooperation and coordination to set up a robust framework and avoid the possibility of regulatory arbitrage. We will touch upon this issue later today. While the prospect of cheaper and more accessible financial Services is appealing, there is an undeniable riskthat some new entrants might not be viable in the long run. Crypto-assets and Decentralised Finance, or DeFi, exemplify this risk. While proponents of crypto and DeFi talk about the democratisation of finance, it is not clear whether it will actually materialise, especially given the highly technical nature of this space. Recent years have witnessed extreme volatility in crypto-asset and DeFi markets. These volatile Products experienced an enormous surge in popularity during the Covid-19 pandemic, but proved to be unsustainable and, unsurprisingly, culminated in the collapse of several products. It is still unclear whether these highly volatile products are here to stay. What is clear, however, is that the European Union has not been idle. In June this year, MiCA, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, entered into force. This uniform EU market rules represent the initial step toward regulating this market comprehensively. But, as in bigtechs, we need further international coordination to address the stillfragmented regulatory landscape. We will discuss if and how this might be achieved. It still needs to be seen how these developments will affect the business model of traditional banks and their ability to provide credit. Regulators will have to strike a careful balance between bringing new players within the regulatory perimeter and avoiding stifling innovation. The principie of same risk, same regulation should guide these efforts. Whether effective supervision will be achieved through an entity-based approach, or an activity-based approach is still an open question. In todays world, climate transition and physical risks are paramount in the newfinancial landscape. In this regard, let me highlight three of the most indisputable conclusions. 1. The first one is that climate-related financial risks are global in nature. They transcend geographical boundaries and economic sectors, impacting us all. 2. Secondly, climate-related financial risks may be a source of systemic risk. 3. And thirdly, as a corollary, addressing such risks and their sources necessitates global coordination and cooperation. The scale and intensity of climate transformations and impacts and the transition to a low-carbon economy represent a paradigm shift for financial institutions, regulators, and supervisors. Against this background, the European framework for Prudential regulation and supervision applicable to banks is currently under discussion. At the microprudential levei, discussions evolve around the need for enhanced Prudential requirements that reflect the intrinsic risk profile of exposures and support the soundness of individual financial institutions. However, microprudential tools alone may not adequately address all dimensions of climate-related financial risks faced by the financial sector. Thus, macroprudential tools may be necessary and complementary to address environmental risks, as we are going to explore today. The complexity and magnitude of the challenges at hand demand a holistic approach by regulators and supervisors across the financial sector. From a financial stability point of view, it is crucial to ensure that measures taken do not lead to the transfer or accumulation of climate-related risks outside the purview of banking supervision. Allow me a quick word on the challenges faced by individual banks in the US and Swiss banking sectors earlier this year. While stemming from distinct causes, they underscore the importance of assessing the resilience of the broader banking system and the need for cooperation and coordination mechanisms. The enhancement of the regulatoryframeworkthrough the full implementation of the Basel III reforms will significantly contribute to the resilience and proper functioning of the banking system, which plays a pivotal role in sustaining economic growth. To conclude, inspired by this wonderful setting, I wish you all a highly productive conference filled with engaging discussions and the exchange of valuable insights. Thankyou.

Title: Note from the Governor on the Release of BPstat - Statistics online
text: Note from the Governor January 19, 2006 The Banco de Portugal is providing from today a new Internet online access to its Statistical Interactive Database, called BPstat - Estatisticas online. It can be found on the Banco de Portugal website ( ). BPstat - Estatisticas online is the outcome of a considerable investment by the Banco de Portugal to provide a web dissemination service for relevant statistical information about the Portuguese economy. Its main aim is to provide easy and quick access to the statistics compiled by the Banco de Portugal, as well as to statistics and economic indicators published by other institutions. This service offers a number of options and facilities allowing for very user-friendly navigation through the statistical information. This comprises:  Multidimensional analysis of the statistical information;  Design of tailor-made statistical tables according to needs;  Creation of favourites;  Subscription to an alert service, which flags the release of new statistical data on pre-selected domains;  Access to the metadata. Two of the main characteristics of this new service are quick and easy access to the statistical series and a very simple method for exploring the information. Significant efforts were made to provide methodological information about the statistical series, and this makes it possible for the users to know the main characteristics of the data and the methods used in their compilation, known in statistics terminology as metadata. This new system is at the cutting-edge of the very best that can be found world-wide in matters of access to and dissemination of statistical data. Obviously, it is for potential users to confirm the usefulness of the system. The Banco de Portugal does not regard this as a final product and will be improving it constantly, especially as regards the statistics made available. Any suggestions from users will therefore be extremely welcome. Vitor Constancio Governor of the Banco de Portugal

Title: Note from the Governor - Statistical Bulletin (January 2005)
text: Note from the Governor January 20, 2005 With the aim of improving the dissemination of the statistical information compiled within the scope of its responsibilities, the Banco de Portugal has introduced a number of changes in the information content of its Statistical Bulletin effective with the January 2005 issue now available on its website. I would like to call your attention to the Bulletins Introductory Note where these changes are explained in detail. The Statistical Bulletin of the Banco de Portugal has been published monthly since January 1995. In addition to the printed version, the Statistical Bulletin was made available beginning in October 2000 on the Banco de Portugals website ( ). Since then, the Banco de Portugal has ensured the regular publication of the Bulletin according to a pre-announced annual schedule, making it possible to have electronic access to the statistical data. In the course of the present year, a significant improvement is slated with the introduction of a new dissemination system of these statistics on its website. As of the present month, the Banco de Portugal will also make available the Statistical Bulletin in a CD-ROM version. It will include not only the image file of the Bulletin (in pdf format), but also the electronic files of all statistical series of the Bulletin (in csv format). An important feature of this CD-ROM version, particularly relevant in terms of archive and data search, is the fact that each monthly issue will include the data published in all previous monthly issues of the same year. Vitor Constancio Governor of the Banco de Portugal

Title: "The challenge of the absorption of structural unemployment in Portugal" - Speech by Governor Carlos da Silva Costa at the ACEGE Conference "A Christian Reflection on Labor and Employment in Portugal"
text: ACEGE Conference "A Christian Reflection on Labour and Employment in Portugal" January 30, 2014 The challenge of absorbing structural unemployment in Portugal Carlos da Silva Costa Governor of Banco de Portugal I would like to begin by saying that it is an honor and a pleasure to participate with Mr. Manuel Clemente and Mr. Antonio Pinto Leite in this reflection organized by ACEGE on work and employment in Portugal. My presentation is structured in four parts. A first part on some characteristics of the labour market that I consider necessary to be present in the framework of reflection. A second part about recent labour market developments and the challenges they pose to us. A third part of the strategy that I believe must be followed to absorb the structural unemployment of the Portuguese economy. Finally, a fourth part, where I make some considerations about the immediate challenges facing us and on the need to ensure a credible exit from the Economic and Financial Assistance Programme. 1. Some characteristics of the labour market in Portugal Portuguese legislation led to the segmentation of the labor market into two groups with very different characteristics: (i) Workers with fixed-term (fixed-term) contracts, who have high rotation between jobs, frequent unemployment and receive lower wages. In the period 2008-2012, fixed-term contracts accounted for about 18% of employees, with mainly young people with higher education levels than the population average (Table 1). (ii) Workers with permanent (no term) contracts, with rotation rates between very low employment and higher wages. Picture 1 Employees: total and type of contract Source: INE - Employment Survey Estimates by Boeri (2010) suggest that, all the rest the same, in Portugal workers with permanent contracts receive, on average, wages 16% higher than workers with fixed-term contracts. In addition, only about 12% of fixed-term contracts are converted into permanent contracts, a very low value both in absolute terms and compared to other European countries (Table 2). Framework 2 Employment gap with permanent and term contracts Source: Boeri (2010). In this context, in Portugal, workers on term contracts bear the majority of adjustment costs in the labour market, both through employment and salary. Thus, data from the INE employment survey show that, in recent years, the drop in employment has been particularly significant in fixed-term contracts (Figure 1). This segmentation of the labor market conditions the growth potential of the Portuguese economy, as it leads to investments in human resources lower than desirable and inadequate transmission and reinforcement of tacit knowledge, which determines a lower productivity of labor and a progressive reduction in the number of skilled workers available to the economy. Indeed, the high rotation of fixed-term workers and the low conversion rate into fixed-term contracts, on the one hand, and the low remuneration of human capital, on the other, discourage young people from investing in formal education and then, when they reach the labour market, from investing in the acquisition of specific professional skills related to the job they occupy. At the same time, this situation promotes the emigration of the most skilled workers. In turn, companies do not have incentives to bet on the professional training of workers with temporary ties, since the return of this training is not guaranteed. As a consequence, specific knowledge and, in particular, tacit knowledge associated with the production processes of companies tends to be limited to the group of workers hired without term, a group that, with the passage of time, tends to be subject to a process of loss and obsolescence of competencies, both in terms of the capacity to revitalize the organization and nature of the productive processes and in terms of the number of workers. Graph 1 Developments in employment on behest of others (rate of change in %) Source: INE - Employment Survey In recent years, and like other developed economies, there has been a polarization of employment and remuneration in Portugal. Centeno and Novo (2009) find evidence of greater increases in employment and wages at the bottom and top of the distribution of qualifications since 1995 (Graph 2). Job search by companies has focused on higher and lower qualifications and has decreased relative demand for intermediate qualifications. Graph 2 Source: Reproduced from Centeno and Novo (2009), update provided by the authors. Job creation in Portugal has thus been concentrated in low-skilled occupations  which involve manual tasks that require physical presence and interaction between people  and activities that require high capacity for abstraction and problem solving and therefore require high qualifications. This reduction in the demand for intermediate qualifications reflects the automation of various professional activities, as a result of the introduction of new technologies in production processes, and the relocation of parts of the production process to regions with lower wage levels. Repetitive and standardisable activities are particularly exposed to the developments of mechanization and automation, with the disappearance of the corresponding jobs, or to the provision at a distance, as is the case of call centers. This is a long-term trend that will determine the nature of production processes and the future configuration of the labour market and will therefore have to be taken into due account of the formulation of education and vocational training policies. In a recent study for the US, Frey and Osborne (2013) estimate that in the coming decades, 47% of current professions are likely to be self-employed and consequently lost jobs. According to these authors, the professions least likely to be sacrificed by automation are those: i) that require greater skills of perception and manipulation (such as surgery); ii) involving creative intelligence (cases of musical composer, poet, biologist, chef, etc.); (iii) or requiring social intelligence (e.g. professions requiring great bargaining, persuasion and personal relationships, such as public relations, social workers and various tourism-related professions). Table 3 presents estimated automation probabilities for some professions by Frey and Osborne (2013). Framework 3 Probability of automation and consequent loss of jobs by profession Fonte: Frey e Osborne (2013). This phenomenon has many consequences both on the labour market and on the international specialisation model, as well as strong social implications. These implications will be all the greater the less anticipated by the policies that determine the acquisition of formal and professional knowledge and by the productive/business structures that specialize in the links of the production chains that are most exposed to the effects of automation. Thus, and first, this phenomenon will put under heavy pressure the middle class, which typically carries out intermediate qualification activities in the value chain. Secondly, it increases wage inequalities, creating problems of social cohesion. Rodrigues et al. (2010) show an increase in wage inequality in Portugal in the period 1993-2008, with a progressive increase in the share of the total gain earned by individuals with higher salary levels. Thirdly, this phenomenon will have implications for requalification needs and future balances. The question is what jobs will occupy those who are displaced from activities that are no longer carried out using human work: do they start to perform less qualified activities - which is problematic from the point of view of social acceptance - or are they in a situation of latent unemployment, barely visible? Therefore, it is necessary to reflect on the challenge of requalifying individuals from the intermediate area of the distribution of qualifications taking into account our training system and our standard of productive specialization. Part of the response will necessarily create conditions to extend the proportion of workers with higher qualifications, which presupposes a change in the standard of specialisation of the Portuguese economy through the attraction of foreign direct investment and, essentially, through a regeneration of the Portuguese business fabric, in particular from the point of view of the product range, the technology used and the speed and intensity of the absorption of knowledge and, desirably, the production of applied knowledge. But it is not enough: institutional frameworks are needed that generate an alignment of attitudes and values with the new determinants of wealth production and distribution on a global scale. Thus, Lindsey (2013) who looked at the polarization of the labor market in the USA, concluded that, in overcoming this problem, it is not enough to intervene at the level of government and education: a substantial cultural and family change is needed that promotes meritocracy. 2. Recent labour market developments The significant increase in unemployment is one of the most striking  and negative  phenomena of the ongoing adjustment of the Portuguese economy. In the first quarter of 2013, the unemployment rate reached an all-time high of 17.7%; in the third quarter of 2013, it was set at 15.6%, equivalent to about 840 000 unemployed people (Figure 3). These figures are alarming from a social point of view. Graph 3 Unemployment rate: as a percentage of the working population in each age group Source: INE - Employment Survey The problem of high youth unemployment The increase in unemployment affected all age groups, but was particularly pronounced in young people (Figure 3). In the first quarter of 2013, the youth unemployment rate reached 42.1%, well above the 18% rate recorded in 2008. These figures show that we are wasting a new generation of human resources  highly skilled and able to compete at European and global level  which is essential to increasing the growth potential of the economy. There are several studies suggesting that, in times of recession, the circumstances surrounding the arrival of young people in the labour market have significant and persistent negative consequences on their professional career, their income, mentality and social inclusion. Thus, those who arrive in the labor market in the midst of recession tend to fall behind: when the recovery of the economy and employment begins the first to be hired tend to be the recent graduates and, only later, the young people of the previous degrees. In terms of long-term effects, a study by Kanh (2010) for the USA shows that, for the same function, graduates who arrive in the labor market in a period of recession receive, 15 years later, a salary about 2.5% lower than those arriving in the labor market in a period of expansion. Moreover, on average, in the long term, those who arrive on the labour market in times of recession have lower occupations. In addition, Giuliano and Spilimbergo (2009) conclude that the arrival in the labour market of young adults (between 18 and 25 years) in times of economic recession has important psychological consequences for these individuals. These young people tend to believe that individual success depends more on luck than effort and tend to support state redistributive policies more and have less confidence in institutions. For these reasons, reducing youth unemployment should be a priority for the Portuguese economy and society. Solving this problem requires an alignment of efforts between the government, the education and vocational training sectors and companies with a view to promoting the acquisition of skills and skills that enable young people to make the most of their talents and respond to the needs of the productive sector of a competitive economy. Increase in long-term unemployment Long-term unemployment (more than 12 months) increased significantly, representing around 62% of total unemployment in the three quarters of 2013. This is a very high value when compared to the average of 46% observed in the past decade (Graph 4). Graph 4 Unemployment rate: contribution by duration Source: INE - Employment Survey The high duration of unemployment creates serious economic and social problems and creates increased difficulties in employability. It must be taken into mind that many of the unemployed have particularly active low income levels and liquidity constraints. The duration of unemployment also has an effect on productivity and future labour market developments, as human capital tends to depreciate. Stigmas are often created that can severely affect links to the labour market and culminate in discouragement and the transition to inactivity. This phenomenon is particularly serious, given that in recent years there has been a reduction in both the active population and the activity rate (Graph 5). At first glance, the reduction of the working population could be perceived as positive, since it reduces the pressure on employment. It would be a short-sighted view, given that, in the long run, the reduction of the working population has devastating effects on the economy and on society. The reduction of the working population, accompanied by a reduction in the rate of activity, reduces the growth potential of GDP and further reduces the growth potential of GDP per capita. It is thus more difficult to achieve the sustainability of both public debt and the social model, with harmful effects on the mechanisms of intergenerational equity, on the safety net against the risks of exclusion and on equal opportunities in access to education, the basis of a socio-economic system that takes full advantage of talent and merit. Graph 5 Rate of variation of the working population As a percentage Source: INE - Employment Survey The increase in unemployment is not only cyclical; there is a sharp rise in structural unemployment Since 2000, there has been a sharp and continuous increase in the structural unemployment rate (Figure 6). Estimates from Banco de Portugal point to a structural unemployment rate above 11.5% in 2013. This is one of the most serious phenomena of the evolution of the Portuguese economy in the last decade and reveals dysfunctions and misadjustments between supply and job demand. The absorption of structural unemployment will not be achieved with the mere resumption of economic activity. For more than a decade, jobs have been created in the non-tradable goods sector as a result of a strong dynamic of domestic demand fuelled by abundant and cheap credit. This demand was deanated when the financial crisis revealed that the present levels of indebtedness of all economic operators were at the limit of their sustainability. The crisis has precipitated the need for debt of national economic agents and made visible the unsustainable levels of demand in the sectors producing non-tradable goods; and, by drag, revealed the artificiality of part of the jobs that had been created in these sectors during the debt boom of households and the State. Graph 6 Unemployment rate: observed and structural (as a percentage) Source: INE and Calculations of Banco de Portugal This means that the crisis has resulted not only in a fluctuation in production and employment, resulting from the contraction of demand determined by the reduction in disposable income, but also a structural adjustment, determined by the reduction in demand fuelled by household and state indebtedness. Therefore, in a context where the fall in demand from non-tradable sectors was permanently, and was perceived as such, there was a destruction of employment clearly greater than that which would result from the reduction of the product or disposable income of households. This is the case of construction, a labor-intensive sector dependent on the indebtedness of buyers, where the reduction in employment in recent years has been very high and higher than that of the manufacturing industry (Graph 7). This means that part of the employment that has been lost in the non-tradable sector will not be recovered with the economic recovery, all the more so as part of the demand corresponded to non-productive investment, such as leisure equipment without the capacity to generate return, or to areas where there is already a situation of equipment, such as road infrastructure, or a situation of lasting market saturation, as is the case in the new housing market. Graph 7 Cumulative employment variation in key sectors of activity since 1999 Notes: Serial break in 2011 due to the change in employment survey methodology. The figures for 2013 are calculated using the annual employment variation in the first three quarters of the year. Source: INE - Employment Survey Thus, the resolution of the problem of structural unemployment will necessarily depend on the restructuring of the economy and the transfer of resources from the non-tradable sector to the tradable sector. The transfer of human capital will never be instantaneous: it requires economically viable investments, that is, based on revealed demand and the competitiveness of supply, and requires the adequacy of workers who are currently unemployed to the qualification and attitude requirements inherent in the viability of those investments. Which means that it will take time, certainly much more than desirable from the point of view of managing the impact of long-term unemployment. And that, for this reason, it requires the strengthening or creation of mechanisms that mitiguous the effects of the structural adjustment of the economy on the cohesion of Portuguese society, in addition to strengthening and establishing mechanisms to support the requalification of the long-term unemployed. They must be requalified in order to adjust to new job opportunities and to prevent them from going into inactivity by obsolescence of previously acquired knowledge. In a moment, we have to define and implement policies that favour the creation of jobs in the sectors producing tradable goods, that absorb unemployment resulting from the adjustment of the non-tradable goods sector and that absorb young people who are unemployed and those who will reach the labour market. At the same time, it is necessary to create jobs that compensate for job losses in the sectors that are now viable, reflecting productivity improvements and the introduction of automated processes inherent in the need to remain competitive. That is, we have to create jobs and, at the same time, improve the standard of international specialization of the Portuguese economy, which means reducing the incorporation of work per unit of product and improving positioning in the value chain  that is, strengthening competitiveness and generating employment. In other words, we cannot face the problem of youth and structural unemployment without asking ourselves about the quality and vitality of our business fabric. 3. Strategy for absorbing structural unemployment The solution to both youth and structural unemployment is therefore to ensure sustained economic growth, which requires a significant increase in investment. The strategy to be adopted should be based on four pillars: i) optimisation of installed production capacity; ii) evolution to higher segments of the value chain in the sectors where we are already installed; iii) sectoral diversification by endogenous means; iv) attraction of foreign investment. First, it is necessary to optimize the use of installed productive capacity, taking advantage of the investment already made, increasing production and looking for new markets and new customers. Today we benefit from a remarkable response from the tradable goods sector, which has moved from the domestic market to the export market and increased its market shares there. It is essential to continue to redirect the production of tradable sectors to foreign markets, which requires increased installed capacity. In the services sector, the use of installed capacity must be increased. There is also scope for production and, consequently, the absorption of unemployment in the area of services and, in particular, in tourism-related services. It is necessary to make Portugal a country providing tourism services throughout the year and take advantage of a series of equipment that is currently underused either because they have entered insolvency or due to lack of operating capacity or, also, for lack of market-based capacity. It is potential for job creation and production that, because they do not materialize, means a waste of capital. In addition, the endogenous improvement of the pattern of intrasectoral specialization should be promoted by inducing a sustained process of incremental innovation. This process will have a significant impact on the added value generated by each sector, and consequently on the ability to pay salaries compatible with the country's development stage. To implement this strategy, it is crucial that companies have the capacity to increase their production scale and take advantage of new knowledge and qualifications on products and production processes. That is, it is an objective that presupposes a scale that allows to sustain an organization with strategic functions, production, market approach and knowledge absorption and innovation, which presupposes investment and financing capacity; and, last but not least, manageability. These are the elements that need to be scrutinised in the business Portuguese. The development of Portuguese companies is now dependent on several restrictions that block it, namely the high level of indebtedness, the poor quality of management and the scale of production that translate into a lack of strategy and functional limitations of the organization, namely the lack of endogenous capacity to monitor markets and innovation. The majority of Portuguese SMEs have extremely low levels of financial autonomy, which compromises their investment and growth capacity (Table 4). Framework 4 Indicators of the financial situation of non-financial undertakings Source: Banco de Portugal (Central Balance Sheet) The low financial autonomy of companies, one of the lowest in the euro area, is now the biggest weakness and the first major obstacle to the regeneration of the business Portuguese. These levels of indebtedness limit investment capacity and, consequently, both their response to competition and the increase in their scale, a necessary condition for moving to a higher stage of organisation, management and strategic orientation. In this context, it is urgent to address the problem of over-indebtedness. In the immediate future, we must seek to reduce the mortality rate of economically viable or viable companies as they represent an important share capital. When a company disappears, the capital invested by the owners and the capital borrowed by the banks is destroyed, but, more importantly, the share capital that represents, for example, the routines and tacit knowledge that existing. With regard to viable companies that are currently under financial stress, it is necessary to ensure compliance with processes that safeguard their continuity, preserving the capital of technological and market knowledge they incorporate. In addition, it is necessary to ensure a sustainable financial structure, the improvement of its efficiency, and in particular procedures that ensure the effectiveness and the appropriateness of the restructuring process itself, namely:  Speed of the agreement between the parties involved - the tendency of public authorities to postpone decisions often implies the bankruptcy of the company, with the consequent loss of share capital;  Neutralization of free riding behaviors by some creditors, which disturb or make the process unfeasible as a way of not sharing the burden of restructuring;  Penalties for creditors who do not cooperate;  Clear separation between negotiations and decisions to restructure accumulated debts and decisions related to the continuation of the company's operation;  Solutions for recapitalisation of companies, that is, that encourage the strengthening of equity, as an alternative to more indebtedness. It is therefore important to act on two fronts: conversion of debt into capital or near-capital, in particular by the correct allocation of Community resources of the next NMR and by the sale of bank credits to funds specialised in risk-taking in the so-called mid-caps; and, secondly, capital strengthening by current owners or third parties. Any recapitalisation solution requires enhanced transparency of accounts, which should be audited by certified entities, an appropriate governance model, providing, inter alia, for the professionalisation of business management and, in the case of medium-sized enterprises, with the opening up of third parties' participation in capital, the separation between ownership and management. The development of a dynamic of scale implies a professionalized management, clearly separated from the property, which is able to provide transparent and reliable information to the different stakeholders. It is not always true that the owner of the company's capital has management capacity, although this does not exclude cases of business owners with strategic vision and management capacity - which happens very often in companies owned by the founder or the second generation. In family businesses, the quality of management tends to degrade, first, in the transition from the management of the founder to the second generation and from the second to the third generation; secondly, when they have an accelerated growth process and reach a scale that requires an organisation model, a definition of functions and a delegation of competences and responsibilities that are not compatible with the centralised management model; and, thirdly, when the balance of the financing structure requires a volume of equity that exceeds the financing capacity of the owners. The intergenerational transmission of family businesses is one of the biggest challenges we face in the short term. Mechanisms must be found to speed up the transmission of companies between heirs or to third parties, for example through Management Buy-Out Operations (MBO). To this end, correct incentives should be established in terms of account transparency, banks' tolerance of corporate mismanagement and, in particular, taxation, defining a tax framework that does not pre-ememdebt indebtedness. We must also improve intersectoral specialisation, with new production sectors, through the use of radical innovation. In today's knowledge-based economies, innovation is the key to productivity gains, economic growth and long-term well-being. These changes should be made from existing entrepreneurial capacity and through dialogue between the national innovation system  composed of education, vocational training and research subsystems  and businesses. Portugal has a great lack in this area, because the subsystems of education, vocational training and research have a poor articulation, a fact that determines a reduction in the efficiency of the national innovation system: and secondly, because the national innovation system, in turn, also manifests deficiencies or even lack of articulation with the business sector, difficulties and lack of qualified interlocutors on the business side. The success of the footwear, moulding and metallomechanics sectors in Portugal are excellent examples of the advantages of the articulation between the innovation system, national or regional, and the business fabric having clearly delimited application points and well organized projects. 4. Final considerations In a sense, in addition to solving the problem of structural unemployment and youth unemployment we need sustained economic growth, supported by increases in productivity and employment. Economic growth is therefore crucial to the success of Portugal's economic adjustment. We must promote investment by creating a fiscal, competitive and regulatory environment conducive to entrepreneurship. We must also ensure the efficient allocation of resources. We can't spend money badly, repeating the mistakes of the past. The investment has to be productive. Companies must invest in continuous productivity improvement so that they can adapt to the competitive demands of the globalized market. In this sense, it is necessary to provide the economy with entrepreneurs, managers and workers with high qualifications. Qualification is a key tool for tackling a constantly changing market. With regard to public investment, it is necessary to introduce a cost-benefit assessment mechanism, allocated projects according to their social and economic return. Public investment cannot be made just because there is an unmet aspiration: the social and economic return must be demonstrated and must justify the priority assigned. But first of all, we must ensure a credible exit from the Economic and Financial Assistance Programme. How can we ensure a credible exit from the Programme? The credible exit from the Programme requires a broad commitment between the political forces of the governance arc to ensure:  A sustainable trajectory of public finances in the medium term;  The fulfilment of our European obligations established under the Fiscal Compact;  Financing the economy with low interest rate spreads, which support economic growth;  The solidarity of our international partners in case of need. Irish experience shows that the degree of credibility of the programme's exit determines the cost of financing the economy, i.e. the levels of low interest rate spreads, and thus conditions the sustainability of the trajectory of public finances in the medium term. Greater credibility induces a lower cost of financing and, consequently, greater margin of manoeuvre, albeit reduced, to ensure the medium-term sustainability of the path of public finances. Given that the cost of financing is an important constraint on investment and economic growth and that it, in turn, is fundamental both for the sustainability of public finances and for the absorption of structural unemployment and for social cohesion, it will be understood that the degree of credibility of leaving the adjustment programme will be one of the most determining factors not only of the intensity of the recovery but also of the development trajectory the Portuguese economy in the medium term.
